paragraphs: The paper extends backpropagation to networks that contain feedback connections. Its architecture organizes neurons into interconnected groups. Within a group, neurons may be fully connected, and the weights in opposite directions need not be equal. This allows recurrent processing inside a group while keeping a particular structure across the whole network.

The structural restriction is that connections between groups cannot form loops. The learning procedure also imposes an inequality constraint on the weight matrix inside each group. This constraint ensures that every input produces a unique equilibrium state for the network. In other words, for a given input there is one equilibrium response under the stated conditions.

A stochastic descent algorithm is applied within this constrained setting. The significance is that the paper broadens the network structures available to backpropagation while explicitly controlling their equilibrium behavior. Its generalization permits feedback and asymmetric weights locally, with the absence of loops between groups and the weight constraints providing the conditions under which the proposed learning approach operates.
summary.tldr: Backpropagation is extended to grouped recurrent networks whose connection structure and weight constraints ensure a unique equilibrium for each input.

title: Learning on a General Network

paragraphs: This paper introduces a learning algorithm for multilayer networks built from binary linear threshold units. Such units produce binary outputs according to whether their weighted inputs cross a threshold. The algorithm makes the network's internal representations the primary objects to determine during training.

This changes the organization of the learning problem. Instead of beginning with a cost function over connection weights, the method seeks a correct set of internal representations. Once those representations have been established, the weights are learned using the Perceptron Learning Rule. The authors describe that rule as local and biologically plausible, giving the representation choices a route to concrete connection strengths.

The algorithm is tested on adjacency, symmetry, parity, and a combined symmetry-parity problem. These tasks provide distinct settings for examining the approach. The main contribution is the separation between deciding what the intermediate units should represent and determining weights that realize those decisions. That separation offers an alternative way to formulate multilayer learning around the internal organization of the solution.
summary.tldr: The algorithm learns multilayer threshold networks by choosing internal representations first and then fitting weights with the Perceptron Learning Rule.

title: Learning by Choice of Internal Representations

Training is based on a novel approach that combines stochastic approximation ideas with back(cid:173) propagation. The method is applied to control admission into a queueing sys(cid:173) tem operating in a time-varying environment.

The method is applied to control admission into a queueing sys(cid:173) tem operating in a time-varying environment.

paragraphs: This paper uses a layered feedforward neural network to implement a mapping needed for control. The system being controlled is unknown, nonlinear, and stochastic: its behavior is not fully specified, its relationships need not be linear, and randomness affects its evolution. Learning the control mapping provides a way to act under those conditions.

The training method combines stochastic approximation ideas with backpropagation. Stochastic approximation supplies an approach to learning from uncertain observations, while backpropagation adjusts the network's weights. The contribution centers on bringing these ideas together to train a neural component for a dynamical control problem.

The application is admission control for a queueing system operating in a changing environment. Admission decisions determine what is allowed into the queue, so the learned mapping participates directly in regulating the system. This setting brings together uncertainty about the dynamics and variation over time. The paper's stated contribution is the training approach and its application to queue admission, showing how neural learning can be formulated around a practical control mapping.
summary.tldr: A feedforward network trained through stochastic approximation and backpropagation controls admission to a queue in a changing environment.

title: Neural Network Implementation of Admission Control

abstract: An novel class of locally excitatory, globally inhibitory oscillator networks is proposed. The model of each oscillator corresponds to a standard relaxation oscillator with two time scales. The network exhibits a mechanism of selective gating, whereby an oscillator jumping up to its active phase rapidly recruits the oscillators stimulated by the same pattern, while preventing others from jumping up. We show analytically that with the selective gating mechanism the network rapidly achieves both synchronization within blocks of oscillators that are stimulated by connected regions and desynchronization between different blocks. Computer simulations demonstrate the network's promising ability for segmenting multiple input patterns in real time. This model lays a physical foundation for the oscillatory correlation theory of feature binding, and may provide an effective computational framework for scene segmentation and figure/ground segregation.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an oscillator network for grouping parts of an input into separate patterns. Each unit is a relaxation oscillator with two time scales. Connections provide local excitation and global inhibition, creating a system in which nearby related activity can be encouraged while competing activity is suppressed across the network.

Its central mechanism is selective gating. When one oscillator enters its active phase, it rapidly recruits oscillators driven by the same pattern and prevents others from activating at that moment. The authors analytically show that this produces synchronization within blocks stimulated by connected regions and desynchronization between different blocks.

Computer simulations demonstrate promising real-time segmentation of multiple input patterns. The timing relationships serve two complementary purposes: shared timing groups a region’s elements, while separated timing distinguishes different regions. The authors present the model as a physical basis for oscillatory accounts of feature binding and as a possible computational framework for scene segmentation and separating figures from their backgrounds.
summary.tldr: Local excitation and global inhibition synchronize oscillators within patterns while separating different patterns in time.

title: Synchrony and Desynchrony in Neural Oscillator Networks

abstract: This paper presents a new approach to speech recognition with hybrid HMM/ANN technology. While the standard approach to hybrid HMMI ANN systems is based on the use of neural networks as posterior probability estimators, the new approach is based on the use of mutual information neural networks trained with a special learning algorithm in order to maximize the mutual information between the input classes of the network and its resulting sequence of firing output neurons during training. It is shown in this paper that such a neural network is an optimal neural vector quantizer for a discrete hidden Markov model system trained on Maximum Likelihood principles. One of the main advantages of this approach is the fact, that such neural networks can be easily combined with HMM's of any complexity with context-dependent capabilities. It is shown that the resulting hybrid system achieves very high recognition rates, which are now already on the same level as the best conventional HMM systems with continuous parameters, and the capabilities of the mutual information neural networks are not yet entirely exploited.

paragraphs: This paper changes the role of a neural network within a speech recognizer that also uses a hidden Markov model. Conventional hybrid systems use the network to estimate posterior class probabilities. Here, the network instead learns outputs that preserve information about the classes presented during training.

A special learning procedure maximizes mutual information between input classes and the sequence of output neurons that fire. The authors show that the resulting network acts as an optimal neural vector quantizer for a discrete hidden Markov model trained by maximum likelihood. In this role, the network converts inputs into discrete representations suitable for the sequence model.

The design matters because these networks can be combined with hidden Markov models of varying complexity, including models that account for context. The reported recognition rates reach the level of the best conventional continuous-parameter hidden Markov systems in the comparison. The authors also state that the network’s capabilities remain incompletely exploited, presenting the results as a strong demonstration of the approach’s potential.
summary.tldr: Mutual-information training turns a neural network into a discrete representation builder for a competitive hybrid speech recognizer.

title: A New Approach to Hybrid HMM/ANN Speech Recognition using Mutual Information Neural Networks

Since BLHT learns a stochastic model based on Bayesian Learning, the over(cid:173) fitting problem is reasonably solved. Moreover, BLHT has an efficient implementation. This paper shows that the model learned by BLHT con(cid:173) verges to one which provides the most accurate predictions of percepts and rewards, given short-term memory.

Since BLHT learns a stochastic model based on Bayesian Learning, the over(cid:173) fitting problem is reasonably solved. Moreover, BLHT has an efficient implementation. This paper shows that the model learned by BLHT con(cid:173) verges to one which provides the most accurate predictions of percepts and rewards, given short-term memory.

paragraphs: BLHT is a reinforcement learning algorithm for environments where the learner cannot directly observe everything relevant to its decisions. It uses short-term memory to supplement current observations. This gives the learner a limited history to work with when predicting what it will perceive and what rewards it will receive, rather than treating the present observation as a complete description of the situation.

The algorithm learns a probabilistic model through Bayesian learning. Its predictions can therefore describe uncertainty about future observations and rewards. The authors report that this approach reasonably addresses overfitting and has an efficient implementation. The overfitting claim is qualified: the abstract presents Bayesian learning as a practical response to the problem, rather than a guarantee that overfitting is impossible.

The main theoretical finding concerns convergence of the learned model. BLHT approaches a model providing the most accurate predictions available given its short-term memory. That qualification defines the result: predictive optimality is tied to the information retained in memory, rather than to unrestricted access to the environment's hidden state or entire history.
summary.tldr: BLHT uses Bayesian learning and short-term memory to learn optimal predictions of observations and rewards within the information its memory retains.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Algorithm in Partially Observable Environments Using Short-Term Memory

paragraphs: This paper develops an approach for helping engineers design analog circuits using Markov fields. It represents even highly nonlinear and discontinuous circuit behavior through potential functions based on Kirchhoff's current law. Those functions translate circuit relationships into an objective that a computational procedure can optimize.

The supplied description uses discrete variables with finitely many possible values and a graph that specifies their neighborhood relationships. Potential functions express preferences for combinations of values within connected groups. This representation connects local circuit constraints with an overall design objective. The paper also describes a relatively efficient optimization algorithm and sketches a proof of its convergence.

The empirical example concerns a JFET transistor circuit model. The algorithm selects circuit components that accurately reproduce the desired characteristic curves, demonstrating the approach on a concrete design problem. The paper presents the example as illustrating both strengths and limitations. Its main contribution combines a circuit representation, an optimization method, and evidence that their combination can recover components producing specified electrical behavior.
summary.tldr: A Markov-field formulation based on Kirchhoff's current law selects components that reproduce desired curves in a JFET circuit model.

title: Kirchoff Law Markov Fields for Analog Circuit Design

abstract: Principal components analysis (PCA) is one of the most widely used techniques in machine learning and data mining. Minor components analysis (MCA) is less well known, but can also play an important role in the presence of constraints on the data distribution. In this paper we present a probabilistic model for “extreme components analysis” (XCA) which at the maximum likelihood solution extracts an optimal combina- tion of principal and minor components. For a given number of compo- nents, the log-likelihood of the XCA model is guaranteed to be larger or equal than that of the probabilistic models for PCA and MCA. We de- scribe an efﬁcient algorithm to solve for the globally optimal solution. For log-convex spectra we prove that the solution consists of principal components only, while for log-concave spectra the solution consists of minor components. In general, the solution admits a combination of both. In experiments we explore the properties of XCA on some synthetic and real-world datasets.

In this paper we present a probabilistic model for “extreme components analysis” (XCA) which at the maximum likelihood solution extracts an optimal combina- tion of principal and minor components. For a given number of compo- nents, the log-likelihood of the XCA model is guaranteed to be larger or equal than that of the probabilistic models for PCA and MCA. We de- scribe an efﬁcient algorithm to solve for the globally optimal solution. For log-convex spectra we prove that the solution consists of principal components only, while for log-concave spectra the solution consists of minor components. In general, the solution admits a combination of both. In experiments we explore the properties of XCA on some synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis focuses on directions of large variation, while minor components analysis can capture constraints through directions of small variation. Extreme components analysis brings both into one probabilistic model. At its maximum-likelihood solution, the model selects an optimal combination of principal and minor components.

For a fixed number of components, the authors guarantee that the model's log-likelihood is at least as high as that of the probabilistic PCA and MCA models. This is a guarantee about the stated likelihood objective. They also describe an efficient algorithm that reaches the global optimum, making the selection between the two types of components part of a solvable optimization problem.

The shape of the spectrum determines some special cases. For log-convex spectra, the solution uses only principal components; for log-concave spectra, it uses minor components. More general spectra can yield a mixture. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets explore these properties, illustrating why choosing only one end of the spectrum need not always be the best fit.
summary.tldr: Extreme components analysis optimally combines principal and minor components under a probabilistic likelihood objective.

title: Extreme Components Analysis

abstract: Recent research suggests that neural systems employ sparse coding. However, there is limited theoretical understanding of fundamental resolution limits in such sparse coding. This paper considers a general sparse estimation problem of detecting the sparsity pattern of a $k$-sparse vector in $\R^n$ from $m$ random noisy measurements. Our main results provide necessary and sufficient conditions on the problem dimensions, $m$, $n$ and $k$, and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for asymptotically-reliable detection. We show a necessary condition for perfect recovery at any given SNR for all algorithms, regardless of complexity, is $m = \Omega(k\log(n-k))$ measurements. This is considerably stronger than all previous necessary conditions. We also show that the scaling of $\Omega(k\log(n-k))$ measurements is sufficient for a trivial ``maximum correlation'' estimator to succeed. Hence this scaling is optimal and does not require lasso, matching pursuit, or more sophisticated methods, and the optimal scaling can thus be biologically plausible.

We also show that the scaling of $\Omega(k\log(n-k))$ measurements is sufficient for a trivial ``maximum correlation'' estimator to succeed. Hence this scaling is optimal and does not require lasso, matching pursuit, or more sophisticated methods, and the optimal scaling can thus be biologically plausible.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many noisy measurements are needed to identify which entries of a high-dimensional sparse vector are nonzero. The unknown vector has n coordinates, of which k are active, and is observed through m random measurements. The goal is reliable recovery of the active pattern, connecting sparse coding to a precise statistical detection problem.

The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions involving the dimensions and signal-to-noise ratio. Their necessary condition says that, at a given signal-to-noise ratio, perfect recovery requires measurements scaling at least as k times log(n−k). This restriction applies to all algorithms, regardless of computational complexity, and strengthens previous necessary conditions.

They also show that this measurement scaling is sufficient for a simple maximum-correlation estimator to succeed under their analysis. The matching scaling establishes optimality at that level without requiring more sophisticated sparse-recovery methods. Because the sufficient estimator is simple, the authors argue that achieving the optimal scaling can be biologically plausible. The reliability statements are asymptotic, concerning behavior as problem dimensions grow.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes an optimal measurement scaling for sparse-pattern recovery and shows that a simple maximum-correlation estimator can achieve it.

title: Resolution Limits of Sparse Coding in High Dimensions

abstract: We investigate methods for selecting sets of labeled vertices for use in predicting the labels of vertices on a graph. We specifically study methods which choose a single batch of labeled vertices (i.e. offline, non sequential methods). In this setting, we find common graph smoothness assumptions directly motivate simple label selection methods with interesting theoretical guarantees. These methods bound prediction error in terms of the smoothness of the true labels with respect to the graph. Some of these bounds give new motivations for previously proposed algorithms, and some suggest new algorithms which we evaluate. We show improved performance over baseline methods on several real world data sets.

In this setting, we find common graph smoothness assumptions directly motivate simple label selection methods with interesting theoretical guarantees. paragraphs: The paper asks which vertices of a graph should be labeled to support prediction at the remaining vertices. It focuses on selecting one batch in advance. The selection process is therefore offline and nonsequential, rather than choosing additional vertices in response to labels already obtained.

The authors derive simple selection methods from graph smoothness assumptions. These assumptions describe how labels vary across the graph, making them directly relevant to whether a chosen set of labeled vertices can support accurate predictions elsewhere. The resulting theoretical bounds express prediction error in terms of the smoothness of the true labels.

Some bounds provide new explanations for previously proposed selection algorithms, while others motivate new algorithms. The authors evaluate those methods and report improvements over baselines on several real-world datasets. The contribution connects a modeling assumption to a practical choice of where to obtain labels: graph structure helps guide selection, and the guarantees explicitly depend on how well the true labels conform to that structure.
summary.tldr: Graph smoothness assumptions motivate batch label-selection methods with error bounds and empirical improvements over baselines.

title: Label Selection on Graphs

abstract: Kernel-based reinforcement-learning (KBRL) is a method for learning a decision policy from a set of sample transitions which stands out for its strong theoretical guarantees. However, the size of the approximator grows with the number of transitions, which makes the approach impractical for large problems. In this paper we introduce a novel algorithm to improve the scalability of KBRL. We resort to a special decomposition of a transition matrix, called stochastic factorization, to fix the size of the approximator while at the same time incorporating all the information contained in the data. The resulting algorithm, kernel-based stochastic factorization (KBSF), is much faster but still converges to a unique solution. We derive a theoretical upper bound for the distance between the value functions computed by KBRL and KBSF. The effectiveness of our method is illustrated with computational experiments on four reinforcement-learning problems, including a difficult task in which the goal is to learn a neurostimulation policy to suppress the occurrence of seizures in epileptic rat brains. We empirically demonstrate that the proposed approach is able to compress the information contained in KBRL's model. Also, on the tasks studied, KBSF outperforms two of the most prominent reinforcement-learning algorithms, namely least-squares policy iteration and fitted Q-iteration.

paragraphs: Kernel-based reinforcement learning learns a decision policy from sampled transitions and has strong theoretical guarantees. Its practical difficulty is that the model grows with the number of transitions. This paper introduces kernel-based stochastic factorization, or KBSF, to keep the approximator's size fixed while incorporating information from all the data.

The method uses a special factorization of a transition matrix. The resulting algorithm is much faster and still converges to a unique solution. The authors also derive an upper bound on the difference between the value functions computed by the original method and KBSF, giving a theoretical way to assess the approximation.

Experiments cover four reinforcement-learning problems, including learning a neurostimulation policy to suppress seizures in epileptic rat brains. The results demonstrate compression of the original model's information. On the tasks studied, KBSF also outperforms least-squares policy iteration and fitted Q-iteration. These comparisons support its practical effectiveness in those settings alongside the separate convergence and approximation guarantees.
summary.tldr: Stochastic factorization makes kernel-based reinforcement learning more scalable while retaining convergence and bounding value-function approximation error.

title: Reinforcement Learning using Kernel-Based Stochastic Factorization

abstract: We study the problem of learning local metrics for nearest neighbor classification. Most previous works on local metric learning learn a number of local unrelated metrics. While this ''independence'' approach delivers an increased flexibility its downside is the considerable risk of overfitting. We present a new parametric local metric learning method in which we learn a smooth metric matrix function over the data manifold. Using an approximation error bound of the metric matrix function we learn local metrics as linear combinations of basis metrics defined on anchor points over different regions of the instance space. We constrain the metric matrix function by imposing on the linear combinations manifold regularization which makes the learned metric matrix function vary smoothly along the geodesics of the data manifold. Our metric learning method has excellent performance both in terms of predictive power and scalability. We experimented with several large-scale classification problems, tens of thousands of instances, and compared it with several state of the art metric learning methods, both global and local, as well as to SVM with automatic kernel selection, all of which it outperforms in a significant manner.

paragraphs: Different regions of a dataset may need different notions of distance for nearest-neighbor classification. Learning unrelated local metrics supplies that flexibility but also creates a considerable risk of overfitting. This paper instead learns a metric matrix that changes smoothly over the data manifold, tying local distance measures together.

Using an approximation-error bound, the authors represent local metrics as linear combinations of basis metrics attached to anchor points in different regions. Manifold regularization constrains those combinations so that the metric varies smoothly along geodesics, or paths following the manifold's geometry. Local adaptation is therefore coordinated through a shared parametric representation and a smoothness requirement.

The method is evaluated on several large classification problems containing tens of thousands of instances. The authors report strong predictive performance and scalability, significantly outperforming the compared global and local metric-learning methods and an SVM with automatic kernel selection. These findings support the proposed way of retaining local flexibility while constraining how neighboring parts of the data space change their distance measures.
summary.tldr: Smooth combinations of anchor-based metrics provide local distance adaptation and strong large-scale nearest-neighbor classification performance.

title: Parametric Local Metric Learning for Nearest Neighbor Classification

abstract: Reliance on computationally expensive algorithms for inference has been limiting the use of Bayesian nonparametric models in large scale applications. To tackle this problem, we propose a Bayesian learning algorithm for DP mixture models. Instead of following the conventional paradigm -- random initialization plus iterative update, we take an progressive approach. Starting with a given prior, our method recursively transforms it into an approximate posterior through sequential variational approximation. In this process, new components will be incorporated on the fly when needed. The algorithm can reliably estimate a DP mixture model in one pass, making it particularly suited for applications with massive data. Experiments on both synthetic data and real datasets demonstrate remarkable improvement on efficiency -- orders of magnitude speed-up compared to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Bayesian nonparametric mixture models offer flexibility, but expensive inference can make them difficult to use on large datasets. This paper addresses that computational obstacle for Dirichlet process mixture models. The goal is to estimate the model progressively as data are processed, while allowing additional mixture components to appear when needed.

The algorithm begins with a specified prior and recursively transforms it into an approximate posterior through sequential variational approximation. It departs from a workflow based on random initialization followed by repeated updates. New components are incorporated during the sequential procedure, so the evolving approximation can expand its representation as learning proceeds.

The authors report that the algorithm can reliably estimate a Dirichlet process mixture model in a single pass, making it particularly suitable for massive datasets. Experiments on synthetic and real data show speedups of orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art methods. The main practical finding is that progressive approximate inference can substantially reduce the computational burden of fitting this flexible model family.
summary.tldr: Sequential variational approximation fits Dirichlet process mixtures in one pass, adding components as needed and delivering large experimental speedups.

title: Online Learning of Nonparametric Mixture Models via Sequential Variational Approximation

abstract: We introduce Natural Neural Networks, a novel family of algorithms that speed up convergence by adapting their internal representation during training to improve conditioning of the Fisher matrix. In particular, we show a specific example that employs a simple and efficient reparametrization of the neural network weights by implicitly whitening the representation obtained at each layer, while preserving the feed-forward computation of the network. Such networks can be trained efficiently via the proposed Projected Natural Gradient Descent algorithm (PRONG), which amortizes the cost of these reparametrizations over many parameter updates and is closely related to the Mirror Descent online learning algorithm. We highlight the benefits of our method on both unsupervised and supervised learning tasks, and showcase its scalability by training on the large-scale ImageNet Challenge dataset.

The target is the conditioning of the Fisher matrix, which describes a geometry relevant to parameter updates. Improving that conditioning makes the parameterization more suitable for optimization, so the method changes how learning is organized within the network.

The paper gives a concrete construction that reparameterizes weights to implicitly whiten the representation at each layer. This transformation preserves the network's feed-forward computation. The proposed Projected Natural Gradient Descent algorithm, PRONG, trains these networks while spreading the cost of reparameterization across many parameter updates, making the additional transformations more affordable.

The authors connect PRONG closely to the Mirror Descent online learning algorithm. They demonstrate benefits on supervised and unsupervised tasks and illustrate scalability by training on the ImageNet Challenge dataset. The reported applications support its practical use across the learning settings examined.
summary.tldr: Natural Neural Networks accelerate training through internal reparameterization, with PRONG amortizing the cost across many updates.

title: Natural Neural Networks

abstract: Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) is a leading algorithm for finding a Nash equilibrium in large zero-sum imperfect-information games. CFR is an iterative algorithm that repeatedly traverses the game tree, updating regrets at each information set.We introduce an improvement to CFR that prunes any path of play in the tree, and its descendants, that has negative regret. It revisits that sequence at the earliest subsequent CFR iteration where the regret could have become positive, had that path been explored on every iteration. The new algorithm maintains CFR's convergence guarantees while making iterations significantly faster---even if previously known pruning techniques are used in the comparison. This improvement carries over to CFR+, a recent variant of CFR. Experiments show an order of magnitude speed improvement, and the relative speed improvement increases with the size of the game.

paragraphs: Counterfactual Regret Minimization, or CFR, finds Nash equilibria in large zero-sum games with imperfect information by repeatedly traversing a game tree and updating regrets. This repeated traversal can be expensive. The paper introduces a way to skip parts of the tree temporarily while preserving the algorithm’s convergence guarantees.

The method prunes a path and its descendants when that path has negative regret. It returns at the earliest later iteration when the regret could have become positive if the path had continued to be explored. This revisit rule connects skipped computation to the evolution of regret, so pruning is governed by when a path could become relevant again.

The improvement also applies to CFR+. Experiments report an order-of-magnitude speedup, with larger relative improvements as games grow. Iterations remain significantly faster even when comparisons include previously known pruning techniques. The contribution is a principled reduction in the work performed during equilibrium computation, supported by both retained convergence guarantees and measured speed improvements.
summary.tldr: Regret-based pruning skips temporarily unpromising game-tree paths while retaining CFR’s convergence guarantees.

title: Regret-Based Pruning in Extensive-Form Games

abstract: In high-dimensional settings, where the number of features p is typically much larger than the number of samples n, methods which can systematically examine arbitrary combinations of features, a huge 2^p-dimensional space, have recently begun to be explored. However, none of the current methods is able to assess the association between feature combinations and a target variable while conditioning on a categorical covariate, in order to correct for potential confounding effects. We propose the Fast Automatic Conditional Search (FACS) algorithm, a significant discriminative itemset mining method which conditions on categorical covariates and only scales as O(k log k), where k is the number of states of the categorical covariate. Based on the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel Test, FACS demonstrates superior speed and statistical power on simulated and real-world datasets compared to the state of the art, opening the door to numerous applications in biomedicine.

paragraphs: When a dataset has many features, potentially useful associations may involve combinations of them. Examining arbitrary combinations creates a search space of size 2^p for p features. The paper addresses an additional statistical challenge: checking whether a combination remains associated with a target after accounting for a categorical covariate that could confound the relationship.

The proposed Fast Automatic Conditional Search algorithm, or FACS, performs significant discriminative itemset mining while conditioning on categorical covariates. It builds on the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test. The stated O(k log k) scaling concerns k, the number of categories of the covariate, giving an efficient way to incorporate that conditioning into the search.

On simulated and real-world datasets, FACS shows better speed and statistical power than the compared state-of-the-art methods. These results matter because searching feature combinations and controlling for a potential confounder are both necessary parts of the intended analysis. The authors identify biomedical applications as a promising use for this ability to discover conditionally significant combinations.
summary.tldr: FACS efficiently searches for significant feature combinations while conditioning on categorical covariates, improving speed and statistical power in the reported evaluations.

title: Finding significant combinations of features in the presence of categorical covariates

abstract: In modern data analysis, random sampling is an efficient and widely-used strategy to overcome the computational difficulties brought by large sample size. In previous studies, researchers conducted random sampling which is according to the input data but independent on the response variable, however the response variable may also be informative for sampling. In this paper we propose an adaptive sampling called the gradient-based sampling which is dependent on both the input data and the output for fast solving of least-square (LS) problems. We draw the data points by random sampling from the full data according to their gradient values. This sampling is computationally saving, since the running time of computing the sampling probabilities is reduced to O(nd) where n is the full sample size and d is the dimension of the input. Theoretically, we establish an error bound analysis of the general importance sampling with respect to LS solution from full data. The result establishes an improved performance of the use of our gradient-based sampling. Synthetic and real data sets are used to empirically argue that the gradient-based sampling has an obvious advantage over existing sampling methods from two aspects of statistical efficiency and computational saving.

paragraphs: Solving a least-squares problem on a large dataset can be expensive, so sampling a smaller collection of observations is a useful shortcut. The paper questions sampling rules that consider the input features but ignore the response values. Responses also carry information relevant to deciding which observations should receive attention.

The proposed gradient-based sampling method uses both inputs and outputs by assigning sampling probabilities according to data points' gradient values. Computing those probabilities takes O(nd) time, where n is the full number of observations and d is the input dimension. This matters because the preparation needed to choose a sample is itself part of the computational cost.

The authors analyze error for general importance sampling relative to the least-squares solution obtained from the complete dataset. Their analysis establishes improved performance from the proposed gradient-based choice. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also support advantages over existing sampling approaches in statistical efficiency and computational savings. The method therefore ties the selection of observations directly to information relevant to the fitting problem.
summary.tldr: Gradient-based sampling uses inputs and responses to select observations for faster, statistically efficient least-squares fitting.

title: Gradient-based Sampling: An Adaptive Importance Sampling for Least-squares

abstract: In this paper, we study the stochastic combinatorial multi-armed bandit (CMAB) framework that allows a general nonlinear reward function, whose expected value may not depend only on the means of the input random variables but possibly on the entire distributions of these variables. Our framework enables a much larger class of reward functions such as the $\max()$ function and nonlinear utility functions. Existing techniques relying on accurate estimations of the means of random variables, such as the upper confidence bound (UCB) technique, do not work directly on these functions. We propose a new algorithm called stochastically dominant confidence bound (SDCB), which estimates the distributions of underlying random variables and their stochastically dominant confidence bounds. We prove that SDCB can achieve $O(\log T)$ distribution-dependent regret and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ distribution-independent regret, where $T$ is the time horizon. We apply our results to the $K$-MAX problem and expected utility maximization problems. In particular, for $K$-MAX, we provide the first polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for its offline problem, and give the first $\tilde{O}(\sqrt T)$ bound on the $(1-\epsilon)$-approximation regret of its online problem, for any $\epsilon>0$.

We prove that SDCB can achieve $O(\log T)$ distribution-dependent regret and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ distribution-independent regret, where $T$ is the time horizon. paragraphs: In combinatorial bandit problems, a learner repeatedly selects combinations of uncertain options. This paper considers nonlinear rewards whose expected values can depend on entire outcome distributions, rather than just their means. Maximum-based rewards and nonlinear utilities fit this setting, where accurately estimating average outcomes alone may leave out information needed to choose well.

The proposed stochastically dominant confidence bound algorithm, SDCB, estimates the underlying distributions and constructs optimistic bounds on them. This extends confidence-based decision making beyond methods that work directly with means. The authors prove regret bounds growing logarithmically with the time horizon when distribution-specific quantities are included, and approximately with its square root in a distribution-independent bound.

The results apply to K-MAX and expected utility maximization. For K-MAX, the authors also provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the offline problem. Online, they establish the first approximately square-root regret bound against a benchmark scaled by one minus epsilon, for any positive epsilon. This approximation qualification is part of the guarantee, rather than a claim of exact online optimization.
summary.tldr: SDCB learns outcome distributions to handle nonlinear combinatorial bandit rewards and establishes logarithmic or approximately square-root regret bounds.

title: Combinatorial Multi-Armed Bandit with General Reward Functions

abstract: We present a new type of probabilistic model which we call DISsimilarity COefficient Networks (DISCO Nets). DISCO Nets allow us to efficiently sample from a posterior distribution parametrised by a neural network. During training, DISCO Nets are learned by minimising the dissimilarity coefficient between the true distribution and the estimated distribution. This allows us to tailor the training to the loss related to the task at hand. We empirically show that (i) by modeling uncertainty on the output value, DISCO Nets outperform equivalent non-probabilistic predictive networks and (ii) DISCO Nets accurately model the uncertainty of the output, outperforming existing probabilistic models based on deep neural networks.
originalAbstract: We present a new type of probabilistic model which we call DISsimilarity COefficient Networks (DISCO Nets). DISCO Nets allow us to efficiently sample from a posterior distribution parametrised by a neural network. During training, DISCO Nets are learned by minimising the dissimilarity coefficient between the true distribution and the estimated distribution. This allows us to tailor the training to the loss related to the task at hand. We empirically show that (i) by modeling uncertainty on the output value, DISCO Nets outperform equivalent non-probabilistic predictive networks and (ii) DISCO Nets accurately model the uncertainty of the output, outperforming existing probabilistic models based on deep neural networks.

paragraphs: DISCO Nets are neural-network-based probabilistic models designed to represent uncertainty about an output. Instead of supplying only a single predicted value, the model permits efficient sampling from a posterior distribution. Those samples provide a way to express multiple possible outcomes and the uncertainty associated with the prediction.

Training minimizes a dissimilarity coefficient between the true distribution and the distribution estimated by the network. A useful feature of this objective is that it can be tailored to the loss associated with the particular task. The method therefore connects distribution learning with how prediction errors are judged in the application, rather than treating the training objective as independent of that task.

The authors report two empirical findings. Modeling output uncertainty improves predictive performance over equivalent non-probabilistic networks, and DISCO Nets represent uncertainty more accurately than existing deep probabilistic models in their evaluations. These results support treating uncertainty as part of the prediction problem itself. They are empirical comparisons, rather than a claim that probabilistic prediction always improves every task.
summary.tldr: DISCO Nets learn task-sensitive output distributions, with reported improvements in both prediction and uncertainty modeling.

title: DISCO Nets : DISsimilarity COefficients Networks

abstract: Tensor train (TT) decomposition provides a space-efficient representation for higher-order tensors. Despite its advantage, we face two crucial limitations when we apply the TT decomposition to machine learning problems: the lack of statistical theory and of scalable algorithms. In this paper, we address the limitations. First, we introduce a convex relaxation of the TT decomposition problem and derive its error bound for the tensor completion task. Next, we develop a randomized optimization method, in which the time complexity is as efficient as the space complexity is. In experiments, we numerically confirm the derived bounds and empirically demonstrate the performance of our method with a real higher-order tensor.

In experiments, we numerically confirm the derived bounds and empirically demonstrate the performance of our method with a real higher-order tensor.

paragraphs: Tensor train decomposition offers a compact representation of higher-order tensors, which organize data across multiple dimensions. This paper addresses two obstacles to using that representation in machine learning: insufficient statistical theory and a lack of scalable algorithms. Compact storage is valuable, but practical learning also needs an understanding of reconstruction error and an efficient computation method.

The authors introduce a convex relaxation of the tensor train decomposition problem. For tensor completion, where the aim is to recover a tensor from partial observations, they derive an error bound. They also develop a randomized optimization method whose time complexity is described as being as efficient as its space complexity, connecting computational scalability to the representation’s storage advantage.

Experiments numerically confirm the derived bounds and demonstrate the method on a real higher-order tensor. These findings supply both theoretical and empirical support for the proposed approach. The paper’s contribution is the combination of a statistically analyzed relaxation and scalable optimization, addressing separate requirements for making tensor train methods useful in learning problems.
summary.tldr: A convex relaxation and randomized optimizer give tensor train learning statistical error bounds and scalable computation.

title: On Tensor Train Rank Minimization : Statistical Efficiency and Scalable Algorithm

abstract: Existing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are either based on general-purpose and domain-agnostic schemes, which can lead to slow convergence, or require hand-crafting of problem-specific proposals by an expert. We propose A-NICE-MC, a novel method to train flexible parametric Markov chain kernels to produce samples with desired properties. First, we propose an efficient likelihood-free adversarial training method to train a Markov chain and mimic a given data distribution. Then, we leverage flexible volume preserving flows to obtain parametric kernels for MCMC. Using a bootstrap approach, we show how to train efficient Markov Chains to sample from a prescribed posterior distribution by iteratively improving the quality of both the model and the samples. A-NICE-MC provides the first framework to automatically design efficient domain-specific MCMC proposals. Empirical results demonstrate that A-NICE-MC combines the strong guarantees of MCMC with the expressiveness of deep neural networks, and is able to significantly outperform competing methods such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo generates samples by repeatedly moving between possible states. General-purpose movement rules can converge slowly, while specialized rules often require expert design. A-NICE-MC addresses this tradeoff by learning flexible transition rules, aiming to make the sampling process suit the distribution of interest automatically.

The method first uses adversarial training to teach a Markov chain to imitate a supplied data distribution without requiring likelihood evaluation for that training procedure. It then uses flexible, volume-preserving flows to construct parameterized MCMC kernels. These learned transformations provide expressive proposals within an MCMC framework, connecting neural-network flexibility with the guarantees associated with MCMC.

For sampling a prescribed posterior distribution, the authors introduce a bootstrap procedure that iteratively improves both the model and its samples. Better samples support better training, and improved transitions support subsequent sampling. The reported experiments show significant gains over competing methods, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. These are empirical comparisons supporting automated, distribution-specific proposal design, rather than a claim that the learned sampler always dominates every alternative.
summary.tldr: A-NICE-MC learns distribution-specific MCMC proposals through adversarial training and iterative sample improvement, with strong reported empirical performance.

title: A-NICE-MC: Adversarial Training for MCMC

abstract: Quick Shift is a popular mode-seeking and clustering algorithm. We present finite sample statistical consistency guarantees for Quick Shift on mode and cluster recovery under mild distributional assumptions. We then apply our results to construct a consistent modal regression algorithm.
originalAbstract: Quick Shift is a popular mode-seeking and clustering algorithm. We present finite sample statistical consistency guarantees for Quick Shift on mode and cluster recovery under mild distributional assumptions. We then apply our results to construct a consistent modal regression algorithm.

paragraphs: Quick Shift is an algorithm for finding modes and forming clusters. This paper studies the statistical reliability of those outputs: whether structures recovered from sampled observations correspond to the modes and clusters of the underlying distribution. Its contribution is theoretical analysis of an established algorithm.

The authors provide finite-sample consistency guarantees for both mode recovery and cluster recovery under mild distributional assumptions. Finite-sample guarantees address behavior with a limited collection of observations, while consistency connects recovery to increasing amounts of data. Treating modes and clusters separately matters because identifying a distribution's peaks and recovering its grouping structure are distinct recovery goals.

The paper then uses these results to construct a consistent modal regression algorithm, extending the analysis beyond the original clustering task. The same statistical foundations thus support both recovery of distributional structure and a regression procedure centered on modes. The guarantees remain conditional on the distributional assumptions stated by the authors; their significance is to establish a principled basis for recovery in that setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional consistency guarantees for Quick Shift's mode and cluster recovery and derives a consistent modal regression method.

title: On the Consistency of Quick Shift

abstract: This paper presents a probabilistic-graphical model that can be used to infer characteristics of instantaneous brain activity by jointly analyzing spatial and temporal dependencies observed in electroencephalograms (EEG). Specifically, we describe a factor-graph-based model with customized factor-functions defined based on domain knowledge, to infer pathologic brain activity with the goal of identifying seizure-generating brain regions in epilepsy patients. We utilize an inference technique based on the graph-cut algorithm to exactly solve graph inference in polynomial time. We validate the model by using clinically collected intracranial EEG data from 29 epilepsy patients to show that the model correctly identifies seizure-generating brain regions. Our results indicate that our model outperforms two conventional approaches used for seizure-onset localization (5-7% better AUC: 0.72, 0.67, 0.65) and that the proposed inference technique provides 3-10% gain in AUC (0.72, 0.62, 0.69) compared to sampling-based alternatives.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a probabilistic-graphical model that can be used to infer characteristics of instantaneous brain activity by jointly analyzing spatial and temporal dependencies observed in electroencephalograms (EEG). Specifically, we describe a factor-graph-based model with customized factor-functions defined based on domain knowledge, to infer pathologic brain activity with the goal of identifying seizure-generating brain regions in epilepsy patients. We utilize an inference technique based on the graph-cut algorithm to exactly solve graph inference in polynomial time. We validate the model by using clinically collected intracranial EEG data from 29 epilepsy patients to show that the model correctly identifies seizure-generating brain regions. Our results indicate that our model outperforms two conventional approaches used for seizure-onset localization (5-7% better AUC: 0.72, 0.67, 0.65) and that the proposed inference technique provides 3-10% gain in AUC (0.72, 0.62, 0.69) compared to sampling-based alternatives.

paragraphs: EEG-GRAPH uses relationships across recording locations and time to infer pathological brain activity from electroencephalograms. Its application is identifying brain regions that generate seizures in people with epilepsy. The model jointly considers these dependencies so that evidence about instantaneous activity is interpreted in its spatial and temporal context.

The authors represent the problem with a factor graph and design its factor functions using domain knowledge. These functions express how different pieces of evidence relate within the model. A graph-cut-based inference procedure solves the resulting graph inference exactly in polynomial time. Exactness concerns solving the model’s inference problem; it does not make the biological predictions automatically certain.

Evaluation uses clinically collected intracranial EEG from 29 patients. The reported AUC is 0.72, compared with 0.67 and 0.65 for two conventional localization approaches. The proposed inference method also exceeds sampling-based alternatives with AUCs of 0.62 and 0.69. These results support both the joint modeling approach and the particular inference procedure for the evaluated localization task.
summary.tldr: EEG-GRAPH combines spatial and temporal EEG evidence with exact graph-cut inference to improve seizure-region localization in the reported patient evaluation.

title: EEG-GRAPH: A Factor-Graph-Based Model for Capturing Spatial, Temporal, and Observational Relationships in Electroencephalograms

abstract: Automatic neural architecture design has shown its potential in discovering powerful neural network architectures. Existing methods, no matter based on reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms (EA), conduct architecture search in a discrete space, which is highly inefficient. In this paper, we propose a simple and efficient method to automatic neural architecture design based on continuous optimization. We call this new approach neural architecture optimization (NAO). There are three key components in our proposed approach: (1) An encoder embeds/maps neural network architectures into a continuous space. (2) A predictor takes the continuous representation of a network as input and predicts its accuracy. (3) A decoder maps a continuous representation of a network back to its architecture. The performance predictor and the encoder enable us to perform gradient based optimization in the continuous space to find the embedding of a new architecture with potentially better accuracy. Such a better embedding is then decoded to a network by the decoder. Experiments show that the architecture discovered by our method is very competitive for image classification task on CIFAR-10 and language modeling task on PTB, outperforming or on par with the best results of previous architecture search methods with a significantly reduction of computational resources. Specifically we obtain $2.11\%$ test set error rate for CIFAR-10 image classification task and $56.0$ test set perplexity of PTB language modeling task. The best discovered architectures on both tasks are successfully transferred to other tasks such as CIFAR-100 and WikiText-2. Furthermore, combined with the recent proposed weight sharing mechanism, we discover powerful architecture on CIFAR-10 (with error rate $3.53\%$) and on PTB (with test set perplexity $56.6$), with very limited computational resources (less than $10$ GPU hours) for both tasks.

summary.tldr: NAO encodes network architectures into a continuous space, improves their predicted accuracy with gradients, and decodes promising new designs.

title: Neural Architecture Optimization

abstract: We introduce the community exploration problem that has various real-world applications such as online advertising. In the problem, an explorer allocates limited budget to explore communities so as to maximize the number of members he could meet. We provide a systematic study of the community exploration problem, from offline optimization to online learning. For the offline setting where the sizes of communities are known, we prove that the greedy methods for both of non-adaptive exploration and adaptive exploration are optimal. For the online setting where the sizes of communities are not known and need to be learned from the multi-round explorations, we propose an ``upper confidence'' like algorithm that achieves the logarithmic regret bounds. By combining the feedback from different rounds, we can achieve a constant regret bound.

By combining the feedback from different rounds, we can achieve a constant regret bound.

paragraphs: The community exploration problem asks how to distribute a limited exploration budget among communities to meet as many members as possible. The authors study both planning with known community sizes and learning those sizes through repeated exploration. Online advertising is one motivating application for this allocation problem.

When community sizes are known, the paper establishes optimality of greedy methods in two settings. A non-adaptive strategy commits to its allocation without adjusting to observations, while an adaptive strategy can respond as exploration unfolds. Proving greedy optimality in both cases gives a direct way to solve the respective offline problems.

When community sizes are unknown, exploration must also provide information for future decisions. The authors propose an algorithm based on an upper-confidence idea and prove logarithmic regret bounds, measuring accumulated loss from learning rather than already knowing the best allocation. They further obtain a constant regret bound by combining feedback across rounds. This stronger result depends on that use of information from different rounds, connecting how feedback is retained with how effectively repeated exploration improves.
summary.tldr: The paper proves greedy optimality for known community sizes and develops learning algorithms with logarithmic, or with combined feedback constant, regret.

title: Community Exploration: From Offline Optimization to Online Learning

abstract: We present a novel approach for LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) topic reconstruction. The main technical idea is to show that the distribution over the documents generated by LDA can be transformed into a distribution for a much simpler generative model in which documents are generated from {\em the same set of topics} but have a much simpler structure: documents are single topic and topics are chosen uniformly at random. Furthermore, this reduction is approximation preserving, in the sense that approximate distributions-- the only ones we can hope to compute in practice-- are mapped into approximate distribution in the simplified world. This opens up the possibility of efficiently reconstructing LDA topics in a roundabout way. Compute an approximate document distribution from the given corpus, transform it into an approximate distribution for the single-topic world, and run a reconstruction algorithm in the uniform, single topic world-- a much simpler task than direct LDA reconstruction. Indeed, we show the viability of the approach by giving very simple algorithms for a generalization of two notable cases that have been studied in the literature, $p$-separability and Gibbs sampling for matrix-like topics.

This paper proposes an indirect route: transform the distribution of LDA documents into a distribution generated by a simpler model. In that model, each document uses just one topic, and topics are selected with equal probability. Crucially, the underlying topics remain the same.

The transformation also preserves approximation. An approximate distribution in the original setting becomes an approximate distribution in the simplified setting. This matters because a finite collection of documents gives only an estimate of the document distribution. The proposed route therefore accommodates the kind of imperfect input that a reconstruction procedure can realistically obtain.

The resulting workflow is to estimate the document distribution, transform it, and reconstruct topics in the simpler model. The authors demonstrate viability through simple algorithms covering generalizations of two previously studied cases: p-separability and Gibbs sampling for matrix-like topics. These results support the reduction as a route toward efficient reconstruction, rather than establishing an unrestricted solution to every LDA reconstruction problem.
summary.tldr: An approximation-preserving transformation reduces LDA topic reconstruction to a simpler model with uniformly chosen, single-topic documents.

title: A Reduction for Efficient LDA Topic Reconstruction

abstract: Recent developments in high throughput profiling of individual neurons have spurred data driven exploration of the idea that there exist natural groupings of neurons referred to as cell types. The promise of this idea is that the immense complexity of brain circuits can be reduced, and effectively studied by means of interactions between cell types. While clustering of neuron populations based on a particular data modality can be used to define cell types, such definitions are often inconsistent across different characterization modalities. We pose this issue of cross-modal alignment as an optimization problem and develop an approach based on coupled training of autoencoders as a framework for such analyses. We apply this framework to a Patch-seq dataset consisting of transcriptomic and electrophysiological profiles for the same set of neurons to study consistency of representations across modalities, and evaluate cross-modal data prediction ability. We explore the problem where only a subset of neurons is characterized with more than one modality, and demonstrate that representations learned by coupled autoencoders can be used to identify types sampled only by a single modality.

This paper treats that disagreement as a problem of aligning representations across measurement modalities.

The authors formulate alignment as an optimization problem and develop a framework that trains autoencoders together. Autoencoders learn compact representations of their inputs; coupling their training provides a way to study how those representations correspond across modalities. The framework is applied to Patch-seq data containing both transcriptomic and electrophysiological measurements of the same neurons. The authors examine representation consistency and evaluate prediction between modalities.

The paper also considers incomplete measurement coverage, where only some neurons have multiple kinds of measurements. It demonstrates that the coupled representations can identify cell types sampled through just one modality. This extends the framework's usefulness beyond datasets in which every neuron has a complete set of measurements.
summary.tldr: Coupled autoencoders align different measurements of neurons and can identify cell types even when some neurons have only one measurement modality.

title: A coupled autoencoder approach for multi-modal analysis of cell types

abstract: Disentangled representation learning finds compact, independent and easy-to-interpret factors of the data. Learning such has been shown to require an inductive bias, which we explicitly encode in a generative model of images. Specifically, we propose a model with two latent spaces: one that represents spatial transformations of the input data, and another that represents the transformed data. We find that the latter naturally captures the intrinsic appearance of the data. To realize the generative model, we propose a Variationally Inferred Transformational Autoencoder (VITAE) that incorporates a spatial ransformer into a variational autoencoder. We show how to perform inference in the model efficiently by carefully designing the encoders and restricting the transformation class to be diffeomorphic. Empirically, our model separates the visual style from digit type on MNIST, separates shape and pose in images of human bodies and facial features from facial shape on CelebA.

paragraphs: A useful image representation would separate what an object looks like from how it is spatially transformed. The paper builds this distinction directly into a generative model, supplying an inductive bias that encourages interpretable factors. It uses two latent spaces: one represents spatial transformations, while the other represents the data after those transformations have been accounted for.

The authors find that the second latent space naturally captures intrinsic appearance. To make inference efficient, they carefully design the encoders and restrict transformations to a diffeomorphic class, meaning smooth, invertible transformations with smooth inverses. This restriction is part of the model’s computational approach.

The reported experiments demonstrate several kinds of separation: visual style from digit identity on MNIST, body shape from pose in human images, and facial features from facial shape on CelebA. These findings support explicitly representing spatial transformations as a way to learn more interpretable image factors. The evidence concerns the separations demonstrated in those image settings.
summary.tldr: VITAE explicitly models spatial transformations and appearance in separate latent spaces, producing interpretable separations across several image datasets.

title: Explicit Disentanglement of Appearance and Perspective in Generative Models

abstract: This paper proposes a partitioning structure learning method for segmented linear regression trees (SLRT), which assigns linear predictors over the terminal nodes. The recursive partitioning process is driven by an adaptive split selection algorithm that maximizes, at each node, a criterion function based on a conditional Kendall’s τ statistic that measures the rank dependence between the regressors and the fit- ted linear residuals. Theoretical analysis shows that the split selection algorithm permits consistent identification and estimation of the unknown segments. A suffi- ciently large tree is induced by applying the split selection algorithm recursively. Then the minimal cost-complexity tree pruning procedure is applied to attain the right-sized tree, that ensures (i) the nested structure of pruned subtrees and (ii) consistent estimation to the number of segments. Implanting the SLRT as the built-in base predictor, we obtain the ensemble predictors by random forests (RF) and the proposed weighted random forests (WRF). The practical performance of the SLRT and its ensemble versions are evaluated via numerical simulations and empirical studies. The latter shows their advantageous predictive performance over a set of state-of-the-art tree-based models on well-studied public datasets.

At each node, an adaptive procedure chooses a split using a criterion based on conditional Kendall's tau, measuring rank dependence between the predictors and the residuals of the fitted linear model.

The split criterion connects the remaining pattern in the residuals to the decision to subdivide a region. The theoretical analysis shows that the procedure permits consistent identification and estimation of unknown segments. Repeated splitting first builds a sufficiently large tree, after which cost-complexity pruning selects its size while preserving nested subtrees and consistent estimation of the number of segments.

The authors also use these trees as base predictors for random forests and a proposed weighted random forest method. Simulations and empirical studies evaluate the individual trees and ensembles. On well-studied public datasets, the empirical results show advantageous predictive performance compared with a set of leading tree-based models.
summary.tldr: A residual-dependence split criterion learns segmented linear regression trees, with consistency results and strong empirical performance for trees and ensembles.

title: Partitioning Structure Learning for Segmented Linear Regression Trees

abstract: We investigate time-dependent data analysis from the perspective of recurrent kernel machines, from which models with hidden units and gated memory cells arise naturally. By considering dynamic gating of the memory cell, a model closely related to the long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network is derived. Extending this setup to $n$-gram filters, the convolutional neural network (CNN), Gated CNN, and recurrent additive network (RAN) are also recovered as special cases. Our analysis provides a new perspective on the LSTM, while also extending it to $n$-gram convolutional filters. Experiments are performed on natural language processing tasks and on analysis of local field potentials (neuroscience). We demonstrate that the variants we derive from kernels perform on par or even better than traditional neural methods. For the neuroscience application, the new models demonstrate significant improvements relative to the prior state of the art.

paragraphs: This paper approaches time-dependent data through recurrent kernel machines and derives connections to familiar neural sequence models. Within that perspective, hidden units and gated memory cells arise naturally. The contribution is a common mathematical viewpoint for understanding several architectures, together with new variants motivated by that viewpoint.

Allowing the memory gate to change dynamically produces a model closely related to an LSTM recurrent network. Extending the construction to n-gram filters recovers convolutional networks, gated convolutional networks, and recurrent additive networks as special cases. The same framework therefore connects recurrent memory with filters that operate over short sequences, and extends the LSTM-related construction to those filters.

The authors test their derived variants on natural language processing tasks and on neuroscience data involving local field potentials. They report performance matching or exceeding traditional neural methods, with significant improvements over the prior state of the art in the neuroscience application. These experiments support the practical value of the kernel perspective alongside its role in explaining relationships between model families.
summary.tldr: Recurrent kernel machines unify several neural sequence architectures and motivate variants with competitive language and neuroscience results.

title: Kernel-Based Approaches for Sequence Modeling: Connections to Neural Methods

abstract: Tight estimation of the Lipschitz constant for deep neural networks (DNNs) is useful in many applications ranging from robustness certification of classifiers to stability analysis of closed-loop systems with reinforcement learning controllers. Existing methods in the literature for estimating the Lipschitz constant suffer from either lack of accuracy or poor scalability. In this paper, we present a convex optimization framework to compute guaranteed upper bounds on the Lipschitz constant of DNNs both accurately and efficiently. Our main idea is to interpret activation functions as gradients of convex potential functions. Hence, they satisfy certain properties that can be described by quadratic constraints. This particular description allows us to pose the Lipschitz constant estimation problem as a semidefinite program (SDP). The resulting SDP can be adapted to increase either the estimation accuracy (by capturing the interaction between activation functions of different layers) or scalability (by decomposition and parallel implementation). We illustrate the utility of our approach with a variety of experiments on randomly generated networks and on classifiers trained on the MNIST and Iris datasets. In particular, we experimentally demonstrate that our Lipschitz bounds are the most accurate compared to those in the literature. We also study the impact of adversarial training methods on the Lipschitz bounds of the resulting classifiers and show that our bounds can be used to efficiently provide robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: A Lipschitz constant bounds how much a network's output can change relative to changes in its input. Tight upper bounds can support classifier robustness certificates and stability analysis for systems using learned controllers. This paper addresses the difficulty of obtaining bounds that are both accurate and computationally manageable for deep networks.

The authors interpret activation functions as gradients of convex potential functions. Properties of those gradients can then be represented through quadratic constraints, yielding a semidefinite optimization problem. The formulation can emphasize accuracy by capturing interactions between activations across layers, or emphasize scalability through decomposition and parallel computation. These are adjustable computational choices within the framework.

Experiments cover randomly generated networks and classifiers trained on MNIST and Iris. The authors report more accurate bounds than the compared literature methods and demonstrate efficient robustness guarantees. They also examine how adversarial training affects the resulting bounds. The upper-bound guarantee is mathematical; the comparative accuracy claim is supported by the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: A semidefinite optimization framework computes guaranteed neural-network Lipschitz upper bounds with adjustable accuracy and scalability.

title: Efficient and Accurate Estimation of Lipschitz Constants for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Neural decoders were shown to outperform classical message passing techniques for short BCH codes. In this work, we extend these results to much larger families of algebraic block codes, by performing message passing with graph neural networks. The parameters of the sub-network at each variable-node in the Tanner graph are obtained from a hypernetwork that receives the absolute values of the current message as input. To add stability, we employ a simplified version of the arctanh activation that is based on a high order Taylor approximation of this activation function. Our results show that for a large number of algebraic block codes, from diverse families of codes (BCH, LDPC, Polar), the decoding obtained with our method outperforms the vanilla belief propagation method as well as other learning techniques from the literature.

The authors seek to extend those gains to a much broader collection of codes, while retaining a graph-based procedure for exchanging decoding information.

The distinctive mechanism is a hypernetwork that produces the parameters of a subnetwork at each variable node in the Tanner graph. Its input is the absolute values of the current message, so the subnetwork's parameters depend on the messages being processed. The reported results cover many codes from the BCH, LDPC, and Polar families. Across that evaluation, the method outperforms ordinary belief propagation and other learning techniques considered in the work. The contribution combines message-dependent neural computation with a stability-oriented activation change, extending the empirical reach of neural decoding beyond the narrower code setting that motivated the study.
summary.tldr: A hypernetwork-driven graph decoder improves decoding across tested BCH, LDPC, and Polar codes by adapting computations to current messages.

title: Hyper-Graph-Network Decoders for Block Codes

abstract: Dynamic functional connectivity, as measured by the time-varying covariance of neurological signals, is believed to play an important role in many aspects of cognition. While many methods have been proposed, reliably establishing the presence and characteristics of brain connectivity is challenging due to the high dimensionality and noisiness of neuroimaging data. We present a latent factor Gaussian process model which addresses these challenges by learning a parsimonious representation of connectivity dynamics. The proposed model naturally allows for inference and visualization of the time-varying connectivity. As an illustration of the scientific utility of the model, application to a data set of rat local field potential activity recorded during a complex non-spatial memory task provides evidence of stimuli differentiation.
