paragraphs: Dynamic functional connectivity describes how the covariance between neurological signals changes over time. Such changes are believed to matter for cognition, but establishing their presence and character is difficult. Neuroimaging data contain many variables and substantial noise, making a reliable description of changing relationships a demanding statistical problem.

This paper introduces a latent factor Gaussian process model to learn a compact representation of those connectivity dynamics. The latent-factor formulation provides a parsimonious account of the evolving relationships. The resulting model supports both inference and visualization, allowing the estimated time-varying connectivity to be examined as part of the analysis.

The authors illustrate its scientific use with rat local field potential recordings collected during a complex non-spatial memory task. Applying the model provides evidence of stimulus differentiation. This result demonstrates how the representation can help investigate task-related patterns in neural activity. The contribution combines a statistical model for noisy, high-dimensional connectivity with an example of how its inferred dynamics can inform interpretation of a neuroscience experiment.
summary.tldr: A latent factor Gaussian process models changing neural connectivity compactly and reveals evidence of stimulus differentiation in rat recordings.

title: Modeling Dynamic Functional Connectivity with Latent Factor Gaussian Processes

abstract: Communication bottleneck has been identified as a significant issue in distributed optimization of large-scale learning models. Recently, several approaches to mitigate this problem have been proposed, including different forms of gradient compression or computing local models and mixing them iteratively. In this paper we propose Qsparse-local-SGD algorithm, which combines aggressive sparsification with quantization and local computation along with error compensation, by keeping track of the difference between the true and compressed gradients. We propose both synchronous and asynchronous implementations of Qsparse-local-SGD. We analyze convergence for Qsparse-local-SGD in the distributed case, for smooth non-convex and convex objective functions. We demonstrate that Qsparse-local-SGD converges at the same rate as vanilla distributed SGD for many important classes of sparsifiers and quantizers. We use Qsparse-local-SGD to train ResNet-50 on ImageNet, and show that it results in significant savings over the state-of-the-art, in the number of bits transmitted to reach target accuracy.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial resources communicating updates between workers. Qsparse-local-SGD combines several ways to reduce that burden: sending sparse updates, quantizing their numerical values, and performing computation locally. The aim is to reduce transmitted information while maintaining effective optimization.

Compression changes the gradients that are communicated. The algorithm therefore tracks the difference between the true and compressed gradients through error compensation. This incorporates the compression discrepancy into the method instead of simply discarding it. The authors provide both synchronous and asynchronous implementations, covering two ways of coordinating distributed computation.

The convergence analysis addresses smooth convex and nonconvex objectives. For many important classes of sparsifiers and quantizers, Qsparse-local-SGD achieves the same convergence rate as ordinary distributed stochastic gradient descent. In experiments training ResNet-50 on ImageNet, it substantially reduces the number of transmitted bits needed to reach target accuracy compared with the state of the art. The theoretical and empirical results jointly support combining compression with local computation under the analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: Qsparse-local-SGD combines compression, local computation, and error compensation to reduce communication while retaining standard convergence rates for many compression choices.

title: Qsparse-local-SGD: Distributed SGD with Quantization, Sparsification and Local Computations

abstract: Individual characteristics in human decision-making are often quantified by fitting a parametric cognitive model to subjects' behavior and then studying differences between them in the associated parameter space. However, these models often fit behavior more poorly than recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which are more flexible and make fewer assumptions about the underlying decision-making processes. Unfortunately, the parameter and latent activity spaces of RNNs are generally high-dimensional and uninterpretable, making it hard to use them to study individual differences. Here, we show how to benefit from the flexibility of RNNs while representing individual differences in a low-dimensional and interpretable space. To achieve this, we propose a novel end-to-end learning framework in which an encoder is trained to map the behavior of subjects into a low-dimensional latent space. These low-dimensional representations are used to generate the parameters of individual RNNs corresponding to the decision-making process of each subject. We introduce terms into the loss function that ensure that the latent dimensions are informative and disentangled, i.e., encouraged to have distinct effects on behavior. This allows them to align with separate facets of individual differences. We illustrate the performance of our framework on synthetic data as well as a dataset including the behavior of patients with psychiatric disorders.

Recurrent neural networks can fit behavior more flexibly, but their large parameter and activity spaces are difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a way to retain that modeling flexibility while expressing differences between people in a small, interpretable representation.

An encoder maps each subject's behavior into a low-dimensional latent space. That representation then generates the parameters of an individual RNN modeling the subject's decision process. The complete system is trained end to end, linking the compact description of a person directly to the flexible model of their behavior.

This is intended to align separate dimensions with separate facets of individual differences. The authors illustrate the framework using synthetic data and behavioral data from patients with psychiatric disorders. The contribution is an approach to comparing individuals through interpretable representations while using RNNs to model their decisions.
summary.tldr: A compact latent representation generates individual RNNs, combining flexible behavioral modeling with interpretable dimensions of individual differences.

title: Disentangled behavioural representations

abstract: We present a simple, flexible, and general framework titled Partial Registration Network (PRNet), for partial-to-partial point cloud registration. Inspired by recently-proposed learning-based methods for registration, we use deep networks to tackle non-convexity of the alignment and partial correspondence problem. While previous learning-based methods assume the entire shape is visible, PRNet is suitable for partial-to-partial registration, outperforming PointNetLK, DCP, and non-learning methods on synthetic data. PRNet is self-supervised, jointly learning an appropriate geometric representation, a keypoint detector that finds points in common between partial views, and keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. We show PRNet predicts keypoints and correspondences consistently across views and objects. Furthermore, the learned representation is transferable to classification.

Inspired by recently-proposed learning-based methods for registration, we use deep networks to tackle non-convexity of the alignment and partial correspondence problem. While previous learning-based methods assume the entire shape is visible, PRNet is suitable for partial-to-partial registration, outperforming PointNetLK, DCP, and non-learning methods on synthetic data. PRNet is self-supervised, jointly learning an appropriate geometric representation, a keypoint detector that finds points in common between partial views, and keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. paragraphs: Point-cloud registration aligns two collections of spatial points describing a shape. When both collections show only part of the shape, the system must work out which visible points correspond while also determining the alignment. PRNet addresses this partial-to-partial setting, extending beyond earlier learning-based methods that assume the entire shape is visible.

The network jointly learns three connected components: a geometric representation, a detector for keypoints shared between partial views, and correspondences between those keypoints. It uses self-supervision to learn these components together. Deep networks tackle the non-convex alignment and partial-correspondence problem, linking the choice of useful points to the task of matching them.

On synthetic data, PRNet outperforms PointNetLK, DCP, and the non-learning methods considered. The authors also show consistent keypoint and correspondence predictions across views and objects. Beyond registration, the learned representation transfers to classification. These results suggest that learning to connect partial observations can produce both useful alignment information and geometric features applicable to another task.
summary.tldr: PRNet jointly learns representations, shared keypoints, and correspondences to align partial point clouds through self-supervision.

title: PRNet: Self-Supervised Learning for Partial-to-Partial Registration

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of computing the barycenter of a set of probability distributions under the Sinkhorn divergence. This problem has recently found applications across various domains, including graphics, learning, and vision, as it provides a meaningful mechanism to aggregate knowledge. Unlike previous approaches which directly operate in the space of probability measures, we recast the Sinkhorn barycenter problem as an instance of unconstrained functional optimization and develop a novel functional gradient descent method named \texttt{Sinkhorn Descent} (\texttt{SD}). We prove that \texttt{SD} converges to a stationary point at a sublinear rate, and under reasonable assumptions, we further show that it asymptotically finds a global minimizer of the Sinkhorn barycenter problem. Moreover, by providing a mean-field analysis, we show that \texttt{SD} preserves the {weak convergence} of empirical measures. Importantly, the computational complexity of \texttt{SD} scales linearly in the dimension $d$ and we demonstrate its scalability by solving a $100$-dimensional Sinkhorn barycenter problem.

paragraphs: A barycenter combines several probability distributions into a representative distribution according to a chosen notion of difference. This paper studies barycenters defined using Sinkhorn divergence, a formulation useful for aggregating information in graphics, learning, and vision. The computational task is to find the distribution that best serves as that shared representative.

The authors reformulate the problem as unconstrained optimization over functions, rather than optimizing directly over probability measures. This leads to Sinkhorn Descent, a functional gradient descent method. They prove sublinear convergence to a stationary point and, under additional assumptions, asymptotic convergence to a global minimizer. The distinction matters because the stronger global conclusion depends on those assumptions.

A mean-field analysis also shows that the method preserves weak convergence of empirical measures, linking its behavior on empirical distributions to their limiting behavior. Its computational complexity grows linearly with dimension, and the authors demonstrate scalability on a 100-dimensional barycenter problem. Together, these results connect an alternative optimization formulation with convergence properties and a concrete demonstration of higher-dimensional computation.
summary.tldr: Sinkhorn Descent reformulates distribution averaging as functional optimization, with convergence guarantees and computational complexity linear in dimension.

title: Sinkhorn Barycenter via Functional Gradient Descent

abstract: We present a novel system that gets as an input, video frames of a musician playing the piano, and generates the music for that video. The generation of music from visual cues is a challenging problem and it is not clear whether it is an attainable goal at all. Our main aim in this work is to explore the plausibility of such a transformation and to identify cues and components able to carry the association of sounds with visual events. To achieve the transformation we built a full pipeline named 'Audeo' containing three components. We first translate the video frames of the keyboard and the musician hand movements into raw mechanical musical symbolic representation Piano-Roll (Roll) for each video frame which represents the keys pressed at each time step. We then adapt the Roll to be amenable for audio synthesis by including temporal correlations. This step turns out to be critical for meaningful audio generation. In the last step, we implement Midi synthesizers to generate realistic music. Audeo converts video to audio smoothly and clearly with only a few setup constraints. We evaluate Audeo on piano performance videos collected from Youtube and obtain that their generated music is of reasonable audio quality and can be successfully recognized with high precision by popular music identification software.

paragraphs: Audeo explores whether video of someone playing a piano contains enough visual information to generate recognizable music. Its input is the performance's video frames, including the keyboard and the musician's hand movements. The work aims to establish the plausibility of this transformation and identify the visual cues and processing stages that connect visible actions to sound.

The system uses three stages. First, it translates the frames into a piano roll: a symbolic record of which keys are pressed at each time step. Next, it incorporates temporal correlations so that this mechanically inferred sequence becomes suitable for audio synthesis. The authors identify this middle stage as critical for meaningful sound. Finally, MIDI synthesizers turn the adapted representation into music.

Evaluations use piano performance videos collected from YouTube. The generated music has reasonable audio quality and is recognized with high precision by popular music identification software. The authors describe smooth, clear conversion with a few setup constraints, supporting the feasibility of this particular visual-to-musical pipeline.
summary.tldr: Audeo generates recognizable piano music from silent performance video by inferring key presses, refining their temporal structure, and synthesizing audio.

title: Audeo: Audio Generation for a Silent Performance Video

abstract: Verification and regression are two general methodologies for prediction in neural networks. Each has its own strengths: verification can be easier to infer accurately, and regression is more efficient and applicable to continuous target variables. Hence, it is often beneficial to carefully combine them to take advantage of their benefits. In this paper, we take this philosophy to improve state-of-the-art object detection, specifically by RepPoints. Though RepPoints provides high performance, we find that its heavy reliance on regression for object localization leaves room for improvement. We introduce verification tasks into the localization prediction of RepPoints, producing RepPoints v2, which proves consistent improvements of about 2.0 mAP over the original RepPoints on COCO object detection benchmark using different backbones and training methods. RepPoints v2 also achieves 52.1 mAP on the COCO \texttt{test-dev} by a single model. Moreover, we show that the proposed approach can more generally elevate other object detection frameworks as well as applications such as instance segmentation.

paragraphs: Object localization requires a detector to predict where an object is. Regression efficiently predicts continuous quantities, while verification tasks can be easier to infer accurately. This paper combines these strengths in RepPoints, whose localization predictions previously relied heavily on regression. The resulting detector is called RepPoints v2.

The contribution adds verification tasks to the localization process so that the detector uses both methodologies. The motivation is that strong overall detection performance can still leave room to improve the way locations are inferred. Combining verification with regression provides an additional source of supervision for the localization prediction.

On the COCO benchmark, the authors report consistent gains of about 2.0 mAP over the original RepPoints across different backbones and training methods. A single RepPoints v2 model reaches 52.1 mAP on COCO test-dev. They also demonstrate improvements in other detection frameworks and instance segmentation. These results suggest that the combination has usefulness beyond the particular detector where it was introduced.
summary.tldr: RepPoints v2 adds verification tasks to regression-based localization, delivering consistent COCO detection gains and benefits in related vision frameworks.

title: RepPoints v2: Verification Meets Regression for Object Detection

abstract: By searching for shared inductive biases across tasks, meta-learning promises to accelerate learning on novel tasks, but with the cost of solving a complex bilevel optimization problem. We introduce and rigorously define the trade-off between accurate modeling and optimization ease in meta-learning. At one end, classic meta-learning algorithms account for the structure of meta-learning but solve a complex optimization problem, while at the other end domain randomized search (otherwise known as joint training) ignores the structure of meta-learning and solves a single level optimization problem. Taking MAML as the representative meta-learning algorithm, we theoretically characterize the trade-off for general non-convex risk functions as well as linear regression, for which we are able to provide explicit bounds on the errors associated with modeling and optimization. We also empirically study this trade-off for meta-reinforcement learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Meta-learning seeks shared structure across tasks so that learning a new task becomes easier. Representing this goal directly often requires bilevel optimization: learning across tasks while accounting for learning within each task. The paper examines the tension between faithfully modeling that structure and solving the resulting optimization problem efficiently.

The comparison places classic meta-learning at one end and joint training, also called domain randomized search here, at the other. Joint training simplifies the problem to a single optimization level but leaves out the structure that distinguishes meta-learning. Using MAML as its representative meta-learning method, the paper formally separates errors associated with modeling from errors associated with optimization.

The authors characterize this trade-off for general nonconvex risk functions and for linear regression, where they provide explicit error bounds. They also investigate it empirically on meta-reinforcement learning benchmarks. The contribution gives a framework for assessing when a more faithful task model is worth its optimization burden, without asserting that either meta-learning or joint training is universally preferable.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes how meta-learning trades more accurate task modeling against harder optimization, using MAML and joint training.

title: Modeling and Optimization Trade-off in Meta-learning

abstract: Generative neural networks have been empirically found very promising in providing effective structural priors for compressed sensing, since they can be trained to span low-dimensional data manifolds in high-dimensional signal spaces. Despite the non-convexity of the resulting optimization problem, it has also been shown theoretically that, for neural networks with random Gaussian weights, a signal in the range of the network can be efficiently, approximately recovered from a few noisy measurements. However, a major bottleneck of these theoretical guarantees is a network \emph{expansivity} condition: that each layer of the neural network must be larger than the previous by a logarithmic factor. Our main contribution is to break this strong expansivity assumption, showing that \emph{constant} expansivity suffices to get efficient recovery algorithms, besides it also being information-theoretically necessary. To overcome the theoretical bottleneck in existing approaches we prove a novel uniform concentration theorem for random functions that might not be Lipschitz but satisfy a relaxed notion which we call ``pseudo-Lipschitzness.'' Using this theorem we can show that a matrix concentration inequality known as the \emph{Weight Distribution Condition (WDC)}, which was previously only known to hold for Gaussian matrices with logarithmic aspect ratio, in fact holds for constant aspect ratios too. Since WDC is a fundamental matrix concentration inequality in the heart of all existing theoretical guarantees on this problem, our tighter bound immediately yields improvements in all known results in the literature on compressed sensing with deep generative priors, including one-bit recovery, phase retrieval, and more.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing with a generative prior seeks a signal from a small number of measurements by restricting reconstruction to outputs of a neural generator. Existing theory supports efficient approximate recovery from noisy measurements for signals in the range of networks with random Gaussian weights. However, those guarantees required every layer to grow over the previous one by a logarithmic factor.

This makes the architectural growth required by the theory substantially less demanding. The result retains the stated generative-network setting rather than establishing recovery for arbitrary generators.

It uses that theorem to establish the Weight Distribution Condition for Gaussian matrices with constant aspect ratios. Because this condition underpins existing recovery guarantees, the improvement carries over to related results, including one-bit recovery and phase retrieval. The contribution is therefore both a sharper recovery guarantee and a reusable theoretical tool.
summary.tldr: For the studied Gaussian-weight generators, constant layer expansion suffices for efficient compressed-sensing recovery, weakening a previous logarithmic expansion requirement.

title: Constant-Expansion Suffices for Compressed Sensing with Generative Priors

abstract: In this work we study online rent-or-buy problems as a sequential decision making problem. We show how one can integrate predictions, typically coming from a machine learning (ML) setup, into this framework. Specifically, we consider the ski-rental problem and the dynamic TCP acknowledgment problem. We present new online algorithms and obtain explicit performance bounds in-terms of the accuracy of the prediction. Our algorithms are close to optimal with accurate predictions while hedging against less accurate predictions.
originalAbstract: In this work we study online rent-or-buy problems as a sequential decision making problem. We show how one can integrate predictions, typically coming from a machine learning (ML) setup, into this framework. Specifically, we consider the ski-rental problem and the dynamic TCP acknowledgment problem. We present new online algorithms and obtain explicit performance bounds in-terms of the accuracy of the prediction. Our algorithms are close to optimal with accurate predictions while hedging against less accurate predictions.

paragraphs: Online rent-or-buy problems require decisions before the full future is known. This paper studies them as sequential decision-making problems and asks how predictions, typically supplied by machine learning, can improve those decisions. Its focus is on combining predictive information with algorithms whose performance can still be analyzed when the predictions are inaccurate.

The authors consider two specific problems: ski rental and dynamic TCP acknowledgment. They develop new online algorithms within the sequential framework and derive explicit performance bounds in terms of prediction accuracy. This makes the quality of the forecast part of the mathematical performance statement, connecting the usefulness of prediction to the decisions the algorithm makes over time.

The algorithms approach optimal performance when predictions are accurate while hedging against less accurate forecasts. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and analytical: it provides ways to use predictions and describes how performance depends on their reliability. The stated findings support prediction-assisted online decision-making without requiring every prediction to be treated as dependable.
summary.tldr: New rent-or-buy algorithms exploit accurate predictions while bounding performance in terms of prediction error.

title: Improving Online Rent-or-Buy Algorithms with Sequential Decision Making and ML Predictions

abstract: Document intelligence automates the extraction of information from documents and supports many business applications. Recent self-supervised learning methods on large-scale unlabeled document datasets have opened up promising directions towards reducing annotation efforts by training models with self-supervised objectives. However, most of the existing document pretraining methods are still language-dominated. We present UDoc, a new unified pretraining framework for document understanding. UDoc is designed to support most document understanding tasks, extending the Transformer to take multimodal embeddings as input. Each input element is composed of words and visual features from a semantic region of the input document image. An important feature of UDoc is that it learns a generic representation by making use of three self-supervised losses, encouraging the representation to model sentences, learn similarities, and align modalities. Extensive empirical analysis demonstrates that the pretraining procedure learns better joint representations and leads to improvements in downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Document understanding requires extracting information from documents, and self-supervised pretraining can reduce dependence on manual annotation. The paper observes that many existing pretraining approaches are dominated by language. Its proposed framework, UDoc, learns a joint representation from both the words and the visual information contained in document images.

Three self-supervised losses encourage complementary behavior: modeling sentences, learning similarities, and aligning the modalities. Together, these objectives are intended to produce a general representation that supports a broad range of document-understanding tasks.

The reported empirical analysis finds that this pretraining procedure learns better joint representations and improves downstream task performance. The significance lies in learning text and visual information together during pretraining, so later tasks can benefit from their combined representation. The framework’s broad task coverage is a design aim, while the stated improvements are supported by the paper’s empirical evaluations.
summary.tldr: UDoc combines regional text and visual features with three self-supervised objectives to improve joint document representations and downstream performance.

title: UniDoc: Unified Pretraining Framework for Document Understanding

abstract: Out-of-domain (OOD) generalization is a significant challenge for machine learning models. Many techniques have been proposed to overcome this challenge, often focused on learning models with certain invariance properties. In this work, we draw a link between OOD performance and model calibration, arguing that calibration across multiple domains can be viewed as a special case of an invariant representation leading to better OOD generalization. Specifically, we show that under certain conditions, models which achieve \emph{multi-domain calibration} are provably free of spurious correlations. This leads us to propose multi-domain calibration as a measurable and trainable surrogate for the OOD performance of a classifier. We therefore introduce methods that are easy to apply and allow practitioners to improve multi-domain calibration by training or modifying an existing model, leading to better performance on unseen domains. Using four datasets from the recently proposed WILDS OOD benchmark, as well as the Colored MNIST, we demonstrate that training or tuning models so they are calibrated across multiple domains leads to significantly improved performance on unseen test domains. We believe this intriguing connection between calibration and OOD generalization is promising from both a practical and theoretical point of view.

paragraphs: Models often lose accuracy when tested in environments different from those used for training. This paper connects that problem to calibration: whether a classifier’s confidence agrees with how often it is correct. The authors focus on calibration across several domains and relate it to the invariant representations commonly pursued for out-of-domain generalization.

Their theoretical result shows that, under certain conditions, models calibrated across multiple domains are free of spurious correlations. This motivates multi-domain calibration as a measurable, trainable surrogate for performance in unseen domains. The authors introduce methods for improving it either while training a model or by modifying an existing one.

Experiments use four datasets from the WILDS benchmark and Colored MNIST. Training or tuning for calibration across domains significantly improves performance on unseen test domains in these evaluations. The evidence combines a conditional theoretical connection with practical improvements. It does not make calibration an unconditional guarantee of transfer, but identifies a concrete property that can help guide efforts to improve it.
summary.tldr: Multi-domain calibration has a conditional theoretical link to avoiding spurious correlations and improves unseen-domain performance in the reported experiments.

title: On Calibration and Out-of-Domain Generalization

abstract: Thanks to their scalability, two-stage recommenders are used by many of today's largest online platforms, including YouTube, LinkedIn, and Pinterest. These systems produce recommendations in two steps: (i) multiple nominators—tuned for low prediction latency—preselect a small subset of candidates from the whole item pool; (ii) a slower but more accurate ranker further narrows down the nominated items, and serves to the user. Despite their popularity, the literature on two-stage recommenders is relatively scarce, and the algorithms are often treated as mere sums of their parts. Such treatment presupposes that the two-stage performance is explained by the behavior of the individual components in isolation. This is not the case: using synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate that interactions between the ranker and the nominators substantially affect the overall performance. Motivated by these findings, we derive a generalization lower bound which shows that independent nominator training can lead to performance on par with uniformly random recommendations. We find that careful design of item pools, each assigned to a different nominator, alleviates these issues. As manual search for a good pool allocation is difficult, we propose to learn one instead using a Mixture-of-Experts based approach. This significantly improves both precision and recall at $K$.

paragraphs: Two-stage recommenders first use fast nominators to select candidates and then apply a slower, more accurate ranker. This architecture scales recommendation to large item pools. The paper asks whether understanding each component independently is enough to explain the quality of the complete system.

Using synthetic and real-world data, the authors show that interactions between nominators and the ranker substantially affect performance. A generalization lower bound further establishes that training nominators independently can produce performance comparable to uniformly random recommendations. This is a possible failure of independent training, rather than a claim that all independently trained systems perform randomly.

Because manually finding a good allocation is difficult, they learn the allocation using a Mixture-of-Experts approach. This significantly improves precision and recall at K in their evaluations. The findings make candidate-pool allocation part of the learning problem and show why the quality of a two-stage system depends on how its components work together.
summary.tldr: Learning which item pools nominators handle improves two-stage recommendations by addressing harmful interactions with the ranker.

title: On Component Interactions in Two-Stage Recommender Systems

abstract: More recently, there has been a surge of interest in employing machine learning approaches to expedite the drug discovery process where virtual screening for hit discovery and ADMET prediction for lead optimization play essential roles. One of the main obstacles to the wide success of machine learning approaches in these two tasks is that the number of compounds labeled with activities or ADMET properties is too small to build an effective predictive model. This paper seeks to remedy the problem by transferring the knowledge from previous assays, namely in-vivo experiments, by different laboratories and against various target proteins. To accommodate these wildly different assays and capture the similarity between assays, we propose a functional rationalized meta-learning algorithm FRML for such knowledge transfer. FRML constructs the predictive model with layers of neural sub-networks or so-called functional regions. Building on this, FRML shares an initialization for the weights of the predictive model across all assays, while customizes it to each assay with a region localization network choosing the pertinent regions. The compositionality of the model improves the capacity of generalization to various and even out-of-distribution tasks. Empirical results on both virtual screening and ADMET prediction validate the superiority of FRML over state-of-the-art baselines powered with interpretability in assay relationship.

paragraphs: Drug discovery models often have too few compounds with measured activities or ADMET properties to learn effective predictions. This paper addresses that shortage by transferring knowledge from earlier assays conducted by different laboratories and against different protein targets. The challenge is to share useful information despite substantial differences between the source and destination tasks.

The proposed FRML method builds its predictor from layers of neural subnetworks called functional regions. All assays share an initial setting of the predictor's weights. A separate region localization network then selects the regions relevant to each assay, allowing the common starting model to be customized rather than transferred identically to every task.

This compositional design is intended to improve generalization across varied tasks, including tasks outside the training distribution. Experiments on virtual screening and ADMET prediction report better performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered. The method also offers interpretability concerning relationships among assays. Its contribution is a structured way to combine shared learning with task-specific selection when labeled compounds are scarce.
summary.tldr: FRML transfers knowledge between drug discovery assays through shared initialization and assay-specific selection of neural subnetworks.

title: Functionally Regionalized Knowledge Transfer for Low-resource Drug Discovery

abstract: Recent advances in implicit neural representations show great promise when it comes to generating numerical solutions to partial differential equations. Compared to conventional alternatives, such representations employ parameterized neural networks to define, in a mesh-free manner, signals that are highly-detailed, continuous, and fully differentiable. In this work, we present a novel machine learning approach for topology optimization---an important class of inverse problems with high-dimensional parameter spaces and highly nonlinear objective landscapes. To effectively leverage neural representations in the context of mesh-free topology optimization, we use multilayer perceptrons to parameterize both density and displacement fields. Our experiments indicate that our method is highly competitive for minimizing structural compliance objectives, and it enables self-supervised learning of continuous solution spaces for topology optimization problems.

paragraphs: Topology optimization searches for structural designs in a large space of possible material arrangements. The paper treats it as an inverse problem with many parameters and a highly nonlinear objective. NTopo uses implicit neural representations to express the relevant physical fields continuously, making a mesh-free approach central to its design.

Specifically, multilayer perceptrons parameterize both density and displacement fields. Density represents the distribution of material, while displacement represents how the structure deforms. Expressing both through neural networks provides continuous, differentiable representations, bringing the same general representation strategy to the design variables and the structural response involved in the optimization.

The reported experiments indicate that NTopo is highly competitive for minimizing structural compliance objectives, which concern how readily a structure deforms. The method also enables self-supervised learning of continuous solution spaces for topology optimization. These findings support neural fields as a useful computational representation for structural design, connecting the optimization of individual structures with learning continuous families of solutions within the proposed framework.
summary.tldr: NTopo represents material density and displacement with neural networks for competitive mesh-free structural topology optimization.

title: NTopo: Mesh-free Topology Optimization using Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: There have been long-standing controversies and inconsistencies over the experiment setup and criteria for identifying the "winning ticket" in literature. To reconcile such, we revisit the definition of lottery ticket hypothesis, with comprehensive and more rigorous conditions. Under our new definition, we show concrete evidence to clarify whether the winning ticket exists across the major DNN architectures and/or applications. Through extensive experiments, we perform quantitative analysis on the correlations between winning tickets and various experimental factors, and empirically study the patterns of our observations. We find that the key training hyperparameters, such as learning rate and training epochs, as well as the architecture characteristics such as capacities and residual connections, are all highly correlated with whether and when the winning tickets can be identified. Based on our analysis, we summarize a guideline for parameter settings in regards of specific architecture characteristics, which we hope to catalyze the research progress on the topic of lottery ticket hypothesis. Our codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/boone891214/sanity-check-LTH.

Under our new definition, we show concrete evidence to clarify whether the winning ticket exists across the major DNN architectures and/or applications. Through extensive experiments, we perform quantitative analysis on the correlations between winning tickets and various experimental factors, and empirically study the patterns of our observations. paragraphs: Research on the lottery ticket hypothesis has used inconsistent experimental setups and criteria for identifying a winning ticket. This paper revisits the definition and introduces more comprehensive, rigorous conditions. Its purpose is to make claims about winning tickets easier to assess across neural-network architectures and applications.

Using those conditions, the authors conduct extensive experiments and analyze how identification of winning tickets relates to experimental choices. Learning rate and training duration are strongly correlated with whether and when a ticket can be identified. Architectural properties, including model capacity and residual connections, also show strong correlations with those outcomes.

These findings make the experimental setup part of the interpretation of a winning-ticket result. They are reported correlations, rather than a claim that one setting universally determines success. Based on the observed patterns, the authors provide guidance for choosing parameters in light of architectural characteristics. The contribution combines clearer evaluation criteria with empirical evidence about which factors accompany successful identification across the settings studied.
summary.tldr: Stricter winning-ticket criteria reveal strong correlations between ticket identification, training choices, and neural-network architecture.

title: Sanity Checks for Lottery Tickets: Does Your Winning Ticket Really Win the Jackpot?

abstract: Recently, game-playing agents based on AI techniques have demonstrated super-human performance in several sequential games, such as chess, Go, and poker. Surprisingly, the multi-agent learning techniques that allowed to reach these achievements do not take into account the actual behavior of the human player, potentially leading to an impressive gap in performances. In this paper, we address the problem of designing artificial agents that learn how to effectively exploit unknown human opponents while playing repeatedly against them in an online fashion. We study the case in which the agent's strategy during each repetition of the game is subject to constraints ensuring that the human's expected utility is within some lower and upper thresholds. Our framework encompasses several real-world problems, such as human engagement in repeated game playing and human education by means of serious games. As a first result, we formalize a set of linear inequalities encoding the conditions that the agent's strategy must satisfy at each iteration in order to do not violate the given bounds for the human's expected utility. Then, we use such formulation in an upper confidence bound algorithm, and we prove that the resulting procedure suffers from sublinear regret and guarantees that the constraints are satisfied with high probability at each iteration. Finally, we empirically evaluate the convergence of our algorithm on standard testbeds of sequential games.

This paper studies agents that learn an unknown human opponent's behavior through repeated play and use that knowledge to improve their own performance. The setting also imposes bounds on the human's expected utility during each repetition of the game.

Those bounds allow the framework to express applications where winning is not the only consideration, including continued player engagement and educational games. summary.tldr: An online game-playing algorithm learns to exploit opponents while respecting bounds on their expected utility with high probability.

title: Exploiting Opponents Under Utility Constraints in Sequential Games

abstract: Deep learning systems frequently fail at out-of-context (OOC) prediction, the problem of making reliable predictions on uncommon or unusual inputs or subgroups of the training distribution. To this end, a number of benchmarks for measuring OOC performance have been recently introduced. In this work, we introduce a framework unifying the literature on OOC performance measurement, and demonstrate how rich auxiliary information can be leveraged to identify candidate sets of OOC examples in existing datasets. We present NOOCh: a suite of naturally-occurring "challenge sets", and show how varying notions of context can be used to probe specific OOC failure modes. Experimentally, we explore the tradeoffs between various learning approaches on these challenge sets and demonstrate how the choices made in designing OOC benchmarks can yield varying conclusions.

paragraphs: This paper examines prediction on unusual examples or uncommon subgroups within a training distribution. These out-of-context cases can expose failures that ordinary evaluation does not adequately characterize. The authors introduce a framework that brings together existing approaches to measuring this behavior and makes the role of context explicit in benchmark construction.

They show how rich auxiliary information can identify candidate out-of-context examples already present in datasets. The resulting NOOCh suite consists of naturally occurring challenge sets. Different definitions of context produce sets that probe different kinds of failure, so the benchmark construction process becomes a way to ask more specific questions about model behavior.

The experiments compare tradeoffs among learning approaches across these challenge sets. They also show that benchmark design choices can lead to different conclusions about out-of-context performance. The practical message is that a result depends in part on which notion of unusualness the evaluation captures. NOOCh provides a framework and concrete challenge sets for examining those distinctions systematically.
summary.tldr: NOOCh uses naturally unusual dataset examples to show how definitions of context affect conclusions about model performance.

title: Identifying and Benchmarking Natural Out-of-Context Prediction Problems

abstract: We propose a simple architecture for deep reinforcement learning by embedding inputs into a learned Fourier basis and show that it improves the sample efficiency of both state-based and image-based RL. We perform infinite-width analysis of our architecture using the Neural Tangent Kernel and theoretically show that tuning the initial variance of the Fourier basis is equivalent to functional regularization of the learned deep network. That is, these learned Fourier features allow for adjusting the degree to which networks underfit or overfit different frequencies in the training data, and hence provide a controlled mechanism to improve the stability and performance of RL optimization. Empirically, this allows us to prioritize learning low-frequency functions and speed up learning by reducing networks' susceptibility to noise in the optimization process, such as during Bellman updates. Experiments on standard state-based and image-based RL benchmarks show clear benefits of our architecture over the baselines.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning must learn from training signals that can contain substantial optimization noise. This paper proposes embedding inputs into a learned Fourier basis before processing them with a network. The architecture improves sample efficiency in experiments involving both state observations and image observations.

An infinite-width analysis using the Neural Tangent Kernel explains how the initialization of these features affects learning. The authors show that changing the Fourier basis’s initial variance corresponds to functional regularization of the network. In particular, it controls the degree to which different frequencies in the data are underfit or overfit, providing a way to influence which patterns the network learns.

Empirically, the method prioritizes low-frequency functions and speeds learning by reducing susceptibility to noise, including noise arising during Bellman updates. Standard state-based and image-based reinforcement learning benchmarks show clear benefits over the evaluated baselines. The contribution connects a simple architectural choice to a theoretical account of frequency-dependent regularization, then demonstrates its usefulness for reinforcement learning optimization.
summary.tldr: Learned Fourier features regulate which frequencies a reinforcement learning network fits and improve sample efficiency on state-based and image-based benchmarks.

title: Functional Regularization for Reinforcement Learning via Learned Fourier Features

abstract: Robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) aim to handle changing or partially known system dynamics. To solve them, one typically resorts to robust optimization methods. However, this significantly increases computational complexity and limits scalability in both learning and planning. On the other hand, regularized MDPs show more stability in policy learning without impairing time complexity. Yet, they generally do not encompass uncertainty in the model dynamics. In this work, we aim to learn robust MDPs using regularization. We first show that regularized MDPs are a particular instance of robust MDPs with uncertain reward. We thus establish that policy iteration on reward-robust MDPs can have the same time complexity as on regularized MDPs. We further extend this relationship to MDPs with uncertain transitions: this leads to a regularization term with an additional dependence on the value function. We finally generalize regularized MDPs to twice regularized MDPs (R${}^2$ MDPs), i.e., MDPs with $\textit{both}$ value and policy regularization. The corresponding Bellman operators enable developing policy iteration schemes with convergence and robustness guarantees. It also reduces planning and learning in robust MDPs to regularized MDPs.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes address uncertainty in rewards or system dynamics, but solving them through robust optimization can increase computational costs. Regularization can stabilize policy learning without the same time-complexity penalty, yet ordinary regularized formulations generally do not capture uncertainty in transition dynamics. The paper develops a connection between these two approaches.

The authors first show that regularized MDPs are a special case of robust MDPs with uncertain rewards. This establishes that policy iteration for reward-robust problems can have the same time complexity as for regularized ones. Extending the relationship to uncertain transitions introduces a regularization term that also depends on the value function.

This leads to twice regularized MDPs, which regularize both the policy and the value function. Their Bellman operators support policy-iteration schemes with convergence and robustness guarantees. The result provides a way to express robust planning and learning through regularization, with value dependence accounting for transition uncertainty. The connection explains how computational tools for regularized problems can serve a broader uncertainty-aware purpose.
summary.tldr: Regularizing both policies and values connects efficient regularized MDP methods to robustness against reward and transition uncertainty.

title: Twice regularized MDPs and the equivalence between robustness and regularization

abstract: Continuous deep learning architectures enable learning of flexible probabilistic models for predictive modeling as neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and for generative modeling as continuous normalizing flows. In this work, we design a framework to decipher the internal dynamics of these continuous depth models by pruning their network architectures. Our empirical results suggest that pruning improves generalization for neural ODEs in generative modeling. We empirically show that the improvement is because pruning helps avoid mode-collapse and flatten the loss surface. Moreover, pruning finds efficient neural ODE representations with up to 98% less parameters compared to the original network, without loss of accuracy. We hope our results will invigorate further research into the performance-size trade-offs of modern continuous-depth models.

paragraphs: Continuous-depth models include neural ordinary differential equations and continuous normalizing flows, supporting predictive and generative modeling. This paper uses network pruning to investigate their internal dynamics. Removing parameters provides a way to examine how much model structure is needed and how model size relates to the behavior of the learned system.

The authors’ empirical results suggest that pruning can improve generalization for neural ODEs used in generative modeling. They present empirical evidence that the improvement comes from avoiding mode collapse and flattening the loss surface. These observations make pruning relevant to the quality of learning as well as to the number of parameters retained.

The framework also finds neural ODE representations with up to 98% fewer parameters than the original networks without losing accuracy in the reported experiments. This is an observed compression result rather than a universal guarantee for continuous-depth models. Together, the findings motivate closer study of performance-size trade-offs and show that substantial parameter removal can coexist with preserved accuracy and improved generalization in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Pruning continuous-depth models empirically improves generative generalization and can remove up to 98% of parameters without accuracy loss.

title: Sparse Flows: Pruning Continuous-depth Models

abstract: As deep networks begin to be deployed as autonomous agents, the issue of how they can communicate with each other becomes important. Here, we train two deep nets from scratch to perform realistic referent identification through unsupervised emergent communication. We show that the largely interpretable emergent protocol allows the nets to successfully communicate even about object types they did not see at training time. The visual representations induced as a by-product of our training regime, moreover, show comparable quality, when re-used as generic visual features, to a recent self-supervised learning model. Our results provide concrete evidence of the viability of (interpretable) emergent deep net communication in a more realistic scenario than previously considered, as well as establishing an intriguing link between this field and self-supervised visual learning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether two neural-network agents can develop useful, understandable communication while learning a visual task from scratch. The agents are trained through unsupervised emergent communication to identify referents: their interaction must convey which object is being referred to. The task provides a setting in which communication develops through the agents' shared objective.

The resulting communication protocol is largely interpretable, and the agents can use it successfully for object types absent from training. This is a meaningful test of the learned protocol because successful interaction extends beyond the object categories encountered while it developed. The finding offers evidence that emergent communication can support this kind of generalization in the studied scenario.

Training also produces visual representations that can be reused as generic features. Their quality is comparable to that of a recent self-supervised learning model. The communication task therefore yields a second useful outcome alongside the protocol itself: a reusable visual representation. Together, these findings connect learning to communicate with learning visual features and demonstrate their compatibility in a more realistic referent-identification setting.
summary.tldr: Two visual agents learn a largely interpretable communication protocol that transfers to unseen object types and produces reusable visual features.

title: Interpretable agent communication from scratch (with a generic visual processor emerging on the side)

abstract: We study Reinforcement Learning for partially observable systems using function approximation. We propose a new PO-bilinear framework, that is general enough to include models such as undercomplete tabular Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG), Predictive State Representations (PSRs), as well as a newly introduced model Hilbert Space Embeddings of POMDPs. Under this framework, we propose an actor-critic style algorithm that is capable to performing agnostic policy learning. Given a policy class that consists of memory based policies (i.e., policy that looks at a fixed-length window of recent observations), and a value function class that consists of functions taking both memory and future observations as inputs, our algorithm learns to compete against the best memory-based policy among the policy class. For certain examples such as undercomplete POMDPs and LQGs, by leveraging their special properties, our algorithm is even capable of competing against the globally optimal policy without paying an exponential dependence on the horizon.

paragraphs: In partially observable reinforcement learning, an agent must act without directly seeing the full state of its environment. This paper introduces a PO-bilinear framework for studying that problem with function approximation. It encompasses undercomplete tabular POMDPs, linear quadratic Gaussian systems, predictive state representations, and a newly introduced model based on Hilbert-space embeddings of POMDPs.

Within this framework, the authors develop an actor-critic-style algorithm for agnostic policy learning. The policy class uses a fixed-length window of recent observations as memory. The value-function class takes both memory and future observations as inputs. The resulting guarantee compares the learned policy with the best memory-based policy in the chosen class.

For particular systems, including undercomplete POMDPs and linear quadratic Gaussian models, additional structure strengthens that comparison to the globally optimal policy without exponential dependence on the horizon. These stronger results rely on properties of those examples. The framework's broader contribution is a shared way to analyze learning across several partially observed system models.
summary.tldr: A unified actor-critic framework learns competitive memory-based policies in partially observed systems, with stronger guarantees for specific model classes.

title: Provably Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Partially Observable Dynamical Systems

abstract: We study the loss surface of DNNs with $L_{2}$ regularization. Weshow that the loss in terms of the parameters can be reformulatedinto a loss in terms of the layerwise activations $Z_{\ell}$ of thetraining set. This reformulation reveals the dynamics behind featurelearning: each hidden representations $Z_{\ell}$ are optimal w.r.t.to an attraction/repulsion problem and interpolate between the inputand output representations, keeping as little information from theinput as necessary to construct the activation of the next layer.For positively homogeneous non-linearities, the loss can be furtherreformulated in terms of the covariances of the hidden representations,which takes the form of a partially convex optimization over a convexcone.This second reformulation allows us to prove a sparsity result forhomogeneous DNNs: any local minimum of the $L_{2}$-regularized losscan be achieved with at most $N(N+1)$ neurons in each hidden layer(where $N$ is the size of the training set). We show that this boundis tight by giving an example of a local minimum that requires $N^{2}/4$hidden neurons. But we also observe numerically that in more traditionalsettings much less than $N^{2}$ neurons are required to reach theminima.

paragraphs: This paper studies feature learning by changing the variables used to describe a neural network's training objective. Instead of expressing the L2-regularized loss only through weights, it rewrites the loss using the activations produced by each layer on the training set. This shifts attention toward the representations that the network learns.

In that formulation, hidden representations solve attraction-and-repulsion problems and interpolate between input and output representations. They preserve as little input information as needed to construct the next layer's activations. For positively homogeneous nonlinearities, a further reformulation uses representation covariances and yields a partially convex optimization problem over a convex cone.

The covariance view supports a sparsity theorem: any local-minimum loss value can be achieved using at most N(N+1) neurons per hidden layer, where N is the training-set size. An example requiring N²/4 neurons shows that quadratic dependence is necessary in general. Numerical observations in more traditional settings require far fewer than N² neurons, distinguishing worst-case representational requirements from the observed behavior of those examples.
summary.tldr: Rewriting regularized neural-network losses in terms of representations reveals feature-learning structure and quadratic worst-case bounds on hidden-layer width.

title: Feature Learning in $L_2$-regularized DNNs: Attraction/Repulsion and Sparsity

abstract: By inferring latent groups in the training data, recent works introduce invariant learning to the case where environment annotations are unavailable. Typically, learning group invariance under a majority/minority split is empirically shown to be effective in improving out-of-distribution generalization on many datasets. However, theoretical guarantee for these methods on learning invariant mechanisms is lacking. In this paper, we reveal the insufficiency of existing group invariant learning methods in preventing classifiers from depending on spurious correlations in the training set. Specifically, we propose two criteria on judging such sufficiency. Theoretically and empirically, we show that existing methods can violate both criteria and thus fail in generalizing to spurious correlation shifts. Motivated by this, we design a new group invariant learning method, which constructs groups with statistical independence tests, and reweights samples by group label proportion to meet the criteria. Experiments on both synthetic and real data demonstrate that the new method significantly outperforms existing group invariant learning methods in generalizing to spurious correlation shifts.

paragraphs: Group invariant learning tries to find reliable predictive mechanisms by dividing training data into inferred groups when environment labels are unavailable. Majority and minority splits have shown empirical promise. This paper asks whether such grouping actually prevents a classifier from using spurious correlations that may change outside the training distribution.

The authors introduce two criteria for assessing that sufficiency. Through theory and experiments, they show that existing methods can violate both criteria and consequently fail when spurious correlations shift. The finding identifies a gap between encouraging performance on some datasets and establishing that a grouping strategy removes reliance on unstable associations.

Their proposed method uses statistical independence tests to construct groups and reweights examples according to group label proportions to meet the criteria. Experiments on synthetic and real data show significant improvements over existing group invariant methods under spurious-correlation shifts. The contribution connects a diagnosis with a remedy: it examines why inferred groups can be inadequate and uses that analysis to guide both group construction and sample weighting.
summary.tldr: Criteria for resisting spurious correlations motivate independence-based grouping and sample reweighting that improve generalization under tested correlation shifts.

title: When Does Group Invariant Learning Survive Spurious Correlations?

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (Offline RL) suffers from the innate distributional shift as it cannot interact with the physical environment during training. To alleviate such limitation, state-based offline RL leverages a learned dynamics model from the logged experience and augments the predicted state transition to extend the data distribution. For exploiting such benefit also on the image-based RL, we firstly propose a generative model, S2P (State2Pixel), which synthesizes the raw pixel of the agent from its corresponding state. It enables bridging the gap between the state and the image domain in RL algorithms, and virtually exploring unseen image distribution via model-based transition in the state space. Through experiments, we confirm that our S2P-based image synthesis not only improves the image-based offline RL performance but also shows powerful generalization capability on unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains from previously collected experience without interacting with the physical environment. That restriction makes it difficult to learn about situations outside the recorded data. State-based approaches can use a learned dynamics model to predict additional transitions, but image-based agents need corresponding visual observations to benefit from that expansion.

S2P, or State2Pixel, supplies this connection through a generative model that synthesizes agent images from states. A dynamics model can predict transitions in state space, and S2P can turn those predicted states into pixels. This allows image-based learning to use virtual experience generated through the more compact state representation.

The authors report that S2P-based image synthesis improves image-based offline reinforcement learning and generalizes strongly to unseen tasks in their experiments. The contribution is a bridge between two forms of experience: states used for predicting transitions and images used by the learner. It gives model-based data augmentation a route into visual offline learning while preserving the setting’s reliance on logged experience during training.
summary.tldr: S2P converts predicted states into images so visual offline reinforcement learning can benefit from model-generated experience.

title: S2P: State-conditioned Image Synthesis for Data Augmentation in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Research in scene graph generation (SGG) usually considers two-stage models, that is, detecting a set of entities, followed by combining them and labeling all possible relationships. While showing promising results, the pipeline structure induces large parameter and computation overhead, and typically hinders end-to-end optimizations. To address this, recent research attempts to train single-stage models that are more computationally efficient. With the advent of DETR, a set-based detection model, one-stage models attempt to predict a set of subject-predicate-object triplets directly in a single shot. However, SGG is inherently a multi-task learning problem that requires modeling entity and predicate distributions simultaneously. In this paper, we propose Transformers with conditional queries for SGG, namely, TraCQ with a new formulation for SGG that avoids the multi-task learning problem and the combinatorial entity pair distribution. We employ a DETR-based encoder-decoder design and leverage conditional queries to significantly reduce the entity label space as well, which leads to 20% fewer parameters compared to state-of-the-art one-stage models. Experimental results show that TraCQ not only outperforms existing single-stage scene graph generation methods, it also beats state-of-the-art two-stage methods on the Visual Genome dataset, yet is capable of end-to-end training and faster inference.

We employ a DETR-based encoder-decoder design and leverage conditional queries to significantly reduce the entity label space as well, which leads to 20% fewer parameters compared to state-of-the-art one-stage models. Experimental results show that TraCQ not only outperforms existing single-stage scene graph generation methods, it also beats state-of-the-art two-stage methods on the Visual Genome dataset, yet is capable of end-to-end training and faster inference.

paragraphs: Scene graph generation describes an image through entities and relationships, such as subject-predicate-object triplets. Traditional systems first detect entities and then label relationships between possible pairs. This pipeline adds computation and parameters and makes joint optimization harder. Single-stage approaches predict triplets directly, but still face the challenge of learning entity and relationship distributions together.

The paper introduces TraCQ, a transformer model with conditional queries and a new formulation of scene graph generation. Built on a DETR-style encoder-decoder, it avoids the stated multitask learning problem and the combinatorial distribution over entity pairs. Conditional queries also reduce the entity label space, narrowing the prediction problem rather than treating every possible label combination in the same way.

TraCQ uses 20% fewer parameters than state-of-the-art single-stage models. On Visual Genome, experiments show that it outperforms existing single-stage approaches and state-of-the-art two-stage methods, while supporting end-to-end training and faster inference. The findings link the reformulation to improvements in both relationship prediction and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: TraCQ uses conditional transformer queries to improve scene graph prediction while reducing parameters and supporting faster inference.

title: Single-Stage Visual Relationship Learning using Conditional Queries

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have triggered the most recent and significant breakthroughs in computer vision. Their efficient designs are mostly guided by the indirect metric of computational complexity, i.e., FLOPs, which however has a clear gap with the direct metric such as throughput. Thus, we propose to use the direct speed evaluation on the target platform as the design principle for efficient ViTs. Particularly, we introduce LITv2, a simple and effective ViT which performs favourably against the existing state-of-the-art methods across a spectrum of different model sizes with faster speed. At the core of LITv2 is a novel self-attention mechanism, which we dub HiLo. HiLo is inspired by the insight that high frequencies in an image capture local fine details and low frequencies focus on global structures, whereas a multi-head self-attention layer neglects the characteristic of different frequencies. Therefore, we propose to disentangle the high/low frequency patterns in an attention layer by separating the heads into two groups, where one group encodes high frequencies via self-attention within each local window, and another group encodes low frequencies by performing global attention between the average-pooled low-frequency keys and values from each window and each query position in the input feature map. Benefiting from the efficient design for both groups, we show that HiLo is superior to the existing attention mechanisms by comprehensively benchmarking FLOPs, speed and memory consumption on GPUs and CPUs. For example, HiLo is 1.4× faster than spatial reduction attention and 1.6× faster than local window attention on CPUs. Powered by HiLo, LITv2 serves as a strong backbone for mainstream vision tasks including image classification, dense detection and segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/ziplab/LITv2.

title: Fast Vision Transformers with HiLo Attention

abstract: In single positive multi-label learning (SPML), only one of multiple positive labels is observed for each instance. The previous work trains the model by simply treating unobserved labels as negative ones, and designs the regularization to constrain the number of expected positive labels. However, in many real-world scenarios, the true number of positive labels is unavailable, making such methods less applicable. In this paper, we propose to solve SPML problems by designing a Label-Aware global Consistency (LAC) regularization, which leverages the manifold structure information to enhance the recovery of potential positive labels. On one hand, we first perform pseudo-labeling for each unobserved label based on its prediction probability. The consistency regularization is then imposed on model outputs to balance the fitting of identified labels and exploring of potential positive labels. On the other hand, by enforcing label-wise embeddings to maintain global consistency, LAC loss encourages the model to learn more distinctive representations, which is beneficial for recovering the information of potential positive labels. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets validate that the proposed method can achieve state-of-the-art performance for solving SPML tasks.

paragraphs: In single-positive multi-label learning, an example may have several correct labels, but training reveals only one. Treating every unobserved label as incorrect can therefore misrepresent the data. Earlier approaches counter this using constraints on the expected number of positive labels, but that number is unavailable in many practical settings.

The proposed Label-Aware global Consistency method, LAC, uses the structure of the data to help recover hidden positive labels. It first assigns provisional labels to unobserved entries using prediction probabilities. A consistency regularizer then balances fitting the labels already identified with exploring other potentially positive labels. This gives the model a way to reconsider missing labels instead of simply treating them as negatives.

LAC also constrains label-specific embeddings to maintain global consistency. The aim is to learn more distinctive representations that help expose additional positive-label information. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance for this setting. The findings support combining consistency in predictions with consistency in representations when training labels reveal only part of each example's true label set.
summary.tldr: LAC combines provisional labels and global consistency to recover missing positives when each training example has only one observed positive label.

title: Label-Aware Global Consistency for Multi-Label Learning with Single Positive Labels

abstract: We propose a projection-free conditional gradient-type algorithm for smooth stochastic multi-level composition optimization, where the objective function is a nested composition of $T$ functions and the constraint set is a closed convex set. Our algorithm assumes access to noisy evaluations of the functions and their gradients, through a stochastic first-order oracle satisfying certain standard unbiasedness and second-moment assumptions. We show that the number of calls to the stochastic first-order oracle and the linear-minimization oracle required by the proposed algorithm, to obtain an $\epsilon$-stationary solution, are of order $\mathcal{O}_T(\epsilon^{-2})$ and $\mathcal{O}_T(\epsilon^{-3})$ respectively, where $\mathcal{O}_T$ hides constants in $T$. Notably, the dependence of these complexity bounds on $\epsilon$ and $T$ are separate in the sense that changing one does not impact the dependence of the bounds on the other. For the case of $T=1$, we also provide a high-probability convergence result that depends poly-logarithmically on the inverse confidence level. Moreover, our algorithm is parameter-free and does not require any (increasing) order of mini-batches to converge unlike the common practice in the analysis of stochastic conditional gradient-type algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems whose objective is built by nesting several functions inside one another, while the solution must remain in a closed convex constraint set. The algorithm receives noisy function values and gradients. Its analysis assumes that these estimates satisfy specified unbiasedness and second-moment conditions.

The proposed method uses conditional-gradient updates, avoiding projection onto the constraint set and instead using linear minimization. To reach an epsilon-stationary solution, it requires stochastic-oracle calls scaling as epsilon to the power minus two and linear-minimization calls scaling as epsilon to the power minus three. Stationarity is the stated target, rather than a guarantee of finding a global optimum.

The number of nested functions affects hidden constants separately from the accuracy dependence, so adding levels does not change those powers of epsilon. The method is also parameter-free and converges without growing mini-batches. For a single function, the authors additionally establish a high-probability result with only polylogarithmic dependence on inverse confidence, extending the analysis beyond its general complexity bounds.
summary.tldr: A projection-free method optimizes noisy nested objectives with convergence bounds that separate accuracy requirements from nesting depth.

title: A Projection-free Algorithm for Constrained Stochastic Multi-level Composition Optimization

abstract: Despite the success achieved in neural abstractive summarization based on pre-trained language models, one unresolved issue is that the generated summaries are not always faithful to the input document.There are two possible causes of the unfaithfulness problem: (1) the summarization model fails to understand or capture the gist of the input text, and (2) the model over-relies on the language model to generate fluent but inadequate words.In this work, we propose a Faithfulness Enhanced Summarization model (FES), which is designed for addressing these two problems and improving faithfulness in abstractive summarization.For the first problem, we propose to use question-answering (QA) to examine whether the encoder fully grasps the input document and can answer the questions on the key information in the input. The QA attention on the proper input words can also be used to stipulate how the decoder should attend to the source.For the second problem, we introduce a max-margin loss defined on the difference between the language and the summarization model, aiming to prevent the overconfidence of the language model.Extensive experiments on two benchmark summarization datasets, CNN/DM and XSum, demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms strong baselines.The evaluation of factual consistency also shows that our model generates more faithful summaries than baselines.
