paragraphs: A generated summary can read fluently while misrepresenting its source document. This paper identifies two possible contributors: the model may fail to capture the document's key information, or it may rely too heavily on language-model preferences when choosing words. Faithfulness Enhanced Summarization addresses these possibilities through separate but connected training mechanisms.

First, question answering tests whether the encoder captures information needed to answer questions about the document's central content. Attention from this task also guides where the summary decoder should attend in the source. Second, a max-margin loss based on the difference between the language model and summarization model aims to prevent excessive confidence from the language model.

These components connect summary generation more closely to source understanding and source-directed attention. Experiments on CNN/DM and XSum show significant improvements over strong baselines, while factual-consistency evaluation finds more faithful summaries. The results support the proposed combination as a way to reduce unfaithfulness; the two motivating causes are presented as possible explanations, not an exhaustive account of every factual error.
summary.tldr: FES combines question-answering guidance with a loss that discourages language-model overconfidence to generate more faithful summaries.

title: Towards Improving Faithfulness in Abstractive Summarization

abstract: We propose a family of First Hitting Diffusion Models (FHDM), deep generative models that generate data with a diffusion process that terminates at a random first hitting time. This yields an extension of the standard fixed-time diffusion models that terminate at a pre-specified deterministic time. Although standard diffusion models are designed for continuous unconstrained data, FHDM is naturally designed to learn distributions on continuous as well as a range of discrete and structure domains. Moreover, FHDM enables instance-dependent terminate time and accelerates the diffusion process to sample higher quality data with fewer diffusion steps. Technically, we train FHDM by maximum likelihood estimation on diffusion trajectories augmented from observed data with conditional first hitting processes (i.e., bridge) derived based on Doob's $h$-transform, deviating from the commonly used time-reversal mechanism. We apply FHDM to generate data in various domains such as point cloud (general continuous distribution), climate and geographical events on earth (continuous distribution on the sphere), unweighted graphs (distribution of binary matrices), and segmentation maps of 2D images (high-dimensional categorical distribution). We observe considerable improvement compared with the state-of-the-art approaches in both quality and speed.

paragraphs: Standard diffusion generators end their sampling process at a predetermined time. First Hitting Diffusion Models instead stop at a random first hitting time, allowing the stopping point to depend on the individual sample. The paper uses this change to extend diffusion generation across continuous data and a range of discrete or structured domains.

Training follows a maximum-likelihood approach built around diffusion trajectories augmented from observed data. These trajectories use conditional first hitting processes, or bridges, derived through Doob's h-transform. This provides a different construction from the time-reversal mechanism commonly used in diffusion models. The variable stopping rule also enables acceleration, with the aim of producing higher-quality samples in fewer diffusion steps.

The authors apply the framework to point clouds, climate and geographical events on the Earth's sphere, unweighted graphs represented as binary matrices, and image segmentation maps with categorical entries. They report considerable improvements in both generation quality and speed over state-of-the-art approaches. The findings demonstrate the approach across substantially different kinds of output structure.
summary.tldr: First Hitting Diffusion Models use sample-dependent stopping times to generate continuous and structured data, with reported gains in quality and speed.

title: First Hitting Diffusion Models for Generating Manifold, Graph and Categorical Data

abstract: State space models (SSM) have recently been shown to be very effective as a deep learning layer as a promising alternative to sequence models such as RNNs, CNNs, or Transformers. The first version to show this potential was the S4 model, which is particularly effective on tasks involving long-range dependencies by using a prescribed state matrix called the HiPPO matrix. While this has an interpretable mathematical mechanism for modeling long dependencies, it also requires a custom representation and algorithm that makes the model difficult to understand and implement. On the other hand, a recent variant of S4 called DSS showed that restricting the state matrix to be fully diagonal can still preserve the performance of the original model when using a specific initialization based on approximating S4's matrix. This work seeks to systematically understand how to parameterize and initialize diagonal state space models. While it follows from classical results that almost all SSMs have an equivalent diagonal form, we show that the initialization is critical for performance. First, we explain why DSS works mathematically, as the diagonal approximation to S4 surprisingly recovers the same dynamics in the limit of infinite state dimension. We then systematically describe various design choices in parameterizing and computing diagonal SSMs, and perform a controlled empirical study ablating the effects of these choices. Our final model S4D is a simple diagonal version of S4 whose kernel computation requires just 3 lines of code and performs comparably to S4 in almost all settings, with state-of-the-art results in image, audio, and medical time-series domains, and 85\% average on the Long Range Arena benchmark.

title: On the Parameterization and Initialization of Diagonal State Space Models

abstract: The Yeo-Johnson (YJ) transformation is a standard parametrized per-feature unidimensional transformation often used to Gaussianize features in machine learning. In this paper, we investigate the problem of applying the YJ transformation in a cross-silo Federated Learning setting under privacy constraints. For the first time, we prove that the YJ negative log-likelihood is in fact convex, which allows us to optimize it with exponential search. We numerically show that the resulting algorithm is more stable than the state-of-the-art approach based on the Brent minimization method. Building on this simple algorithm and Secure Multiparty Computation routines, we propose SECUREFEDYJ, a federated algorithm that performs a pooled-equivalent YJ transformation without leaking more information than the final fitted parameters do. Quantitative experiments on real data demonstrate that, in addition to being secure, our approach reliably normalizes features across silos as well as if data were pooled, making it a viable approach for safe federated feature Gaussianization.

paragraphs: The Yeo-Johnson transformation adjusts individual features to make their distributions more Gaussian-like. Applying it consistently across organizations is challenging when data must remain separated for privacy. This paper develops a federated procedure that fits the transformation as if the organizations' data had been pooled.

The authors first prove that the Yeo-Johnson negative log-likelihood is convex. That result enables an optimization algorithm based on exponential search. Numerical comparisons show greater stability than the existing approach based on Brent minimization. This optimization result forms the computational foundation of the federated method.

SecureFedYJ combines the algorithm with secure multiparty computation. Its privacy guarantee is that the procedure reveals no more information than the final fitted parameters themselves, while producing a pooled-equivalent transformation. Experiments on real data show reliable feature normalization across silos, matching what pooling would achieve. The contribution brings both numerical stability and a specific information-leakage guarantee to a preprocessing step needed before federated model learning, without requiring that the underlying datasets be combined.
summary.tldr: SecureFedYJ fits pooled-equivalent feature transformations across data silos while revealing no more than the fitted parameters.

title: SecureFedYJ: a safe feature Gaussianization protocol for Federated Learning

abstract: Human teammates often form conscious and subconscious expectations of each other during interaction. Teaming success is contingent on whether such expectations can be met. Similarly, for an intelligent agent to operate beside a human, it must consider the human’s expectation of its behavior. Disregarding such expectations can lead to the loss of trust and degraded team performance. A key challenge here is that the human’s expectation may not align with the agent’s optimal behavior, e.g., due to the human’s partial or inaccurate understanding of the task domain. Prior work on explicable planning described the ability of agents to respect their human teammate’s expectations by trading off task performance for more expected or “explicable” behaviors. In this paper, we introduce Explicable Policy Search (EPS) to significantly extend such an ability to stochastic domains in a reinforcement learning (RL) setting with continuous state and action spaces. Furthermore, in contrast to the traditional RL methods, EPS must at the same time infer the human’s hidden expectations. Such inferences require information about the human’s belief about the domain dynamics and her reward model but directly querying them is impractical. We demonstrate that such information can be necessarily and sufficiently encoded by a surrogate reward function for EPS, which can be learned based on the human’s feedback on the agent’s behavior. The surrogate reward function is then used to reshape the agent’s reward function, which is shown to be equivalent to searching for an explicable policy. We evaluate EPS in a set of navigation domains with synthetic human models and in an autonomous driving domain with a user study. The results suggest that our method can generate explicable behaviors that reconcile task performance with human expectations intelligently and has real-world relevance in human-agent teaming domains.

The results suggest that EPS can reconcile performance with human expectations, providing evidence for its relevance to human-agent teamwork rather than assuming that task reward alone captures successful collaboration.
summary.tldr: EPS learns a surrogate reward from human feedback to balance task performance with expected behavior in continuous, stochastic environments.

title: Explicable Policy Search

abstract: Machine learning models will often fail when deployed in an environment with a data distribution that is different than the training distribution. When multiple environments are available during training, many methods exist that learn representations which are invariant across the different distributions, with the hope that these representations will be transportable to unseen domains. In this work, we present a nonparametric strategy for learning invariant representations based on the recently-proposed Nadaraya-Watson (NW) head. The NW head makes a prediction by comparing the learned representations of the query to the elements of a support set that consists of labeled data. We demonstrate that by manipulating the support set, one can encode different causal assumptions. In particular, restricting the support set to a single environment encourages the model to learn invariant features that do not depend on the environment. We present a causally-motivated setup for our modeling and training strategy and validate on three challenging real-world domain generalization tasks in computer vision.

In this work, we present a nonparametric strategy for learning invariant representations based on the recently-proposed Nadaraya-Watson (NW) head. The NW head makes a prediction by comparing the learned representations of the query to the elements of a support set that consists of labeled data. We demonstrate that by manipulating the support set, one can encode different causal assumptions. paragraphs: Models often perform poorly when deployment data differ from their training data. With multiple training environments, one strategy is to learn features that remain useful across environments. This paper pursues that goal using a nonparametric Nadaraya-Watson prediction head, which compares learned representations against a support set of labeled examples.

The main design choice concerns which examples enter that support set. The authors show that manipulating its composition can encode different causal assumptions. In particular, restricting it to one environment encourages the model to learn features that do not depend on the environment. Support-set construction thus becomes a way to shape representation learning.

The paper provides a causally motivated formulation of this modeling and training strategy and validates it on three challenging real-world computer vision tasks involving domain generalization. The approach matters because it places part of the invariance objective in the examples used to make predictions. The stated effect is encouragement toward invariant features, with empirical validation on the selected tasks, rather than a guarantee of successful transfer to every unseen distribution.
summary.tldr: Controlling a Nadaraya-Watson head's labeled support set encodes causal assumptions and can encourage representations that remain invariant across environments.

title: Learning Invariant Representations with a Nonparametric Nadaraya-Watson Head

abstract: We study the implicit bias of gradient flow on linear equivariant steerable networks in group-invariant binary classification. Our findings reveal that the parameterized predictor converges in direction to the unique group-invariant classifier with a maximum margin defined by the input group action. Under a unitary assumption on the input representation, we establish the equivalence between steerable networks and data augmentation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the improved margin and generalization bound of steerable networks over their non-invariant counterparts.

paragraphs: This paper examines how training selects a classifier when a network is designed to respect symmetries in its inputs. The setting is group-invariant binary classification with linear equivariant steerable networks. The authors study gradient flow, asking which predictor its optimization dynamics favor even without explicitly specifying that preference in the learning objective.

They show that the predictor’s direction converges to a unique group-invariant maximum-margin classifier. The relevant margin is defined through the group action on the input. Directional convergence identifies the classifier’s eventual orientation; the result concerns the preference induced by training within this symmetry-aware linear setting.

Under a unitary assumption on the input representation, the authors also establish an equivalence between steerable networks and data augmentation. They further obtain an improved margin and generalization bound relative to non-invariant counterparts. Together, these results connect architectural symmetry, the behavior of optimization, and theoretical generalization, while making the additional assumption behind the augmentation equivalence explicit.
summary.tldr: Gradient flow in linear steerable networks favors a group-invariant maximum-margin classifier, with an augmentation equivalence under a unitary representation assumption.

title: On the Implicit Bias of Linear Equivariant Steerable Networks

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers an appealing approach to real-world tasks by learning policies from pre-collected datasets without interacting with the environment. However, the performance of existing offline RL algorithms heavily depends on the scale and state-action space coverage of datasets. Real-world data collection is often expensive and uncontrollable, leading to small and narrowly covered datasets and posing significant challenges for practical deployments of offline RL. In this paper, we provide a new insight that leveraging the fundamental symmetry of system dynamics can substantially enhance offline RL performance under small datasets. Specifically, we propose a Time-reversal symmetry (T-symmetry) enforced Dynamics Model (TDM), which establishes consistency between a pair of forward and reverse latent dynamics. TDM provides both well-behaved representations for small datasets and a new reliability measure for OOD samples based on compliance with the T-symmetry. These can be readily used to construct a new offline RL algorithm (TSRL) with less conservative policy constraints and a reliable latent space data augmentation procedure. Based on extensive experiments, we find TSRL achieves great performance on small benchmark datasets with as few as 1% of the original samples, which significantly outperforms the recent offline RL algorithms in terms of data efficiency and generalizability. Code is available at:https://github.com/pcheng2/TSRL

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains decision-making policies from previously collected data without gathering new experience from the environment. Small datasets with narrow coverage can make this difficult. This paper uses time-reversal symmetry in system dynamics to extract more useful structure from limited data and to assess samples beyond the observed distribution.

Its Time-reversal symmetry enforced Dynamics Model links forward and reverse dynamics in a learned latent representation. Consistency between these directions serves two purposes: it supports useful representations from small datasets and supplies a reliability measure for out-of-distribution samples. The authors build TSRL around these properties, using less conservative policy constraints and data augmentation within the latent space.

The reported experiments show strong performance on reduced benchmark datasets containing as little as 1% of the original samples. TSRL significantly outperforms the compared recent offline reinforcement-learning algorithms in data efficiency and generalizability. These findings support the method’s use of dynamical consistency as both a learning signal and a guide for augmentation, with the performance claim tied to the evaluated small-data benchmarks.
summary.tldr: TSRL uses consistency between forward and reverse latent dynamics to improve offline reinforcement learning from small datasets.

title: Look Beneath the Surface: Exploiting Fundamental Symmetry for Sample-Efficient Offline RL

abstract: Off-policy Learning to Rank (LTR) aims to optimize a ranker from data collected by a deployed logging policy. However, existing off-policy learning to rank methods often make strong assumptions about how users generate the click data, i.e., the click model, and hence need to tailor their methods specifically under different click models. In this paper, we unified the ranking process under general stochastic click models as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and the optimal ranking could be learned with offline reinforcement learning (RL) directly. Building upon this, we leverage offline RL techniques for off-policy LTR and propose the Click Model-Agnostic Unified Off-policy Learning to Rank (CUOLR) method, which could be easily applied to a wide range of click models. Through a dedicated formulation of the MDP, we show that offline RL algorithms can adapt to various click models without complex debiasing techniques and prior knowledge of the model. Results on various large-scale datasets demonstrate that CUOLR consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art off-policy learning to rank algorithms while maintaining consistency and robustness under different click models.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning to rank improves a ranking system using interaction data collected by a previously deployed system. A difficulty is that observed clicks depend on how users respond to the displayed ranking. Existing approaches often assume a particular click-generation model, requiring their learning procedures to be redesigned when those assumptions change.

This paper formulates ranking under general stochastic click models as a Markov decision process. That reformulation makes it possible to learn the optimal ranking directly through offline reinforcement learning. The resulting method, CUOLR, uses a dedicated decision-process formulation to adapt across a wide range of click models without requiring prior knowledge of the click model or complex debiasing procedures.

Experiments on several large-scale datasets report that CUOLR consistently outperforms leading off-policy ranking algorithms while remaining consistent and robust across different click models. The contribution is a common learning formulation for settings that previously called for specialized methods. Its findings support using offline reinforcement-learning tools to connect logged user behavior with ranking improvement across the studied click-generation settings.
summary.tldr: CUOLR formulates ranking as an offline reinforcement-learning problem that adapts across click models without prior knowledge of their form.

title: Unified Off-Policy Learning to Rank: a Reinforcement Learning Perspective

abstract: One of the remarkable properties of robust computer vision models is that their input-gradients are often aligned with human perception, referred to in the literature as perceptually-aligned gradients (PAGs). Despite only being trained for classification, PAGs cause robust models to have rudimentary generative capabilities, including image generation, denoising, and in-painting. However, the underlying mechanisms behind these phenomena remain unknown. In this work, we provide a first explanation of PAGs via \emph{off-manifold robustness}, which states that models must be more robust off- the data manifold than they are on-manifold. We first demonstrate theoretically that off-manifold robustness leads input gradients to lie approximately on the data manifold, explaining their perceptual alignment. We then show that Bayes optimal models satisfy off-manifold robustness, and confirm the same empirically for robust models trained via gradient norm regularization, randomized smoothing, and adversarial training with projected gradient descent. Quantifying the perceptual alignment of model gradients via their similarity with the gradients of generative models, we show that off-manifold robustness correlates well with perceptual alignment. Finally, based on the levels of on- and off-manifold robustness, we identify three different regimes of robustness that affect both perceptual alignment and model accuracy: weak robustness, bayes-aligned robustness, and excessive robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/tml-tuebingen/pags.

paragraphs: Some robust image classifiers have input gradients that align with human perception, giving them rudimentary image generation and restoration abilities despite classification training. This paper explains that phenomenon through off-manifold robustness. The relevant condition is greater robustness to changes away from the data manifold than to changes along it.

The authors theoretically show that this condition makes input gradients lie approximately on the data manifold, explaining their perceptual alignment. They also show that Bayes-optimal models satisfy the condition. Empirical studies find it in robust models trained using gradient-norm regularization, randomized smoothing, and projected-gradient-descent adversarial training.

To measure alignment, the paper compares classifier gradients with gradients from generative models and finds a strong correlation with off-manifold robustness. It distinguishes weak, Bayes-aligned, and excessive robustness regimes according to on- and off-manifold behavior. These regimes affect both accuracy and gradient alignment. The findings therefore explain why the direction of robustness matters, rather than treating robustness as a single quantity whose increase always has the same effect.
summary.tldr: Greater robustness away from the data manifold explains why some classifiers have gradients aligned with human perception.

title: Which Models have Perceptually-Aligned Gradients? An Explanation via Off-Manifold Robustness

abstract: Item-side group fairness (IGF) requires a recommendation model to treat different item groups similarly, and has a crucial impact on information diffusion, consumption activity, and market equilibrium. Previous IGF notions only focus on the direct utility of the item exposures, i.e., the exposure numbers across different item groups. Nevertheless, the item exposures also facilitate utility gained from the neighboring users via social influence, called social utility, such as information sharing on the social media. To fill this gap, this paper introduces two social attribute-aware IGF metrics, which require similar user social attributes on the exposed items across the different item groups. In light of the trade-off between the direct utility and social utility, we formulate a new multi-objective optimization problem for training recommender models with flexible trade-off while ensuring controllable accuracy. To solve this problem, we develop a gradient-based optimization algorithm and theoretically show that the proposed algorithm can find Pareto optimal solutions with varying trade-off and guaranteed accuracy. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Recommendation fairness across item groups is often assessed by comparing how frequently each group is shown. This captures direct exposure but misses what can happen afterward. An item shown to a socially influential user may gain additional attention through sharing, so similar exposure counts can coexist with different opportunities for social reach.

The paper introduces two fairness metrics that account for the social attributes of users receiving recommendations. They require those attributes to be similar across the audiences exposed to different item groups. The authors then formulate recommendation training as a multi-objective optimization problem, allowing the balance between direct exposure utility and social utility to vary while controlling accuracy.

A gradient-based algorithm solves this formulation. The authors theoretically show that it can find Pareto-optimal solutions with different trade-offs and guaranteed accuracy: improving one objective cannot simply be achieved without sacrificing another at such a solution. Experiments on two real-world datasets support the approach. The contribution broadens fairness assessment to include who receives an exposure and its possible social consequences.
summary.tldr: The paper makes recommendation fairness sensitive to users' social attributes and provides controllable trade-offs between exposure, social utility, and accuracy.

title: Fairly Recommending with Social Attributes: A Flexible and Controllable Optimization Approach

abstract: To solve the spatial problems of mapping, localization and navigation, the mammalian lineage has developed striking spatial representations. One important spatial representation is the Nobel-prize winning grid cells: neurons that represent self-location, a local and aperiodic quantity, with seemingly bizarre non-local and spatially periodic activity patterns of a few discrete periods. Why has the mammalian lineage learnt this peculiar grid representation? Mathematical analysis suggests that this multi-periodic representation has excellent properties as an algebraic code with high capacity and intrinsic error-correction, but to date, synthesis of multi-modular grid cells in deep recurrent neural networks remains absent. In this work, we begin by identifying key insights from four families of approaches to answering the grid cell question: dynamical systems, coding theory, function optimization and supervised deep learning. We then leverage our insights to propose a new approach that elegantly combines the strengths of all four approaches. Our approach is a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework - including data, data augmentations, loss functions and a network architecture - motivated from a normative perspective, with no access to supervised position information. Without making assumptions about internal or readout representations, we show that multiple grid cell modules can emerge in networks trained on our SSL framework and that the networks generalize significantly beyond their training distribution. This work contains insights for neuroscientists interested in the origins of grid cells as well as machine learning researchers interested in novel SSL frameworks.

This paper investigates how such representations can emerge through learning, bringing together insights from dynamical systems, coding theory, function optimization, and supervised deep learning.

The authors construct a self-supervised framework comprising training data, augmentations, loss functions, and a network architecture. It is motivated by the purposes a spatial representation should serve and does not use supervised position information. The method also avoids assuming a particular form for the network’s internal representations or its readout representations.

The result demonstrates that multi-modular grid representations can emerge under the proposed self-supervised setup. This offers a learning-based perspective on their possible origins and a framework of interest for machine learning. It establishes emergence in the trained networks, without establishing that the same learning process explains biological development.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised spatial learning framework produces multiple grid-cell modules without position labels or prescribed internal representations.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Representations for Space Generates Multi-Modular Grid Cells

abstract: Real-world optimization problems often require black-box optimization with observation failure, where we can obtain the objective function value if we succeed, otherwise, we can only obtain a fact of failure. Moreover, this failure region can be complex by several latent constraints, whose number is also unknown. For this problem, we propose a failure-aware Gaussian process upper confidence bound (F-GP-UCB), which only requires a mild assumption for the observation failure that an optimal solution lies on an interior of a feasible region. Furthermore, we show that the number of successful observations grows linearly, by which we provide the first regret upper bounds and the convergence of F-GP-UCB. We demonstrate the effectiveness of F-GP-UCB in several benchmark functions, including the simulation function motivated by material synthesis experiments.

Moreover, this failure region can be complex by several latent constraints, whose number is also unknown. For this problem, we propose a failure-aware Gaussian process upper confidence bound (F-GP-UCB), which only requires a mild assumption for the observation failure that an optimal solution lies on an interior of a feasible region. paragraphs: Some black-box optimization problems return a numerical objective value only when an attempted evaluation succeeds. Otherwise, the optimizer learns just that the attempt failed. Several hidden constraints may determine these failures, and even the number of constraints can be unknown. This makes ordinary observations and failure feedback fundamentally different sources of information.

The paper proposes F-GP-UCB, a failure-aware version of Gaussian process upper confidence bound optimization. Its stated assumption about observation failure is that an optimal solution lies inside a feasible region. This condition provides the basis for analyzing progress despite a potentially complicated pattern of unsuccessful evaluations.

The authors prove that successful observations accumulate linearly, then use that result to establish regret upper bounds and convergence for the method. Regret measures the shortfall associated with optimization choices, so these bounds give a formal account of performance over time. Benchmark experiments, including a simulation motivated by material synthesis, demonstrate effectiveness in settings where failed evaluations are part of the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: F-GP-UCB optimizes despite failed evaluations and has convergence and regret guarantees when an optimum lies inside a feasible region.

title: Failure-Aware Gaussian Process Optimization with Regret Bounds

abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to train deep neural networks efficiently on streaming data while limiting the forgetting caused by new tasks. However, learning transferable knowledge with less interference between tasks is difficult, and real-world deployment of CL models is limited by their inability to measure predictive uncertainties. To address these issues, we propose handling CL tasks with neural processes (NPs), a class of meta-learners that encode different tasks into probabilistic distributions over functions all while providing reliable uncertainty estimates. Specifically, we propose an NP-based CL approach (NPCL) with task-specific modules arranged in a hierarchical latent variable model. We tailor regularizers on the learned latent distributions to alleviate forgetting. The uncertainty estimation capabilities of the NPCL can also be used to handle the task head/module inference challenge in CL. Our experiments show that the NPCL outperforms previous CL approaches. We validate the effectiveness of uncertainty estimation in the NPCL for identifying novel data and evaluating instance-level model confidence. Code is available at https://github.com/srvCodes/NPCL.

paragraphs: Continual learning must absorb new tasks without erasing knowledge from earlier ones. It also needs useful confidence estimates when making predictions. NPCL addresses these issues using neural processes, meta-learning models that represent tasks through probability distributions over functions, giving the model a way to express uncertainty alongside its predictions.

The method arranges task-specific modules in a hierarchical latent-variable model. Regularizers act on the learned latent distributions to reduce forgetting as learning proceeds. The same uncertainty estimates can help infer which task head or module to use, connecting confidence assessment to a practical decision inside a continual-learning system.

Experiments report stronger performance than previous continual-learning approaches. The authors also validate uncertainty estimation for identifying novel data and assessing confidence on individual examples. These results support combining knowledge retention with probabilistic task representations. The method's uncertainty output serves both to evaluate predictions and to help select the appropriate module, making uncertainty part of how the system operates.
summary.tldr: NPCL uses hierarchical neural processes to reduce forgetting, estimate predictive uncertainty, and help select task-specific modules during continual learning.

title: NPCL: Neural Processes for Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning

abstract: Supervised machine learning approaches have been increasingly used in accelerating electronic structure prediction as surrogates of first-principle computational methods, such as density functional theory (DFT). While numerous quantum chemistry datasets focus on chemical properties and atomic forces, the ability to achieve accurate and efficient prediction of the Hamiltonian matrix is highly desired, as it is the most important and fundamental physical quantity that determines the quantum states of physical systems and chemical properties. In this work, we generate a new Quantum Hamiltonian dataset, named as QH9, to provide precise Hamiltonian matrices for 2,399 molecular dynamics trajectories and 130,831 stable molecular geometries, based on the QM9 dataset. By designing benchmark tasks with various molecules, we show that current machine learning models have the capacity to predict Hamiltonian matrices for arbitrary molecules. Both the QH9 dataset and the baseline models are provided to the community through an open-source benchmark, which can be highly valuable for developing machine learning methods and accelerating molecular and materials design for scientific and technological applications. Our benchmark is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/divelab/AIRS/tree/main/OpenDFT/QHBench}.

Many available chemistry datasets emphasize properties or forces, while this paper focuses on predicting the Hamiltonian matrix, a central quantity determining quantum states and chemical properties. Accurate matrix prediction is therefore a valuable target for learned electronic-structure models.

The authors introduce QH9, a dataset built from QM9 molecules that supplies precise Hamiltonian matrices for 2,399 molecular dynamics trajectories and 130,831 stable molecular geometries. Including both trajectories and stable structures gives the benchmark distinct kinds of molecular configurations on which to study prediction.

The paper designs benchmark tasks involving varied molecules and reports evidence that current machine-learning models have the capacity to predict Hamiltonian matrices across molecules. The dataset and baseline models are released as an open-source benchmark to support further method development. Its practical contribution is a shared resource for evaluating this fundamental prediction target, with potential value for accelerating molecular and materials design. The benchmark evidence does not establish uniform accuracy for every possible molecule.
summary.tldr: QH9 provides Hamiltonian matrices, molecular benchmark tasks, and baseline models to advance learned electronic-structure prediction.

title: QH9: A Quantum Hamiltonian Prediction Benchmark for QM9 Molecules

abstract: Energy-based models are a simple yet powerful class of probabilistic models, but their widespread adoption has been limited by the computational burden of training them. We propose a novel loss function called Energy Discrepancy (ED) which does not rely on the computation of scores or expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo. We show that energy discrepancy approaches the explicit score matching and negative log-likelihood loss under different limits, effectively interpolating between both. Consequently, minimum energy discrepancy estimation overcomes the problem of nearsightedness encountered in score-based estimation methods, while also enjoying theoretical guarantees. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that ED learns low-dimensional data distributions faster and more accurately than explicit score matching or contrastive divergence. For high-dimensional image data, we describe how the manifold hypothesis puts limitations on our approach and demonstrate the effectiveness of energy discrepancy by training the energy-based model as a prior of a variational decoder model.

paragraphs: Energy-based models offer a flexible way to describe probability distributions, but training them can be computationally demanding. The paper introduces Energy Discrepancy, a loss function that avoids computing scores and avoids expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo. The aim is to make learning these models more practical while preserving a theoretical foundation.

The authors show that Energy Discrepancy approaches explicit score matching and negative log-likelihood in different limits. This connects two established training objectives within one formulation. They further show that minimizing it overcomes the nearsightedness associated with score-based estimation methods and provides theoretical guarantees.

Numerical experiments on low-dimensional distributions find faster and more accurate learning than explicit score matching or contrastive divergence. The paper also addresses a stated obstacle for high-dimensional images: the manifold hypothesis places limitations on this approach. In that setting, the authors demonstrate Energy Discrepancy by training an energy-based prior for a variational decoder model. The evidence therefore includes both direct low-dimensional density learning and a structured use within an image model.
summary.tldr: Energy Discrepancy trains energy-based models without scores or expensive MCMC and connects score matching with likelihood-based learning.

title: Energy Discrepancies: A Score-Independent Loss for Energy-Based Models

abstract: Compositional reasoning is a hallmark of human visual intelligence. Yet, despite the size of large vision-language models, they struggle to represent simple compositions by combining objects with their attributes. To measure this lack of compositional capability, we design Cola, a text-to-image retrieval benchmark to Compose Objects Localized with Attributes. To solve Cola, a model must retrieve images with the correct configuration of attributes and objects and avoid choosing a distractor image with the same objects and attributes but in the wrong configuration. Cola contains about 1.2k composed queries of 168 objects and 197 attributes on around 30K images. Our human evaluation finds that Cola is 83.33% accurate, similar to contemporary compositionality benchmarks. Using Cola as a testbed, we explore empirical modeling designs to adapt pre-trained vision-language models to reason compositionally. We explore 6 adaptation strategies on 2 seminal vision-language models, using compositionality-centric test benchmarks - Cola and CREPE. We find the optimal adaptation strategy is to train a multi-modal attention layer that jointly attends over the frozen pre-trained image and language features. Surprisingly, training multimodal layers on CLIP performs better than tuning a larger FLAVA model with already pre-trained multimodal layers. Furthermore, our adaptation strategy improves CLIP and FLAVA to comparable levels, suggesting that training multimodal layers using contrastive attribute-object data is key, as opposed to using them pre-trained. Lastly, we show that Cola is harder than a closely related contemporary benchmark, CREPE, since simpler fine-tuning strategies without multimodal layers suffice on CREPE, but not on Cola. However, we still see a significant gap between our best adaptation and human accuracy, suggesting considerable room for further research. Project page: https://cs-people.bu.edu/array/research/cola/

We explore 6 adaptation strategies on 2 seminal vision-language models, using compositionality-centric test benchmarks - Cola and CREPE. We find the optimal adaptation strategy is to train a multi-modal attention layer that jointly attends over the frozen pre-trained image and language features. Surprisingly, training multimodal layers on CLIP performs better than tuning a larger FLAVA model with already pre-trained multimodal layers. Furthermore, our adaptation strategy improves CLIP and FLAVA to comparable levels, suggesting that training multimodal layers using contrastive attribute-object data is key, as opposed to using them pre-trained. Lastly, we show that Cola is harder than a closely related contemporary benchmark, CREPE, since simpler fine-tuning strategies without multimodal layers suffice on CREPE, but not on Cola. However, we still see a significant gap between our best adaptation and human accuracy, suggesting considerable room for further research. Project page: https://cs-people.bu.edu/array/research/cola/

paragraphs: Recognizing objects and attributes separately does not establish that a model knows which attribute belongs to which object. Cola tests this distinction through text-to-image retrieval. A model must select an image with the requested arrangement while rejecting distractors containing the same objects and attributes in a different configuration.

The benchmark contains about 1,200 composed queries covering 168 objects and 197 attributes across roughly 30,000 images. The authors also compare six ways of adapting two pretrained vision-language models. Among the evaluated approaches, the best strategy trains a multimodal attention layer over frozen image and language features, allowing those features to be considered jointly.

Training such layers on CLIP performs better than tuning a larger FLAVA model that already contains pretrained multimodal layers. Both models reach comparable levels with the proposed adaptation, suggesting that training with contrastive attribute-object data matters substantially. Simpler tuning succeeds on CREPE but falls short on Cola, and the best adaptation still trails human accuracy. The findings identify both a useful adaptation strategy and a remaining compositional reasoning gap.
summary.tldr: Cola tests whether image retrieval models bind attributes to the correct objects and exposes a persistent gap despite effective multimodal adaptation.

title: Cola: A Benchmark for Compositional Text-to-image Retrieval

abstract: Gaussian Process Networks (GPNs) are a class of directed graphical models which employ Gaussian processes as priors for the conditional expectation of each variable given its parents in the network. The model allows the description of continuous joint distributions in a compact but flexible manner with minimal parametric assumptions on the dependencies between variables. Bayesian structure learning of GPNs requires computing the posterior over graphs of the network and is computationally infeasible even in low dimensions. This work implements Monte Carlo and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods to sample from the posterior distribution of network structures. As such, the approach follows the Bayesian paradigm, comparing models via their marginal likelihood and computing the posterior probability of the GPN features. Simulation studies show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in recovering the graphical structure of the network and provides an accurate approximation of its posterior distribution.

paragraphs: Gaussian Process Networks describe relationships among continuous variables using a directed graph. Each variable's expected value depends on its parent variables through a function given a Gaussian process prior. This allows flexible dependencies without requiring a tightly specified parametric form, while keeping the joint distribution organized through the network structure.

Learning that structure in a Bayesian way means assigning posterior probabilities to possible graphs. Computing this distribution directly is computationally infeasible even for relatively few variables. The paper implements Monte Carlo and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods that sample network structures, making it possible to approximate the posterior rather than enumerate it exactly.

The approach compares models through marginal likelihood and estimates posterior probabilities for features of the network. This supports reasoning about uncertainty in the learned structure, alongside identifying plausible graphs. In simulation studies, the method recovers network structure better than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms and accurately approximates its posterior distribution. The stated evidence therefore supports both structural recovery and uncertainty estimation in those simulations.
summary.tldr: Sampling-based Bayesian structure learning improves Gaussian Process Network recovery and approximates uncertainty over network graphs in simulation studies.

title: A Bayesian Take on Gaussian Process Networks

abstract: Score matching is an alternative to maximum likelihood (ML) for estimating a probability distribution parametrized up to a constant of proportionality. By fitting the ''score'' of the distribution, it sidesteps the need to compute this constant of proportionality (which is often intractable).While score matching and variants thereof are popular in practice, precise theoretical understanding of the benefits and tradeoffs with maximum likelihood---both computational and statistical---are not well understood. In this work, we give the first example of a natural exponential family of distributions such that the score matching loss is computationally efficient to optimize, and has a comparable statistical efficiency to ML, while the ML loss is intractable to optimize using a gradient-based method. The family consists of exponentials of polynomials of fixed degree, and our result can be viewed as a continuous analogue of recent developments in the discrete setting. Precisely, we show: (1) Designing a zeroth-order or first-order oracle for optimizing the maximum likelihood loss is NP-hard. (2) Maximum likelihood has a statistical efficiency polynomial in the ambient dimension and the radius of the parameters of the family. (3) Minimizing the score matching loss is both computationally and statistically efficient, with complexity polynomial in the ambient dimension.

paragraphs: Estimating a probability distribution can be difficult when its formula is known only up to a normalization constant that is expensive to compute. Score matching avoids computing that constant by fitting the distribution's score. This paper asks whether that computational advantage can be established rigorously without giving up the statistical efficiency associated with maximum likelihood.

The authors identify a natural exponential family whose members are exponentials of fixed-degree polynomials. For this family, they show that providing either function-value or first-order access for optimizing the maximum-likelihood loss is NP-hard. Maximum likelihood nevertheless has statistical efficiency polynomial in the ambient dimension and the radius of the family's parameters, separating statistical feasibility from computational accessibility.

For the same family, minimizing the score-matching loss is both computationally and statistically efficient, with complexity polynomial in the ambient dimension. The result supplies a concrete case where score matching offers a provable computational benefit while retaining comparable statistical efficiency. Its scope is the constructed family; the contribution establishes that this favorable tradeoff exists, rather than asserting it for all distribution-estimation problems.
summary.tldr: For a fixed-degree polynomial exponential family, score matching is efficiently optimizable with statistical efficiency comparable to computationally intractable maximum likelihood.

title: Provable benefits of score matching

abstract: Artificial intelligence for scientific discovery has recently generated significant interest within the machine learning and scientific communities, particularly in the domains of chemistry, biology, and material discovery. For these scientific problems, molecules serve as the fundamental building blocks, and machine learning has emerged as a highly effective and powerful tool for modeling their geometric structures. Nevertheless, due to the rapidly evolving process of the field and the knowledge gap between science ({\eg}, physics, chemistry, \& biology) and machine learning communities, a benchmarking study on geometrical representation for such data has not been conducted. To address such an issue, in this paper, we first provide a unified view of the current symmetry-informed geometric methods, classifying them into three main categories: invariance, equivariance with spherical frame basis, and equivariance with vector frame basis. Then we propose a platform, coined Geom3D, which enables benchmarking the effectiveness of geometric strategies. Geom3D contains 16 advanced symmetry-informed geometric representation models and 14 geometric pretraining methods over 52 diverse tasks, including small molecules, proteins, and crystalline materials. We hope that Geom3D can, on the one hand, eliminate barriers for machine learning researchers interested in exploring scientific problems; and, on the other hand, provide valuable guidance for researchers in computational chemistry, structural biology, and materials science, aiding in the informed selection of representation techniques for specific applications. The source code is available on \href{https://github.com/chao1224/Geom3D}{the GitHub repository}.

paragraphs: Machine learning for molecules, proteins, and crystalline materials depends on how geometric structure is represented. Its contribution combines an organizing framework with a platform for comparing methods across scientific tasks.

The authors group existing approaches into three categories: invariant methods, equivariant methods using spherical frame bases, and equivariant methods using vector frame bases. This classification provides a shared vocabulary for understanding different geometric strategies. Their Geom3D platform brings together 16 symmetry-informed representation models and 14 geometric pretraining methods across 52 tasks.

The intended value is a more accessible basis for benchmarking and informed method selection. The abstract presents this broad comparison infrastructure and taxonomy, rather than claiming that one representation strategy is universally best across the covered applications.
summary.tldr: Geom3D organizes symmetry-informed geometric learning and benchmarks 16 representation models and 14 pretraining methods across 52 scientific tasks.

title: Symmetry-Informed Geometric Representation for Molecules, Proteins, and Crystalline Materials

abstract: Vision and text have been fully explored in contemporary video-text foundational models, while other modalities such as audio and subtitles in videos have not received sufficient attention. In this paper, we resort to establish connections between multi-modality video tracks, including Vision, Audio, and Subtitle, and Text by exploring an automatically generated large-scale omni-modality video caption dataset called VAST-27M. Specifically, we first collect 27 million open-domain video clips and separately train a vision and an audio captioner to generate vision and audio captions. Then, we employ an off-the-shelf Large Language Model (LLM) to integrate the generated captions, together with subtitles and instructional prompts into omni-modality captions. Based on the proposed VAST-27M dataset, we train an omni-modality video-text foundational model named VAST, which can perceive and process vision, audio, and subtitle modalities from video, and better support various tasks including vision-text, audio-text, and multi-modal video-text tasks (retrieval, captioning and QA). Extensive experiments have been conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed VAST-27M corpus and VAST foundation model. VAST achieves 22 new state-of-the-art results on various cross-modality benchmarks.

paragraphs: Video understanding can draw on images, sound, and subtitles, yet video-text foundation models have emphasized vision and text. This paper develops a dataset and model that connect all three video tracks with textual descriptions. The goal is to make audio and subtitles more fully available to the model's understanding of video.

To build VAST-27M, the researchers collect 27 million open-domain clips and train separate vision and audio captioners. An existing large language model then integrates those generated descriptions with subtitles and instructional prompts to produce captions spanning the modalities. The resulting automatically generated corpus is used to train the VAST foundation model.

VAST processes visual, audio, and subtitle information and supports vision-text, audio-text, and multimodal video-text tasks, including retrieval, captioning, and question answering. The authors report 22 state-of-the-art results across cross-modality benchmarks. These findings support the usefulness of both the corpus and the model, demonstrating the practical value of training video-text systems with descriptions that incorporate multiple information streams.
summary.tldr: VAST combines vision, audio, and subtitles through a 27-million-video caption corpus, achieving 22 reported state-of-the-art cross-modality results.

title: VAST: A Vision-Audio-Subtitle-Text Omni-Modality Foundation Model and Dataset

abstract: Recent advances in prompt optimization have notably enhanced the performance of pre-trained language models (PLMs) on downstream tasks. However, the potential of optimized prompts on domain generalization has been under-explored. To explore the nature of prompt generalization on unknown domains, we conduct pilot experiments and find that (i) Prompts gaining more attention weight from PLMs’ deep layers are more generalizable and (ii) Prompts with more stable attention distributions in PLMs’ deep layers are more generalizable. Thus, we offer a fresh objective towards domain-generalizable prompts optimization named ''Concentration'', which represents the ''lookback'' attention from the current decoding token to the prompt tokens, to increase the attention strength on prompts and reduce the fluctuation of attention distribution.We adapt this new objective to popular soft prompt and hard prompt optimization methods, respectively. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our idea improves comparison prompt optimization methods by 1.42% for soft prompt generalization and 2.16% for hard prompt generalization in accuracy on the multi-source domain generalization setting, while maintaining satisfying in-domain performance. The promising results validate the effectiveness of our proposed prompt optimization objective and provide key insights into domain-generalizable prompts.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether optimized prompts remain useful when a language model encounters unfamiliar domains. The authors begin with pilot experiments showing two associations: prompts that receive stronger attention in deeper model layers generalize better, and prompts with more stable attention distributions in those layers also generalize better.

They turn these observations into an optimization objective called Concentration. It measures attention directed backward from the token currently being decoded to the prompt tokens. Optimization encourages stronger attention to the prompt while reducing fluctuations in how that attention is distributed. The objective is incorporated into both soft prompt and hard prompt optimization methods.

In experiments involving generalization from multiple source domains, the authors report accuracy improvements of 1.42% for soft prompts and 2.16% for hard prompts over the comparison methods. Performance within the original domains remains satisfactory. The results support using the model's attention to its instructions as an additional training signal when optimizing prompts for unfamiliar domains.
summary.tldr: Encouraging stronger, steadier attention to prompt tokens improves prompt generalization to unfamiliar domains in the reported experiments.

title: Concentrate Attention: Towards Domain-Generalizable Prompt Optimization for Language Models

abstract: The efficacy of large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks usually hinges on instruction tuning, which relies critically on the quality of training data. Unfortunately, collecting high-quality and diverse data is both expensive and time-consuming. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel Star-Agents framework, which automates the enhancement of data quality across datasets through multi-agent collaboration and assessment. The framework adopts a three-pronged strategy. It initially generates diverse instruction data with multiple LLM agents through a bespoke sampling method. Subsequently, the generated data undergo a rigorous evaluation using a dual-model method that assesses both difficulty and quality. Finaly, the above process evolves in a dynamic refinement phase, where more effective LLMs are prioritized, enhancing the overall data quality. Our empirical studies, including instruction tuning experiments with models such as Pythia and LLaMA, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Optimized datasets have achieved substantial improvements, with an average increase of 12\% and notable gains in specific metrics, such as a 40\% improvement in Fermi, as evidenced by benchmarks like MT-bench, Vicuna bench, and WizardLM testset. Codes will be released soon.

paragraphs: Star-Agents automates the improvement of instruction-tuning datasets. These datasets strongly influence how language models perform on downstream tasks, but collecting varied, high-quality examples is expensive. The framework uses multiple language-model agents to generate and assess instruction data, making dataset refinement an explicit collaborative process.

Its workflow has three parts. First, a specialized sampling method draws on multiple agents to produce diverse instructions. Second, a dual-model assessment evaluates the generated data for both difficulty and quality. Third, a dynamic refinement stage gives greater priority to models that prove more effective, adjusting the process as it proceeds.

The authors report an average improvement of 12% and a 40% improvement on Fermi. These findings support the value of jointly managing generation, evaluation, and model selection when improving training data. The reported gains concern models trained with the optimized datasets, linking the data workflow to downstream performance.
summary.tldr: Star-Agents uses collaborative generation, dual-model assessment, and adaptive refinement to improve instruction-tuning data.

title: Star-Agents: Automatic Data Optimization with LLM Agents for Instruction Tuning

abstract: LLMs are computationally expensive to pre-train due to their large scale.Model growth emerges as a promising approach by leveraging smaller models to accelerate the training of larger ones. However, the viability of these model growth methods in efficient LLM pre-training remains underexplored.This work identifies three critical $\underline{\textit{O}}$bstacles: ($\textit{O}$1) lack of comprehensive evaluation, ($\textit{O}$2) untested viability for scaling, and ($\textit{O}$3) lack of empirical guidelines.To tackle $\textit{O}$1, we summarize existing approaches into four atomic growth operators and systematically evaluate them in a standardized LLM pre-training setting.Our findings reveal that a depthwise stacking operator, called $G_{\text{stack}}$, exhibits remarkable acceleration in training, leading to decreased loss and improved overall performance on eight standard NLP benchmarks compared to strong baselines. Motivated by these promising results, we conduct extensive experiments to delve deeper into $G_{\text{stack}}$ to address $\textit{O}$2 and $\textit{O}$3.For $\textit{O}$2 (untested scalability), our study shows that $G_{\text{stack}}$ is scalable and consistently performs well, with experiments up to 7B LLMs after growth and pre-training LLMs with 750B tokens.For example, compared to a conventionally trained 7B model using 300B tokens, our $G_{\text{stack}}$ model converges to the same loss with 194B tokens, resulting in a 54.6\% speedup. We further address $\textit{O}$3 (lack of empirical guidelines) by formalizing guidelines to determine growth timing and growth factor for $G_{\text{stack}}$, making it practical in general LLM pre-training.We also provide in-depth discussions and comprehensive ablation studies of $G_{\text{stack}}$. Our code and pre-trained model are available at https://llm-stacking.github.io/.

paragraphs: Model growth aims to reduce language-model pretraining costs by using a smaller model to accelerate training of a larger one. This paper examines which growth operations work, whether their benefits persist at larger scales, and how to choose practical growth settings. It organizes existing methods into four basic operators and evaluates them in a standardized pretraining setup.

Depthwise stacking, called G_stack, emerges as particularly effective. It accelerates training, reduces loss, and improves overall performance across eight NLP benchmarks relative to strong baselines. Further experiments reach models with 7 billion parameters after growth and pretraining runs using 750 billion tokens, providing empirical evidence about scaling.

In one comparison, a grown 7-billion-parameter model reaches the loss of a conventionally trained model using 194 billion rather than 300 billion tokens, with a reported 54.6% speedup. The authors also formalize empirical guidelines for when to grow and how much growth to apply. These guidelines make the evaluated strategy more actionable for pretraining decisions.
summary.tldr: Systematic experiments identify depthwise stacking as an effective model-growth strategy for faster LLM pretraining and provide practical growth guidelines.

title: Stacking Your Transformers: A Closer Look at Model Growth for Efficient LLM Pre-Training

abstract: We present RelBench, a public benchmark for solving predictive tasks in relational databases with deep learning. RelBench provides databases and tasks spanning diverse domains, scales, and database dimensions, and is intended to be a foundational infrastructure for future research in this direction. We use RelBench to conduct the first comprehensive empirical study of graph neural network (GNN) based predictive models on relational data, as recently proposed by Fey et al. 2024. End-to-end learned GNNs are capable fully exploiting the predictive signal encoded in links between entities, marking a significant shift away from the dominant paradigm of manual feature engineering combined with tabular machine learning. To thoroughly evaluate GNNs against the prior gold-standard we conduct a user study, where an experienced data scientist manually engineers features for each task. In this study, GNNs learn better models whilst reducing human work needed by more than an order of magnitude. This result demonstrates the power of GNNs for solving predictive tasks in relational databases, opening up new research opportunities.

paragraphs: Relational databases contain predictive information both in individual records and in the links between entities. Conventional workflows often rely on a person to turn that information into features for a tabular model. RelBench provides a public benchmark for studying whether deep learning can learn useful predictions directly from relational data.

The benchmark includes databases and prediction tasks spanning different domains, scales, and database dimensions. The authors use it for a comprehensive empirical study of graph neural networks, which can learn from connections between entities. To compare these models with the established manual approach, they conduct a user study in which an experienced data scientist engineers features for each task.

In that study, the graph neural networks produce better predictive models while reducing required human work by more than an order of magnitude. This supports the usefulness of learning from relational links end to end in the evaluated tasks. RelBench also supplies shared infrastructure for further work, making both model performance and the effort involved in building predictive systems concrete subjects of comparison.
summary.tldr: RelBench shows graph neural networks outperforming manually engineered predictive workflows while requiring substantially less human work in its study.

title: RelBench: A Benchmark for Deep Learning on Relational Databases

abstract: The pursuit of high perceptual quality in image restoration has driven the development of revolutionary generative models, capable of producing results often visually indistinguishable from real data.However, as their perceptual quality continues to improve, these models also exhibit a growing tendency to generate hallucinations – realistic-looking details that do not exist in the ground truth images.Hallucinations in these models create uncertainty about their reliability, raising major concerns about their practical application.This paper investigates this phenomenon through the lens of information theory, revealing a fundamental tradeoff between uncertainty and perception. We rigorously analyze the relationship between these two factors, proving that the global minimal uncertainty in generative models grows in tandem with perception. In particular, we define the inherent uncertainty of the restoration problem and show that attaining perfect perceptual quality entails at least twice this uncertainty. Additionally, we establish a relation between distortion, uncertainty and perception, through which we prove the aforementioned uncertainly-perception tradeoff induces the well-known perception-distortion tradeoff.We demonstrate our theoretical findings through experiments with super-resolution and inpainting algorithms.This work uncovers fundamental limitations of generative models in achieving both high perceptual quality and reliable predictions for image restoration. Thus, we aim to raise awareness among practitioners about this inherent tradeoff, empowering them to make informed decisions and potentially prioritize safety over perceptual performance.

paragraphs: Generative image restoration can produce convincing visual details that were absent from the original image. Such hallucinations create a reliability problem: an output can look realistic while remaining uncertain as a reconstruction. This paper studies that tension through information theory, connecting perceptual quality to unavoidable restoration uncertainty.

The authors define the inherent uncertainty of a restoration problem and prove a tradeoff between uncertainty and perception. In their analysis, the lowest achievable uncertainty increases as perceptual quality improves. Attaining perfect perceptual quality requires at least twice the problem's inherent uncertainty, giving the tension a quantitative form rather than treating hallucinations solely as implementation errors.

The paper also relates distortion, uncertainty, and perception, showing how its uncertainty-perception tradeoff implies the established perception-distortion tradeoff. Experiments involving super-resolution and inpainting illustrate the theoretical findings. The implication is that visual realism and reliable recovery of the original image cannot always be improved together without compromise. For practitioners, the analysis provides a reason to consider restoration uncertainty explicitly when deciding how much to prioritize perceptual performance.
summary.tldr: The paper proves an uncertainty-perception tradeoff in generative restoration, including a lower bound of twice the inherent uncertainty at perfect perceptual quality.

title: Looks Too Good To Be True: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Hallucinations in Generative Restoration Models

abstract: Recently, there have been explorations of generalist segmentation models that can effectively tackle a variety of image segmentation tasks within a unified in-context learning framework. However, these methods still struggle with task ambiguity in in-context segmentation, as not all in-context examples can accurately convey the task information. In order to address this issue, we present SINE, a simple image $\textbf{S}$egmentation framework utilizing $\textbf{in}$-context $\textbf{e}$xamples. Our approach leverages a Transformer encoder-decoder structure, where the encoder provides high-quality image representations, and the decoder is designed to yield multiple task-specific output masks to eliminate task ambiguity effectively. Specifically, we introduce an In-context Interaction module to complement in-context information and produce correlations between the target image and the in-context example and a Matching Transformer that uses fixed matching and a Hungarian algorithm to eliminate differences between different tasks. In addition, we have further perfected the current evaluation system for in-context image segmentation, aiming to facilitate a holistic appraisal of these models. Experiments on various segmentation tasks show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: SINE addresses an ambiguity in teaching image segmentation through examples: an example does not always make clear which segmentation task the model should perform. A generalist model therefore needs to interpret the relationship between the example and the target image, as well as identify the relevant image regions.

The framework uses a Transformer encoder to produce image representations and a decoder that generates multiple task-specific masks. An In-context Interaction module supplements the example information and establishes correlations with the target image. A Matching Transformer then combines fixed matching with the Hungarian algorithm to handle differences between tasks. These components organize how example information becomes a segmentation output.

The authors also refine the evaluation system for in-context segmentation to support a more comprehensive assessment of generalist models. Experiments across several segmentation tasks support SINE's effectiveness. The contribution is a unified approach that explicitly addresses ambiguous task information through interaction, matching, and multiple output masks, alongside an evaluation framework intended to assess that broader capability.
summary.tldr: SINE uses example–image interactions and task-specific masks to address ambiguity in in-context image segmentation.

title: A Simple Image Segmentation Framework via In-Context Examples

abstract: Although Vision Transformers (ViTs) have recently advanced computer vision tasks significantly, an important real-world problem was overlooked: adapting to variable input resolutions. Typically, images are resized to a fixed resolution, such as 224x224, for efficiency during training and inference. However, uniform input size conflicts with real-world scenarios where images naturally vary in resolution. Modifying the preset resolution of a model may severely degrade the performance. In this work, we propose to enhance the model adaptability to resolution variation by optimizing the patch embedding. The proposed method, called Multi-Scale Patch Embedding (MSPE), substitutes the standard patch embedding with multiple variable-sized patch kernels and selects the best parameters for different resolutions, eliminating the need to resize the original image. Our method does not require high-cost training or modifications to other parts, making it easy to apply to most ViT models. Experiments in image classification, segmentation, and detection tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MSPE, yielding superior performance on low-resolution inputs and performing comparably on high-resolution inputs with existing methods.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers commonly process images resized to a preset resolution, although real images naturally have different dimensions. Changing a model's expected resolution can substantially reduce its performance. This paper addresses that problem at the patch-embedding stage, where image regions are converted into representations the Transformer can process.

Multi-Scale Patch Embedding replaces a standard patch embedding with several patch kernels of different sizes. It selects suitable parameters for different resolutions, allowing the original image to be used without resizing. The approach concentrates the adaptation in this input component and does not require changes to other parts of the model or costly training.

Experiments cover image classification, segmentation, and detection. The authors report stronger performance on low-resolution inputs and comparable performance on high-resolution inputs relative to existing methods. These findings support patch embedding as a useful place to handle resolution variation. The method is designed to apply readily to most Vision Transformers, connecting practical flexibility in input size with a localized architectural change.
summary.tldr: MSPE adapts Vision Transformers to varying image resolutions through multiple patch-kernel sizes, improving low-resolution performance without changing the rest of the model.

title: MSPE: Multi-Scale Patch Embedding Prompts Vision Transformers to Any Resolution

abstract: Lip reading aims at transforming the videos of continuous lip movement into textual contents, and has achieved significant progress over the past decade. It serves as a critical yet practical assistance for speech-impaired individuals, with more practicability than speech recognition in noisy environments. With the increasing interpersonal communications in social media owing to globalization, the existing monolingual datasets for lip reading may not be sufficient to meet the exponential proliferation of bilingual and even multilingual users. However, to our best knowledge, research on code-switching is only explored in speech recognition, while the attempts in lip reading are seriously neglected. To bridge this gap, we have collected a bilingual code-switching lip reading benchmark composed of Chinese and English, dubbed CSLR. As the pioneering work, we recruited 62 speakers with proficient foundations in bothspoken Chinese and English to express sentences containing both involved languages. Through rigorous criteria in data selection, CSLR benchmark has accumulated 85,560 video samples with a resolution of 1080x1920, totaling over 71.3 hours of high-quality code-switching lip movement data. To systematically evaluate the technical challenges in CSLR, we implement commonly-used lip reading backbones, as well as competitive solutions in code-switching speech for benchmark testing. Experiments show CSLR to be a challenging and under-explored lip reading task. We hope our proposed benchmark will extend the applicability of code-switching lip reading, and further contribute to the communities of cross-lingual communication and collaboration. Our dataset and benchmark are accessible at https://github.com/cslr-lipreading/CSLR.
