paragraphs: Lip reading converts visible mouth movements into text. Existing progress has largely relied on monolingual datasets, leaving a gap for people who switch languages within their speech. This paper introduces CSLR, a benchmark focused on Chinese-English code switching, to make that mixed-language setting available for systematic study.

The authors recruited 62 speakers proficient in both languages to produce sentences containing Chinese and English. After applying data-selection criteria, the collection contains 85,560 videos at a resolution of 1080 by 1920, covering more than 71.3 hours of lip movement. The dataset therefore provides a substantial collection centered specifically on language changes within the material being transcribed.

To establish benchmark results, the researchers evaluate commonly used lip-reading architectures and competitive methods from code-switching speech recognition. Their experiments identify CSLR as a difficult and underexplored task. The contribution is both the dataset and an initial evaluation framework: together, they support studying how visual speech systems handle bilingual utterances, extending evaluation beyond the monolingual settings emphasized by existing lip-reading resources.
summary.tldr: CSLR provides a large Chinese-English lip-reading dataset and benchmark for sentences that switch between languages.

title: Language Without Borders: A Dataset and Benchmark for Code-Switching Lip Reading

abstract: The reliable recovery and uncertainty quantification of a fixed effect function $\mu$ in a functional mixed model, for modeling population- and object-level variability in noisily observed functional data, is a notoriously challenging task: variations along the $x$ and $y$ axes are confounded with additive measurement error, and cannot in general be disentangled. The question then as to what properties of $\mu$ may be reliably recovered becomes important. We demonstrate that it is possible to recover the size-and-shape of a square-integrable $\mu$ under a Bayesian functional mixed model. The size-and-shape of $\mu$ is a geometric property invariant to a family of space-time unitary transformations, viewed as rotations of the Hilbert space, that jointly transform the $x$ and $y$ axes. A random object-level unitary transformation then captures size-and-shape preserving deviations of $\mu$ from an individual function, while a random linear term and measurement error capture size-and-shape altering deviations. The model is regularized by appropriate priors on the unitary transformations, posterior summaries of which may then be suitably interpreted as optimal data-driven rotations of a fixed orthonormal basis for the Hilbert space. Our numerical experiments demonstrate utility of the proposed model, and superiority over the current state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: When observations are noisy curves, variation along both axes can become entangled with measurement error. This makes recovering a population-level reference function and its uncertainty difficult, and the sources of variation cannot generally be separated. The paper instead asks which geometric properties of that function can be recovered reliably within a probabilistic model.

The authors show that the size-and-shape of a square-integrable reference function can be recovered under their Bayesian functional mixed model. Here, size-and-shape means a property unchanged by a specified family of joint transformations of the two axes. The model describes these transformations as rotations in a Hilbert space and uses random transformations to capture individual differences that preserve this property.

A separate random linear term and measurement error represent changes that alter size-and-shape. Priors regularize the transformations, whose posterior summaries can be interpreted as data-driven rotations of a fixed orthonormal basis. Numerical experiments demonstrate usefulness and superiority over the compared state-of-the-art approach. The recovery claim concerns this invariant geometric property under the proposed model.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian functional mixed model recovers an invariant size-and-shape property of a reference curve despite confounded variation and measurement noise.

title: Probabilistic size-and-shape functional mixed models

abstract: Neural models learn data representations that lie on low-dimensional manifolds, yet modeling the relation between these representational spaces is an ongoing challenge.By integrating spectral geometry principles into neural modeling, we show that this problem can be better addressed in the functional domain, mitigating complexity, while enhancing interpretability and performances on downstream tasks. To this end, we introduce a multi-purpose framework to the representation learning community, which allows to: (i) compare different spaces in an interpretable way and measure their intrinsic similarity; (ii) find correspondences between them, both in unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, and (iii) to effectively transfer representations between distinct spaces.We validate our framework on various applications, ranging from stitching to retrieval tasks, and on multiple modalities, demonstrating that Latent Functional Maps can serve as a swiss-army knife for representation alignment.

To this end, we introduce a multi-purpose framework to the representation learning community, which allows to: (i) compare different spaces in an interpretable way and measure their intrinsic similarity; (ii) find correspondences between them, both in unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, and (iii) to effectively transfer representations between distinct spaces.We validate our framework on various applications, ranging from stitching to retrieval tasks, and on multiple modalities, demonstrating that Latent Functional Maps can serve as a swiss-army knife for representation alignment.

paragraphs: Different neural models can organize information into different representation spaces, making it difficult to compare their internal features or transfer information between them. This paper approaches those spaces as low-dimensional manifolds and draws on spectral geometry to describe their relationships. Its central move is to work in the functional domain, providing another way to express alignment between spaces.

Latent Functional Maps is a framework with three related uses. It can compare representation spaces through interpretable measures of intrinsic similarity, find correspondences with either no supervision or weak supervision, and transfer representations between distinct spaces. Bringing these operations into one framework makes comparison and transfer parts of a shared geometric treatment rather than separate modeling problems.

The authors validate the framework across multiple modalities and applications, including stitching and retrieval tasks. They report reduced complexity, greater interpretability, and improved downstream performance from the functional approach. The stated findings support the framework's versatility across the tested uses, with its contribution centered on a common language for relating learned spaces.
summary.tldr: Latent Functional Maps uses spectral geometry to compare, align, and transfer neural representations across different spaces.

title: Latent Functional Maps: a spectral framework for representation alignment

abstract: Unsupervised semantic segmentation aims to discover groupings within images, capturing objects' view-invariance without external supervision. Moreover, this task is inherently ambiguous due to the varying levels of semantic granularity. Existing methods often bypass this ambiguity using dataset-specific priors. In our research, we address this ambiguity head-on and provide a universal tool for pixel-level semantic parsing of images guided by the latent representations encoded in self-supervised models. We introduce a novel algebraic approach that recursively decomposes an image into nested subgraphs, dynamically estimating their count and ensuring clear separation.The innovative approach identifies scene-specific primitives and constructs a hierarchy-agnostic tree of semantic regions from the image pixels. The model captures fine and coarse semantic details, producing a nuanced and unbiased segmentation. We present a new metric for estimating the quality of the semantic segmentation of discovered elements on different levels of the hierarchy. The metric validates the intrinsic nature of the compositional relations among parts, objects, and scenes in a hierarchy-agnostic domain. Our results prove the power of this methodology, uncovering semantic regions without prior definitions and scaling effectively across various datasets. This robust framework for unsupervised image segmentation proves more accurate semantic hierarchical relationships between scene elements than traditional algorithms. The experiments underscore its potential for broad applicability in image analysis tasks, showcasing its ability to deliver a detailed and unbiased segmentation that surpasses existing unsupervised methods.

paragraphs: An image can be divided meaningfully at several levels: small parts, whole objects, or larger scene regions. This makes unsupervised semantic segmentation ambiguous because there may be no single appropriate level of detail. The paper addresses that ambiguity by discovering nested regions instead of relying on dataset-specific choices about semantic granularity.

The method uses representations learned by self-supervised models to guide an algebraic procedure that recursively splits an image into subgraphs. It estimates how many subgraphs are needed and separates them clearly. The resulting tree organizes scene-specific primitives and semantic regions, capturing both fine and coarse structure without predefined region categories.

The authors also introduce a metric for evaluating discovered elements at different hierarchy levels and assessing compositional relationships among parts, objects, and scenes. Experiments across datasets report better semantic hierarchical relationships and segmentation than existing unsupervised approaches. The contribution is therefore both a way to construct multilevel image structure and a way to evaluate whether the discovered hierarchy reflects meaningful relationships between scene elements.
summary.tldr: A recursive graph-based method discovers nested semantic image regions without predefined categories and evaluates their relationships across hierarchy levels.

title: Hierarchy-Agnostic Unsupervised Segmentation: Parsing Semantic Image Structure

abstract: We introduce BioTrove, the largest publicly accessible dataset designed to advance AI applications in biodiversity. Curated from the iNaturalist platform and vetted to include only research-grade data, BioTrove contains 161.9 million images, offering unprecedented scale and diversity from three primary kingdoms: Animalia ("animals"), Fungi ("fungi"), and Plantae ("plants"), spanning approximately 366.6K species. Each image is annotated with scientific names, taxonomic hierarchies, and common names, providing rich metadata to support accurate AI model development across diverse species and ecosystems.We demonstrate the value of BioTrove by releasing a suite of CLIP models trained using a subset of 40 million captioned images, known as BioTrove-Train. This subset focuses on seven categories within the dataset that are underrepresented in standard image recognition models, selected for their critical role in biodiversity and agriculture: Aves ("birds"), Arachnida} ("spiders/ticks/mites"), Insecta ("insects"), Plantae ("plants"), Fungi ("fungi"), Mollusca ("snails"), and Reptilia ("snakes/lizards"). To support rigorous assessment, we introduce several new benchmarks and report model accuracy for zero-shot learning across life stages, rare species, confounding species, and multiple taxonomic levels.We anticipate that BioTrove will spur the development of AI models capable of supporting digital tools for pest control, crop monitoring, biodiversity assessment, and environmental conservation. These advancements are crucial for ensuring food security, preserving ecosystems, and mitigating the impacts of climate change. BioTrove is publicly available, easily accessible, and ready for immediate use.

paragraphs: BioTrove provides a large collection of biodiversity images curated from research-grade iNaturalist observations. It contains 161.9 million images covering approximately 366,600 species across animals, fungi, and plants. Scientific names, common names, and taxonomic hierarchies accompany the images, connecting visual examples to both individual species and broader biological categories.

The authors also release CLIP models trained on BioTrove-Train, a subset of 40 million captioned images. This subset emphasizes seven groups described as underrepresented in standard image recognition models: birds, arachnids, insects, plants, fungi, mollusks, and reptiles. The training resource therefore directs attention toward organisms relevant to biodiversity and agriculture that general image collections may represent less well.

New benchmarks assess zero-shot recognition across life stages, rare species, confounding species, and different taxonomic levels. These evaluations examine several distinct recognition challenges rather than treating species identification as one uniform task. The authors anticipate applications in pest control, crop monitoring, and conservation; those uses are presented as opportunities the publicly available data and models could support.
summary.tldr: BioTrove releases 161.9 million curated biodiversity images, specialized CLIP models, and benchmarks for recognizing diverse organisms.

title: BioTrove: A Large Curated Image Dataset Enabling AI for Biodiversity

abstract: Understanding how humans interact with each other is key to building realistic multi-human virtual reality systems. This area remains relatively unexplored due to the lack of large-scale datasets. Recent datasets focusing on this issue mainly consist of activities captured entirely in controlled indoor environments with choreographed actions, significantly affecting their diversity. To address this, we introduce Harmony4D, a multi-view video dataset for human-human interaction featuring in-the-wild activities such as wrestling, dancing, MMA,and more. We use a flexible multi-view capture system to record these dynamic activities and provide annotations for human detection, tracking, 2D/3D pose estimation, and mesh recovery for closely interacting subjects. We propose a novel markerless algorithm to track 3D human poses in severe occlusion and close interaction to obtain our annotations with minimal manual intervention. Harmony4D consists of 1.66 million images and 3.32 million human instances from more than 20 synchronized cameras with 208 video sequences spanning diverse environments and 24 unique subjects. We rigorously evaluate existing state-of-the-art methods for mesh recovery and highlight their significant limitations in modeling close interaction scenarios. Additionally, we fine-tune a pre-trained HMR2.0 model on Harmony4D and demonstrate an improved performance of 54.8% PVE in scenes with severe occlusion and contact. “Harmony—a cohesive alignment of human behaviors." Code and data are available at https://jyuntins.github.io/harmony4d/.

paragraphs: Harmony4D addresses the difficulty of understanding people who interact closely, including situations where their bodies overlap or obscure one another. Earlier interaction datasets are described as relying heavily on choreographed activities in controlled indoor environments. This dataset broadens the setting with activities such as wrestling, dancing, and mixed martial arts captured across diverse environments.

A flexible system of more than 20 synchronized cameras records the interactions. The dataset contains 208 video sequences, 24 subjects, 1.66 million images, and 3.32 million human instances. Its annotations support detection, tracking, pose estimation in two and three dimensions, and body-mesh recovery. A markerless tracking algorithm handles severe occlusion and close interaction to produce these annotations with minimal manual intervention.

Evaluations expose substantial limitations in existing mesh-recovery methods when people are in close contact. Fine-tuning a pretrained HMR2.0 model on Harmony4D yields a reported 54.8% improvement in PVE for scenes with severe occlusion and contact. The dataset consequently serves both as a demanding evaluation resource and as training material that improves performance in the interaction conditions it targets.
summary.tldr: Harmony4D provides richly annotated multiview videos of close human interactions, exposing reconstruction weaknesses and improving a model fine-tuned on its data.

title: Harmony4D: A Video Dataset for In-The-Wild Close Human Interactions

abstract: As AI systems pervade human life, ensuring that large language models (LLMs) make safe decisions remains a significant challenge. We introduce the Governance of the Commons Simulation (GovSim), a generative simulation platform designed to study strategic interactions and cooperative decision-making in LLMs. In GovSim, a society of AI agents must collectively balance exploiting a common resource with sustaining it for future use. This environment enables the study of how ethical considerations, strategic planning, and negotiation skills impact cooperative outcomes. We develop an LLM-based agent architecture and test it with the leading open and closed LLMs. We find that all but the most powerful LLM agents fail to achieve a sustainable equilibrium in GovSim, with the highest survival rate below 54%. Ablations reveal that successful multi-agent communication between agents is critical for achieving cooperation in these cases. Furthermore, our analyses show that the failure to achieve sustainable cooperation in most LLMs stems from their inability to formulate and analyze hypotheses about the long-term effects of their actions on the equilibrium of the group. Finally, we show that agents that leverage "Universalization"-based reasoning, a theory of moral thinking, are able to achieve significantly better sustainability. Taken together, GovSim enables us to study the mechanisms that underlie sustainable self-government with specificity and scale. We open source the full suite of our research results, including the simulation environment, agent prompts, and a comprehensive web interface.

paragraphs: GovSim is a simulation for studying whether language-model agents can cooperate over a shared resource. Each agent participates in a society that must balance taking resources now with keeping enough available for the future. The setting brings strategic planning, negotiation, and ethical reasoning into the same repeated decision problem.

The authors build an agent architecture and test leading open and closed language models. All but the most powerful agents fail to reach a sustainable equilibrium, and even the highest reported survival rate remains below 54%. Ablation experiments indicate that successful communication between agents is critical to cooperation in these tested cases.

The analysis links many failures to difficulty forming and assessing hypotheses about how present actions affect the group over time. Agents using Universalization-based moral reasoning achieve significantly better sustainability. The contribution is therefore both a testing environment and evidence about mechanisms associated with cooperation. The released environment, prompts, results, and interface support further investigation of sustainable self-government among agents.
summary.tldr: GovSim exposes widespread failures of sustainable cooperation among tested LLM agents and finds improvements from communication and Universalization-based reasoning.

title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents

abstract: Images are increasingly becoming the currency for documenting biodiversity on the planet, providing novel opportunities for accelerating scientific discoveries in the field of organismal biology, especially with the advent of large vision-language models (VLMs). We ask if pre-trained VLMs can aid scientists in answering a range of biologically relevant questions without any additional fine-tuning. In this paper, we evaluate the effectiveness of $12$ state-of-the-art (SOTA) VLMs in the field of organismal biology using a novel dataset, VLM4Bio, consisting of $469K$ question-answer pairs involving $30K$ images from three groups of organisms: fishes, birds, and butterflies, covering five biologically relevant tasks. We also explore the effects of applying prompting techniques and tests for reasoning hallucination on the performance of VLMs, shedding new light on the capabilities of current SOTA VLMs in answering biologically relevant questions using images.

paragraphs: VLM4Bio asks whether pretrained vision-language models can help scientists answer biological questions from images without further fine-tuning. As images become an increasingly important record of biodiversity, the ability to interpret them could support organismal research. The paper turns this possibility into an evaluation problem focused on biologically relevant questions.

The benchmark contains 469,000 question-answer pairs associated with 30,000 images of fishes, birds, and butterflies. It covers five biological tasks and is used to assess 12 state-of-the-art vision-language models. This provides a shared collection for examining how existing models handle biological image questions across several organism groups and task types.

The study also explores prompting techniques and tests for reasoning hallucination, examining more than whether a model can produce an answer. These analyses investigate how prompting affects performance and whether the reasoning accompanying responses is problematic. The contribution is a domain-focused dataset and comparative evaluation that sheds light on pretrained models’ capabilities for image-based biological inquiry under the stated no-additional-fine-tuning setting.
summary.tldr: VLM4Bio evaluates 12 pretrained vision-language models on biological image questions, including prompting effects and reasoning hallucinations.

title: VLM4Bio: A Benchmark Dataset to Evaluate Pretrained Vision-Language Models for Trait Discovery from Biological Images

abstract: Different from classical one-model-fits-all strategy, individualized models allow parameters to vary across samples and are gaining popularity in various fields, particularly in personalized medicine. Motivated by medical imaging analysis, this paper introduces a novel individualized modeling framework for matrix-valued data that does not require additional information on sample similarity for the individualized coefficients. Under our framework, the model individualization stems from an optimal internal relation map within the samples themselves. We refer to the proposed method as Attention boosted Individualized Regression, due to its close connections with the self-attention mechanism. Therefore, our approach provides a new interpretation for attention from the perspective of individualized modeling. Comprehensive numerical experiments and real brain MRI analysis using an ADNI dataset demonstrated the superior performance of our model.

paragraphs: A conventional regression model uses one set of parameters for all samples. Individualized regression allows those parameters to vary between samples, making it relevant when a shared model cannot adequately describe individual differences. This paper develops that idea for matrix-valued data, motivated by medical imaging and personalized medicine.

The proposed framework derives individualization from an optimized map of relationships within the samples themselves. It does not require additional information specifying how similar different samples are for the individualized coefficients. This makes the internal structure of the supplied data the basis for adapting the model, rather than requiring a separate source of sample relationships.

The authors call the method Attention boosted Individualized Regression because its relationship map is closely connected to self-attention. That connection also offers an interpretation of attention as a way to construct individualized models. Numerical experiments and an analysis of brain MRI data from ADNI report superior performance, providing evidence for the framework in both experimental and medical-imaging settings.
summary.tldr: Attention boosted Individualized Regression learns sample-specific models for matrix data using internal relationships without additional sample-similarity information.

title: Attention boosted Individualized Regression

abstract: Neural collapse ($\mathcal{NC}$) is a phenomenon observed in classification tasks where top-layer representations collapse into their class means, which become equinorm, equiangular and aligned with the classifiers.These behaviors -- associated with generalization and robustness -- would manifest under specific conditions: models are trained towards zero loss, with noise-free labels belonging to balanced classes, which do not outnumber the model's hidden dimension.Recent studies have explored $\mathcal{NC}$ in the absence of one or more of these conditions to extend and capitalize on the associated benefits of ideal geometries.Language modeling presents a curious frontier, as \textit{training by token prediction} constitutes a classification task where none of the conditions exist: the vocabulary is imbalanced and exceeds the embedding dimension; different tokens might correspond to similar contextual embeddings; and large language models (LLMs) in particular are typically only trained for a few epochs.This paper empirically investigates the impact of scaling the architectures and training of causal language models (CLMs) on their progression towards $\mathcal{NC}$.We find that $\mathcal{NC}$ properties that develop with scale (and regularization) are linked to generalization.Moreover, there is evidence of some relationship between $\mathcal{NC}$ and generalization independent of scale.Our work thereby underscores the generality of $\mathcal{NC}$ as it extends to the novel and more challenging setting of language modeling.Downstream, we seek to inspire further research on the phenomenon to deepen our understanding of LLMs -- and neural networks at large -- and improve existing architectures based on $\mathcal{NC}$-related properties.Our code is hosted on GitHub: [`https://github.com/rhubarbwu/linguistic-collapse`](https://github.com/rhubarbwu/linguistic-collapse).

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a geometric pattern in classification models: representations concentrate around class means, and those means acquire regular relationships with one another and with the classifiers. This paper asks whether related behavior appears in causal language models, where predicting the next token also constitutes a classification task.

Language modeling departs from conditions associated with ideal neural collapse. Token frequencies are unbalanced, vocabulary size exceeds embedding dimension, different tokens can have similar contextual representations, and large models typically receive only a few training epochs. The researchers empirically examine how architecture scale and training affect the development of collapse-related properties in this more challenging setting.

They find that properties emerging with scale and regularization are linked to generalization. There is also evidence for some relationship between collapse and generalization independent of scale. These are empirical associations rather than a claim that collapse necessarily causes better performance. The findings extend the study of neural collapse to language modeling and motivate further investigation of its relevance to architecture design.
summary.tldr: The study finds neural-collapse properties in causal language models and empirical links between those properties and generalization.

title: Linguistic Collapse: Neural Collapse in (Large) Language Models

abstract: Despite recent advances in diffusion models, top-tier text-to-image (T2I) models still struggle to achieve precise spatial layout control, *i.e.* accurately generating entities with specified attributes and locations. Segmentation-mask-to-image (S2I) generation has emerged as a promising solution by incorporating pixel-level spatial guidance and regional text prompts. However, existing S2I methods fail to simultaneously ensure semantic consistency and shape consistency. To address these challenges, we propose Seg2Any, a novel S2I framework built upon advanced multimodal diffusion transformers (*e.g.* FLUX). First, to achieve both semantic and shape consistency, we decouple segmentation mask conditions into regional semantic and high-frequency shape components. The regional semantic condition is introduced by a Semantic Alignment Attention Mask, ensuring that generated entities adhere to their assigned text prompts. The high-frequency shape condition, representing entity boundaries, is encoded as an Entity Contour Map and then introduced as an additional modality via multi-modal attention to guide image spatial structure. Second, to prevent attribute leakage across entities in multi-entity scenarios, we introduce an Attribute Isolation Attention Mask mechanism, which constrains each entity’s image tokens to attend exclusively to themselves during image self-attention. To support open-set S2I generation, we construct SACap-1M, a large-scale dataset containing 1 million images with 5.9 million segmented entities and detailed regional captions, along with a SACap-Eval benchmark for comprehensive S2I evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Seg2Any achieves state-of-the-art performance on both open-set and closed-set S2I benchmarks, particularly in fine-grained spatial and attribute control of entities.

paragraphs: Segmentation masks specify where objects should appear, while regional text prompts describe what those objects should be. Seg2Any combines these inputs to address a persistent image-generation challenge: matching object shapes and semantic attributes simultaneously. The framework builds on multimodal diffusion transformers and separates the two kinds of guidance.

Regional semantics enter through an attention mask that connects entities to their assigned prompts. Shape information enters through an Entity Contour Map, which represents boundaries and is processed as an additional modality. A separate attribute-isolation mechanism restricts each entity's image tokens to attending within that entity during image self-attention, aiming to prevent attributes from leaking between objects.

The authors also introduce SACap-1M, with one million images, 5.9 million segmented entities, and detailed regional captions, plus the SACap-Eval benchmark. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on both open-set and closed-set mask-to-image benchmarks, especially for fine spatial and attribute control. These findings support treating boundaries, regional meaning, and inter-entity attribute separation as distinct components of controllable image generation.
summary.tldr: Seg2Any separates regional semantics, object contours, and attribute isolation to improve shape and semantic control in mask-guided image generation.

title: Seg2Any: Open-set Segmentation-Mask-to-Image Generation with Precise Shape and Semantic Control

abstract: Selective prediction [Dru13, QV19] models the scenario where a forecaster freely decides on the prediction window that their forecast spans. Many data statistics can be predicted to a non-trivial error rate *without any* distributional assumptions or expert advice, yet these results rely on that the forecaster may predict at any time. We introduce a model of Prediction with Limited Selectivity (PLS) where the forecaster can start the prediction only on a subset of the time horizon. We study the optimal prediction error both on an instance-by-instance basis and via an average-case analysis. We introduce a complexity measure that gives instance-dependent bounds on the optimal error. For a randomly-generated PLS instance, these bounds match with high probability.

paragraphs: Selective prediction gives a forecaster freedom to choose the time window covered by a forecast. Earlier results show that this flexibility can support nontrivial prediction accuracy for many statistics without distributional assumptions or expert advice. However, those results depend on the ability to begin predicting at any time. This paper examines what happens when that freedom is restricted.

The proposed Prediction with Limited Selectivity model allows prediction to start only at designated times within the overall horizon. The authors study the best achievable error for individual instances as well as through an average-case analysis. This separates the effect of a particular pattern of available start times from behavior across randomly generated instances.

The main tool is a complexity measure that yields instance-dependent bounds on optimal prediction error. For randomly generated instances, the bounds match with high probability. That qualified matching result gives a tight characterization in the stated random setting. More broadly, the work makes the availability of prediction opportunities an explicit part of understanding how accurate a selective forecaster can be.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes prediction error when forecasters can start only at selected times, with bounds that match with high probability for random instances.

title: Online Prediction with Limited Selectivity

abstract: Existing world models for autonomous driving struggle with long-horizon generation and generalization to challenging scenarios. In this work, we develop a model using simple design choices, and without additional supervision or sensors, such as maps, depth, or multiple cameras. We show that our model yields state-of-the-art performance, despite having only 469M parameters and being trained on 280h of video data. It particularly stands out in difficult scenarios like turning maneuvers and urban traffic. We test whether discrete token models possibly have advantages over continuous models based on flow matching. To this end, we set up a hybrid tokenizer that is compatible with both approaches and allows for a side-by-side comparison. Our study concludes in favor of the continuous autoregressive model, which is less brittle on individual design choices and more powerful than the model built on discrete tokens. Project page with code, model checkpoints and visualization can be found here: https://lmb-freiburg.github.io/orbis.github.io/

We test whether discrete token models possibly have advantages over continuous models based on flow matching. To this end, we set up a hybrid tokenizer that is compatible with both approaches and allows for a side-by-side comparison. Project page with code, model checkpoints and visualization can be found here: https://lmb-freiburg.github.io/orbis.github.io/

paragraphs: Driving world models need to generate plausible futures over extended periods, including difficult situations such as turns and urban traffic. This paper develops a model using simple design choices without extra supervision or sensors such as maps, depth, or multiple cameras. It reports state-of-the-art performance with 469 million parameters and training on 280 hours of video.

A central part of the study compares two ways to model the visual sequence: discrete tokens and continuous representations based on flow matching. To make a side-by-side comparison possible, the authors construct a hybrid tokenizer compatible with both approaches. This provides a shared representation mechanism for investigating whether discrete-token modeling offers an advantage.

The study instead favors the continuous autoregressive model. In the reported comparison, it is more capable and less sensitive to individual design choices than the discrete-token model. Its particularly strong performance on turning maneuvers and urban traffic connects that conclusion to challenging driving scenarios. The contribution combines an effective video-based world model with evidence about representation and generation choices within the evaluated setup.
summary.tldr: A video-based driving world model achieves strong long-horizon results, with a shared-tokenizer comparison favoring continuous autoregressive generation.

title: Overcoming Challenges of Long-Horizon Prediction in Driving World Models

abstract:
The canonical approach in generative modeling is to split model fitting into two blocks: define first how to sample noise (e.g. Gaussian) and choose next what to do with it (e.g. using a single map or flows). We explore in this work an alternative route that ties sampling and mapping. We find inspiration in moment measures, a result that states that for any measure $ho$, there exists a unique convex potential $u$ such that $ho=
abla u \sharp e^{-u}$. While this does seem to tie effectively sampling (from log-concave distribution $e^{-u}$) and action (pushing particles through $
abla u$), we observe on simple examples (e.g., Gaussians or 1D distributions) that this choice is ill-suited for practical tasks. We study an alternative factorization, where $ho$ is factorized as $
abla w^* \sharp e^{-w}$, where $w^\ast$ is the convex conjugate of a convex potential $w$. We call this approach conjugate moment measures, and show far more intuitive results on these examples. Because $
abla w^*$ is the Monge map between the log-concave distribution $e^{-w}$ and $ho$, we rely on optimal transport solvers to propose an algorithm to recover $w$ from samples of $ho$, and parameterize $w$ as an input-convex neural network. We also address the common sampling scenario in which the density of $ho$ is known only up to a normalizing constant, and propose an algorithm to learn $w$ in this setting.

paragraphs: Generative modeling commonly separates the choice of a noise distribution from the transformation that turns noise into data. This paper explores linking both choices through one convex function. Its starting point is moment measures, which connect sampling from a log-concave distribution with mapping samples through the gradient of the function defining that distribution.

The authors find that the direct moment-measure construction behaves poorly for practical purposes on simple examples, including Gaussians and one-dimensional distributions. They instead propose conjugate moment measures: sampling uses a convex potential w, while the mapping uses the gradient of its convex conjugate. This alternative gives more intuitive behavior on the examples they study.

The resulting mapping is an optimal transport map between the sampling distribution and the target. The authors use optimal transport solvers to learn the potential from target samples and represent it with an input-convex neural network. They also propose a learning algorithm for targets whose density is known only up to a normalizing constant, extending the construction to another common sampling setting.
summary.tldr: Conjugate moment measures link a generator's sampling distribution and transport map through a single learned convex potential.

title: Sample and Map from a Single Convex Potential: Generation using Conjugate Moment Measures

abstract: Machine unlearning has become a focal point in recent research, yet the specific area of feature unlearning has not been thoroughly explored. Feature unlearning involves the elimination of specific features' effects from an already trained model, presenting distinct challenges that are still not comprehensively addressed. This paper presents a novel and straightforward approach to feature unlearning that employs a tactical shuffling of the features designated for removal. By redistributing the values of the features targeted for unlearning throughout the original training dataset and subsequently fine-tuning the model with this shuffled data, our proposed method provides a theoretical guarantee for effective feature unlearning. Under mild assumptions, our method can effectively disrupt the established correlations between unlearned features and the target outcomes, while preserving the relationships between the remaining features and the predicted outcomes. Our empirical studies across various datasets,validate that our approach not only successfully removes the effects of specified features but also maintains the informational integrity of the remaining features while achieving a faster convergence rate.

paragraphs: Feature unlearning asks how to remove the influence of selected input features from a model that has already been trained. The challenge includes preserving the useful relationships carried by features that should remain. This paper proposes a simple procedure built around shuffling the values of the features targeted for removal.

The method redistributes those feature values across the original training dataset and then fine-tunes the model on the modified data. Shuffling disrupts the original correspondence between the selected features and target outcomes. Under mild assumptions, the authors provide a theoretical guarantee that the procedure can break those correlations while preserving relationships between the remaining features and predicted outcomes.

Empirical studies across multiple datasets report successful removal of the specified features’ effects, preservation of information from other features, and faster convergence. The contribution links a straightforward data modification to a conditional theoretical guarantee and experimental evidence. Its central idea is to make the targeted features lose their predictive association during fine-tuning while keeping the rest of the training signal useful.
summary.tldr: Shuffling selected features before fine-tuning can remove their influence while preserving other predictive relationships under mild assumptions.

title: Feature Unlearning: Theoretical Foundations and Practical Applications with Shuffling

abstract: LLM-agent systems often decompose high-level objectives into subtask dependency graphs, assuming that each subtask’s output is reliable and conditionally independent of others given its parent responses. However, this assumption frequently breaks during execution, as ground-truth responses are inaccessible, leading to inter-agent misalignment—failures caused by inconsistencies and coordination breakdowns among agents. To address this, we propose SeqCV, a dynamic framework for reliable execution under violated conditional independence. SeqCV executes subtasks sequentially, each conditioned on all prior verified responses, and performs consistency checks immediately after agents generate short token sequences. At each checkpoint, a token sequence is accepted only if it represents shared knowledge consistently supported across diverse LLM models; otherwise, it is discarded, triggering recursive subtask decomposition for finer-grained reasoning. Despite its sequential nature, SeqCV avoids repeated corrections on the same misalignment and achieves higher effective throughput than parallel pipelines. Across multiple reasoning and coordination tasks, SeqCV improves accuracy by up to 30\% over existing LLM-agent systems. Code is available at https://github.com/tmllab/2025_NeurIPS_SeqCV.

paragraphs: Multi-agent workflows often represent a task as a graph of dependent subtasks. This structure assumes that parent responses provide enough context to make other subtasks conditionally independent, and that their outputs are reliable. The paper argues that these assumptions frequently break during execution, producing inconsistencies and coordination failures when correct answers are unavailable for direct checking.

SeqCV responds by executing subtasks sequentially and conditioning each one on all previously verified responses. It checks consistency after short stretches of generated text. A stretch is accepted only when diverse language models consistently support it as shared knowledge. Otherwise, the system discards it and recursively divides the subtask into smaller reasoning steps.

The intended benefit is to catch misalignment before it propagates through the workflow. Although execution is sequential, the authors report higher effective throughput than parallel pipelines because SeqCV avoids repeatedly correcting the same inconsistency. Across the evaluated reasoning and coordination tasks, accuracy improves by up to 30% over existing agent systems. The findings connect productive throughput to the amount of corrective work, not simply the amount of parallel execution.
summary.tldr: SeqCV uses sequential execution and frequent cross-model consistency checks to reduce coordination failures in multi-agent reasoning.

title: Can Dependencies Induced by LLM-Agent Workflows Be Trusted?

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing effectiveness in Text-to-SQL tasks. However, another closely related problem, Cross-System SQL Translation (a.k.a., SQL-to-SQL), which adapts a query written for one database system (e.g., MySQL) into its equivalent one for another system (e.g., ClickHouse), is of great practical importance but remains underexplored. Existing SQL benchmarks are not well-suited for SQL-to-SQL evaluation, which (1) focus on a limited set of database systems (often just SQLite) and (2) cannot capture many system-specific SQL dialects (e.g., customized functions, data types, and syntax rules). Thus, in this paper, we introduce PARROT, a Practical And Realistic BenchmaRk for CrOss-System SQL Translation. PARROT comprises 598 translation pairs from 38 open-source benchmarks and real-world business services, specifically prepared to challenge system-specific SQL understanding (e.g., LLMS achieve lower than 38.53% accuracy on average). We also provide multiple benchmark variants, including PARROT-Diverse with 28,003 translation (for extensive syntax testing) and PARROT-Simple with 5,306 representative samples (for focused stress testing), covering 22 production-grade database systems. To promote future research, we release a public leaderboard and source code at: https://code4db.github.io/parrot-bench/.

paragraphs: Moving a SQL query between database systems requires preserving its meaning while adapting system-specific functions, data types, and syntax. This differs from generating SQL from a natural-language request. PARROT targets this translation problem, which existing SQL benchmarks poorly capture because they cover too few systems and too little dialect-specific behavior.

The core benchmark contains 598 translation pairs drawn from 38 open-source benchmarks and real-world business services. These pairs are prepared to challenge understanding of database-specific SQL. Two additional variants serve different evaluation needs: PARROT-Diverse provides 28,003 translations for broad syntax testing, while PARROT-Simple supplies 5,306 representative samples for focused stress testing.

The benchmark variants cover 22 production-grade database systems. Reported LLM results average below 38.53% accuracy, indicating that translating between SQL dialects remains difficult in this evaluation. By making system differences central to the task, PARROT provides a way to assess a practical capability that success on conventional text-to-SQL benchmarks may not adequately establish.
summary.tldr: PARROT tests SQL translation across database systems and exposes substantial difficulty with dialect-specific functions, types, and syntax.

title: PARROT: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs in Cross-System SQL Translation

abstract: We present DEPS, an end-to-end algorithm for discovering parameterized skills from expert demonstrations. Our method learns parameterized skill policies jointly with a meta-policy that selects the appropriate discrete skill and continuous parameters at each timestep. Using a combination of temporal variational inference and information-theoretic regularization methods, we address the challenge of degeneracy common in latent variable models, ensuring that the learned skills are temporally extended, semantically meaningful, and adaptable. We empirically show that learning parameterized skills from multitask expert demonstrations significantly improves generalization to unseen tasks. Our method outperforms multitask as well as skill learning baselines on both LIBERO and MetaWorld benchmarks. We also demonstrate that DEPS discovers interpretable parameterized skills, such as an object grasping skill whose continuous arguments define the grasp location.

Our method outperforms multitask as well as skill learning baselines on both LIBERO and MetaWorld benchmarks. paragraphs: A reusable robot skill can have both a discrete identity and continuous settings. Grasping, for example, can be one skill whose arguments specify where to grasp. DEPS learns this kind of structure directly from expert demonstrations, jointly discovering skill policies and a meta-policy that chooses the skill and its parameters at each timestep.

The learning procedure combines temporal variational inference with information-theoretic regularization. These components address degeneracy in latent-variable models, where the learned internal structure can fail to provide useful skills. The intended result is a collection of behaviors that extend over time, have recognizable meaning, and can adapt through their continuous parameters.

Experiments using multitask demonstrations show improved generalization to unseen tasks, with DEPS outperforming multitask and skill-learning baselines on LIBERO and MetaWorld. The authors also demonstrate interpretable learned skills, including grasping with continuous arguments that determine grasp location. Together, the findings connect the learned representation to both task performance and an understandable division between a behavior and its adjustable settings.
summary.tldr: DEPS learns reusable skills with continuous parameters from demonstrations, improving generalization to unseen robotic tasks.

title: Learning Parameterized Skills from Demonstrations

abstract: We propose Graph Consistency Regularization (GCR), a novel framework that injects relational graph structures, derived from model predictions, into the learning process to promote class-aware, semantically meaningful feature representations. Functioning as a form of *self-prompting*, GCR enables the model to refine its internal structure using its own outputs. While deep networks learn rich representations, these often capture noisy inter-class similarities that contradict the model's predicted semantics. GCR addresses this issue by introducing parameter-free *Graph Consistency Layers* (GCLs) at arbitrary depths. Each GCL builds a batch-level feature similarity graph and aligns it with a global, class-aware masked prediction graph, derived by modulating softmax prediction similarities with intra-class indicators. This alignment enforces that feature-level relationships reflect class-consistent prediction behavior, acting as a *semantic regularizer* throughout the network. Unlike prior work, GCR introduces a multi-layer, cross-space graph alignment mechanism with adaptive weighting, where layer importance is learned from graph discrepancy magnitudes. This allows the model to prioritize semantically reliable layers and suppress noisy ones, enhancing feature quality without modifying the architecture or training procedure. GCR is model-agnostic, lightweight, and improves semantic structure across various networks and datasets. Experiments show that GCR promotes cleaner feature structure, stronger intra-class cohesion, and improved generalization, offering a new perspective on learning from prediction structure.

title: Graph Your Own Prompt

abstract: In this paper, we study differentially private mechanisms for functions whose outputs lie in a Euclidean Jordan algebra. Euclidean Jordan algebras capture many important mathematical structures and form the foundation of linear programming, second-order cone programming, and semidefinite programming. Our main contribution is a generic Gaussian mechanism for such functions, with sensitivity measured in $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$, and $\ell_\infty$ norms. Notably, this framework includes the important case where the function outputs are symmetric matrices, and sensitivity is measured in the Frobenius, nuclear, or spectral norm. We further derive private algorithms for solving symmetric cone programs under various settings, using a combination of the multiplicative weights update method and our generic Gaussian mechanism. As an application, we present differentially private algorithms for semidefinite programming, resolving a major open question posed by [Hsu, Roth, Roughgarden, and Ullman, ICALP 2014].

paragraphs: This paper develops differential privacy methods for outputs belonging to Euclidean Jordan algebras. These mathematical structures provide a shared foundation for linear, second-order cone, and semidefinite programming. Working at this level lets the authors develop a common privacy mechanism for several important kinds of structured output, including symmetric matrices.

The main contribution is a generic Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity measured using three different norms. Sensitivity describes how much an output can change with a change in the underlying data. For symmetric matrices, the framework covers Frobenius, nuclear, and spectral norms. Supporting these different measures allows the privacy analysis to accommodate different ways of expressing changes in a matrix.

The authors then combine their mechanism with multiplicative weights updates to derive private algorithms for symmetric cone programs under several settings. A central application is differentially private semidefinite programming, which they identify as resolving a previously posed major open question. The work's value lies in connecting a general mathematical privacy framework to concrete optimization algorithms, rather than developing an isolated mechanism for only one output type.
summary.tldr: A general Gaussian privacy mechanism for Euclidean Jordan algebras yields private algorithms for symmetric cone and semidefinite programming.

title: Differential Privacy for Euclidean Jordan Algebra with Applications to Private Symmetric Cone Programming

abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as the next generation of models in robotics. However, despite leveraging powerful pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), existing end-to-end VLA systems often lose key capabilities during fine-tuning as the model adapts to specific robotic tasks. We argue that a generalizable VLA model should retain and expand upon the VLM's core competencies: 1) **Open-world reasoning** - the VLA should inherit the knowledge from VLM, i.e., recognize anything that the VLM can recognize, capable of solving math problems, possessing visual-spatial intelligence, 2) **Reasoning following** – effectively translating the open-world reasoning into actionable steps for the robot. In this work, we introduce **ChatVLA-2**, a novel mixture-of-expert VLA model coupled with a specialized three-stage training pipeline designed to preserve the VLM’s original strengths while enabling actionable reasoning. To validate our approach, we design a math-matching task wherein a robot interprets math problems written on a whiteboard and picks corresponding number cards from a table to solve equations. Remarkably, our method exhibits exceptional mathematical reasoning and OCR capabilities, despite these abilities not being explicitly trained within the VLA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the VLA possesses strong spatial reasoning skills, enabling it to interpret novel directional instructions involving previously unseen objects. Overall, our method showcases reasoning and comprehension abilities that significantly surpass state-of-the-art imitation learning methods such as OpenVLA, DexVLA, and $\pi_0$. This work represents a substantial advancement toward developing truly generalizable robotic foundation models endowed with robust reasoning capacities.

paragraphs: Robot models built from pretrained vision-language systems can lose useful capabilities when adapted to particular actions. ChatVLA-2 addresses the problem of preserving broad understanding while turning that understanding into robot behavior. The paper distinguishes recognizing and reasoning about the world from following that reasoning with appropriate physical steps.

Its approach combines a mixture-of-experts vision-language-action model with a specialized three-stage training process. The design aims to preserve the original vision-language model's strengths while developing actionable reasoning. To test this connection, the authors create a task where a robot reads mathematical problems on a whiteboard and selects number cards from a table to solve the equations.

They also show responses to new directional instructions involving previously unseen objects. The authors report stronger reasoning and comprehension than OpenVLA, DexVLA, and π0. These results support progress toward robots that carry pretrained understanding into physical tasks, while grounding the claim in the demonstrated capabilities.
summary.tldr: ChatVLA-2 preserves pretrained reasoning abilities and translates them into robot actions, including solving written math problems with number cards.

title: ChatVLA-2: Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Reasoning

abstract: The integration of logic programs with embedding models resulted in a class of neurosymbolic frameworks that jointly learn symbolic rules and representations for the symbols in the logic (constant or predicate). The key idea that enabled this integration was the differentiable relaxation of unification, the algorithm for variable instantiation during inference in logic programs. Unlike unification, its relaxed counterpart exploits the similarity between symbols in the embedding space to decide when two symbols are semantically equivalent. We show that this similarity between symbols violates the transitive law of equivalence, leading to undesirable side effects in learning and inference. To alleviate those side effects, we are the first to revamp the well-known possible world semantics of probabilistic logic programs into new semantics called equivalence semantics. In our semantics, a probabilistic logic program induces a probability distribution over all possible equivalence relations between symbols, instead of a probability distribution over all possible subsets of probabilistic facts. We propose a factorization of the equivalence distribution using latent random variables and characterize its expressivity. Additionally, we propose both exact and approximate techniques for reasoning in our semantics. Experiments on well-known benchmarks show that the equivalence semantics leads to neurosymbolic models with up to 42% higher results than state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: This paper examines a logical inconsistency in systems that combine symbolic rules with learned embeddings. Such systems can replace exact symbol matching with similarity in an embedding space. However, similarity does not necessarily behave like equivalence: one symbol can resemble a second, and the second a third, without the first resembling the third. The authors show that this failure of transitivity affects learning and inference.

Their solution changes what uncertainty means in a probabilistic logic program. Instead of assigning probabilities to different collections of facts, the proposed equivalence semantics assigns probabilities to complete equivalence relations among symbols. Each possible relation therefore provides a consistent account of which symbols count as equivalent.

The authors introduce a factorization using latent random variables, characterize what it can express, and develop exact and approximate reasoning methods. Benchmark experiments report results up to 42% higher than state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is both semantic and practical: it gives learned symbol matching a logically structured probabilistic foundation and reports improved neurosymbolic performance.
summary.tldr: The paper replaces potentially inconsistent embedding similarity with probability distributions over valid symbol equivalences, improving neurosymbolic reasoning results.

title: Embeddings as Probabilistic Equivalence in Logic Programs

abstract: Robust partially observable Markov decision processes (RPOMDPs) model sequential decision-making problems under partial observability, where an agent must be robust against a range of dynamics. RPOMDPs can be viewed as a two-player game between an agent, who selects actions, and nature, who adversarially selects the dynamics. Evaluating an agent policy requires finding an adversarial nature policy, which is computationally challenging. In this paper, we advance the evaluation of agent policies for RPOMDPs in three ways. First, we discuss suitable benchmarks. We observe that for some RPOMDPs, an optimal agent policy can be found by considering only subsets of nature policies, making them easier to solve. We formalize this concept of solvability and construct three benchmarks that are only solvable for expressive sets of nature policies. Second, we describe a new method to evaluate agent policies for RPOMDPs by solving an equivalent MDP. Third, we lift two well-known upper bounds from POMDPs to RPOMDPs, which can be used to efficiently approximate the optimality gap of a policy and serve as baselines. Our experimental evaluation shows that (1) our proposed benchmarks cannot be solved by assuming naive nature policies, (2) our method of evaluating policies is accurate, and (3) the upper bounds provide solid baselines for evaluation

paragraphs: Robust partially observable Markov decision processes model an agent that sees only part of its environment and must tolerate uncertain dynamics. The paper describes this as a game: the agent chooses actions, while an adversarial nature chooses dynamics. Evaluating a fixed agent policy requires finding a sufficiently challenging nature policy, which is computationally difficult.

The authors first examine benchmark difficulty. Some problems can be solved by considering only restricted subsets of nature policies, potentially making them easier than their formulation suggests. They formalize this notion and construct three benchmarks requiring expressive nature policies. They also introduce an evaluation method based on solving an equivalent MDP and extend two POMDP upper bounds to the robust setting.

Those upper bounds efficiently approximate a policy's optimality gap and provide evaluation baselines. Experiments find that naive nature policies cannot solve the proposed benchmarks, that the evaluation method is accurate, and that the bounds offer solid baselines. Together, these contributions strengthen both the tests used for robust policies and the tools for assessing their quality.
summary.tldr: The paper improves robust POMDP evaluation with demanding benchmarks, an equivalent-MDP method, and useful policy-quality bounds.

title: On Evaluating Policies for Robust POMDPs

abstract: We develop the first parameter-free algorithms for the Stochastically Extended Adversarial (SEA) model, a framework that bridges adversarial and stochastic online convex optimization. Existing approaches for the SEA model require prior knowledge of problem-specific parameters, such as the diameter of the domain $D$ and the Lipschitz constant of the loss functions $G$, which limits their practical applicability. Addressing this, we develop parameter-free methods by leveraging the Optimistic Online Newton Step (OONS) algorithm to eliminate the need for these parameters. We first establish a comparator-adaptive algorithm for the scenario with unknown domain diameter but known Lipschitz constant, achieving an expected regret bound of $\tilde{O}\big(\Vert u\Vert_2^2 + \Vert u\Vert_2(\sqrt{\sigma^2_{1:T}} + \sqrt{\Sigma^2_{1:T}})\big)$, where $u$ is the comparator vector and $\sigma^2_{1:T}$ and $\Sigma^2_{1:T}$ represent the cumulative stochastic variance and cumulative adversarial variation, respectively. We then extend this to the more general setting where both $D$ and $G$ are unknown, attaining the comparator- and Lipschitz-adaptive algorithm. Notably, the regret bound exhibits the same dependence on $\sigma^2_{1:T}$ and $\Sigma^2_{1:T}$, demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed methods even when both parameters are unknown in the SEA model.

paragraphs: Online optimization often involves both random variation and changes that can behave adversarially. The Stochastically Extended Adversarial model brings these sources of difficulty into one framework. Existing algorithms require advance knowledge of quantities such as the domain’s diameter and the Lipschitz constant describing how sharply losses can change.

The paper develops methods based on Optimistic Online Newton Step that remove these requirements in stages. First, it handles an unknown domain diameter while assuming the Lipschitz constant is known. The resulting expected-regret guarantee adapts to the comparator vector used to evaluate performance and depends on cumulative stochastic variance and cumulative adversarial variation.

The authors then extend the approach to the case where both quantities are unknown. The bound preserves the same dependence on the two cumulative variation measures. This matters because adaptation to unknown problem scales does not change that stated dependence. Here, parameter-free refers specifically to avoiding prior knowledge of these problem quantities, giving the SEA framework algorithms that can operate with less advance information.
summary.tldr: The paper gives SEA online-optimization algorithms that adapt without knowing domain diameter or loss Lipschitz constants in advance.

title: Parameter-free Algorithms for the Stochastically Extended Adversarial Model

abstract: Neural Probabilistic Circuits (NPCs), a new class of concept bottleneck models, comprise an attribute recognition model and a probabilistic circuit for reasoning. By integrating the outputs from these two modules, NPCs produce compositional and interpretable predictions. While offering enhanced interpretability and high performance on downstream tasks, the neural-network-based attribute recognition model remains a black box. This vulnerability allows adversarial attacks to manipulate attribute predictions by introducing carefully crafted subtle perturbations to input images, potentially compromising the final predictions. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the adversarial robustness of NPC and demonstrate that it only depends on the robustness of the attribute recognition model and is independent of the robustness of the probabilistic circuit. Moreover, we propose RNPC, the first robust neural probabilistic circuit against adversarial attacks on the recognition module. RNPC introduces a novel class-wise integration for inference, ensuring a robust combination of outputs from the two modules. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that RNPC exhibits provably improved adversarial robustness compared to NPC. Empirical results on image classification tasks show that RNPC achieves superior adversarial robustness compared to existing concept bottleneck models while maintaining high accuracy on benign inputs. The code is available at https://github.com/uiuctml/RNPC.

summary.tldr: RNPC changes how attribute recognition and probabilistic reasoning are combined to provably improve robustness against attacks on recognized attributes.

title: Understanding and Improving Adversarial Robustness of Neural Probabilistic Circuits

abstract: Agnostic learning of Boolean halfspaces is a fundamental problem in computational learning theory, but it is known to be computationally hard even for weak learning. Recent work \citep{chandrasekaran2024smoothed} proposed smoothed analysis as a way to bypass such hardness, but existing frameworks rely on additive Gaussian perturbations, making them unsuitable for discrete domains. We introduce a new smoothed agnostic learning framework for Boolean inputs, where perturbations are modeled via random bit flips. This defines a natural discrete analogue of smoothed optimality generalizing the Gaussian case. Under strictly subexponential assumptions on the input distribution, we give an efficient algorithm for learning halfspaces in this model, with runtime and sample complexity $\tilde{O}(n^{\mathrm{poly}(\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon})})$. Previously, such algorithms were known only with strong structural assumptions for the discrete hypercube—for example, independent coordinates or symmetric distributions. Our result provides the first computationally efficient guarantee for smoothed agnostic learning of halfspaces over the Boolean hypercube, bridging the gap between worst-case intractability and practical learnability in discrete settings.

paragraphs: Learning Boolean halfspaces means learning threshold-based classifiers on inputs made of bits. In the agnostic setting, this is computationally difficult even when the goal is only weak learning. The paper investigates whether smoothing the problem can make it tractable, while preserving the discrete nature of the inputs rather than perturbing them with additive Gaussian noise.

The authors define a smoothing framework based on random bit flips. This creates a discrete counterpart to smoothed optimality and allows them to analyze learning directly on the Boolean hypercube. Under strictly subexponential assumptions on the input distribution, they give an algorithm whose runtime and sample complexity are approximately n raised to a polynomial in 1/(σε), with logarithmic factors suppressed.

Earlier algorithms for this discrete setting required strong structure such as independent coordinates or symmetric distributions. The new result provides an efficient guarantee under the paper’s different distributional assumptions and smoothing model. It therefore establishes a conditional route around worst-case hardness, rather than removing that hardness for unrestricted Boolean learning problems.
summary.tldr: Random-bit-flip smoothing enables provably efficient agnostic learning of Boolean halfspaces under strictly subexponential input-distribution assumptions.

title: Smoothed Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces over the Hypercube

abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) have been proposed as a compromise between white-box and black-box models, aiming to achieve interpretability without sacrificing accuracy. The standard training procedure for CBMs is to predefine a candidate set of human-interpretable concepts, extract their values from the training data, and identify a sparse subset as inputs to a transparent prediction model. However, such approaches are often hampered by the tradeoff between exploring a sufficiently large set of concepts versus controlling the cost of obtaining concept extractions, resulting in a large interpretability-accuracy tradeoff. This work investigates a novel approach that sidesteps these challenges: BC-LLM iteratively searches over a potentially infinite set of concepts within a Bayesian framework, in which Large Language Models (LLMs) serve as both a concept extraction mechanism and prior. Even though LLMs can be miscalibrated and hallucinate, we prove that BC-LLM can provide rigorous statistical inference and uncertainty quantification. Across image, text, and tabular datasets, BC-LLM outperforms interpretable baselines and even black-box models in certain settings, converges more rapidly towards relevant concepts, and is more robust to out-of-distribution samples.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through human-readable concepts, allowing people to inspect the information behind a decision. Typically, developers first choose candidate concepts, extract them from examples, and select a small subset for a transparent predictor. Exploring more concepts can improve the model, but obtaining all those concept values becomes expensive.

BC-LLM replaces this fixed candidate list with an iterative search over a potentially unlimited concept space. Within a Bayesian framework, a large language model supplies both concept extractions and prior information. This lets concept discovery and statistical modeling work together as the search progresses, rather than requiring a broad set of extractions before choosing useful concepts.

The authors prove that the method can support rigorous statistical inference and uncertainty quantification despite language models being capable of hallucination and miscalibration. Evaluations cover images, text, and tabular data. BC-LLM outperforms interpretable baselines, surpasses black-box models in some settings, reaches relevant concepts faster, and shows greater robustness to out-of-distribution examples. These findings support adaptive concept discovery as a route toward useful, interpretable prediction.
summary.tldr: BC-LLM uses language models within Bayesian concept search to improve interpretable prediction while supporting rigorous uncertainty quantification.

title: Bayesian Concept Bottleneck Models with LLM Priors

abstract: We develop an analytical framework for understanding how the learned distribution evolves during diffusion model training. Leveraging the Gaussian equivalence principle, we derived exact solutions for the gradient-flow dynamics of weights in one or two layer linear or linear convolutional denoiser settings with arbitrary data, where linear networks converge along principal components, and convolutional networks converge along Fourier modes. Remarkably, these solutions allow us to derive the generated distribution in closed-form and its KL-divergence through training. These analytical results expose a pronounced \emph{spectral bias}, i.e. for both weights and generated distributions, the convergence time of a mode follows an inverse power law of its variance. Empirical experiments on both Gaussian and natural image datasets demonstrate that the power-law spectral bias—remain robust even when using deeper or convolutional architectures. Our results underscore the importance of the data covariance in dictating the order and rate at which diffusion models learn different modes of the data, providing potential explanations of why earlier stopping could lead to incorrect details in image generative model.
originalAbstract: We develop an analytical framework for understanding how the learned distribution evolves during diffusion model training. Leveraging the Gaussian equivalence principle, we derived exact solutions for the gradient-flow dynamics of weights in one or two layer linear or linear convolutional denoiser settings with arbitrary data, where linear networks converge along principal components, and convolutional networks converge along Fourier modes. Remarkably, these solutions allow us to derive the generated distribution in closed-form and its KL-divergence through training. These analytical results expose a pronounced \emph{spectral bias}, i.e. for both weights and generated distributions, the convergence time of a mode follows an inverse power law of its variance. Empirical experiments on both Gaussian and natural image datasets demonstrate that the power-law spectral bias—remain robust even when using deeper or convolutional architectures. Our results underscore the importance of the data covariance in dictating the order and rate at which diffusion models learn different modes of the data, providing potential explanations of why earlier stopping could lead to incorrect details in image generative model.

The resulting spectral bias has a precise form: the time needed for a mode to converge follows an inverse power law of its variance, so higher-variance modes converge faster.

Experiments on Gaussian data and natural images find that this power-law pattern remains robust with deeper or convolutional architectures. The exact solutions apply to the specified simplified settings, while the experiments support a broader empirical pattern. Together, the findings suggest how data covariance shapes learning order and offer a possible explanation for incorrect image details when training stops early.

title: An Analytical Theory of Spectral Bias in the Learning Dynamics of Diffusion Models

abstract: Training data attribution (TDA) is concerned with understanding model behavior in terms of the training data. This paper draws attention to the common setting where one has access only to the final trained model, and not the training algorithm or intermediate information from training. We reframe the problem in this "final-model-only" setting as one of measuring sensitivity of the model to training instances. To operationalize this reframing, we propose *further training*, with appropriate adjustment and averaging, as a gold standard method to measure sensitivity. We then unify existing gradient-based methods for TDA by showing that they all approximate the further training gold standard in different ways. We investigate empirically the quality of these gradient-based approximations to further training, for tabular, image, and text datasets and models. We find that the approximation quality of first-order methods is sometimes high but decays with the amount of further training. In contrast, the approximations given by influence function methods are more stable but surprisingly lower in quality.

paragraphs: Training data attribution seeks to connect a model's behavior to individual training examples. This paper focuses on a constrained but common situation: only the final trained model is available, with no access to the training algorithm or intermediate training information. It reframes attribution in this setting as measuring sensitivity to training instances.

To make that idea operational, the authors propose further training, combined with appropriate adjustments and averaging, as a reference procedure for measuring sensitivity. They then show that existing gradient-based attribution methods can be understood as different approximations to this same procedure. This creates a shared target against which methods can be interpreted and compared.
