Influence-function methods provide more stable approximations, yet their quality is surprisingly lower. These results distinguish stability from fidelity and clarify what different attribution methods measure when the original training process cannot be inspected.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies gradient-based data attribution as approximations to model sensitivity measured through further training of the final model.

title: Final-Model-Only Data Attribution with a Unifying View of Gradient-Based Methods

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture offers enhanced efficiency for Large Language Models (LLMs) with modularized computation, yet its inherent sparsity poses significant hardware deployment challenges, including memory locality issues, communication overhead, and inefficient computing resource utilization. Inspired by the modular organization of the human brain, we propose $\texttt{Mozart}$, a novel algorithm-hardware co-design framework tailored for efficient training of MoE-based LLMs on 3.5D wafer-scale chiplet architectures. On the algorithm side, $\texttt{Mozart}$ exploits the inherent modularity of chiplets and introduces: ($1$) an expert allocation strategy that enables efficient on-package all-to-all communication, and ($2$) a fine-grained scheduling mechanism that improves communication-computation overlap through streaming tokens and experts. On the architecture side, $\texttt{Mozart}$ adaptively co-locates heterogeneous modules on specialized chiplets with a 2.5D NoP-Tree topology and hierarchical memory structure. Evaluation across three popular MoE models demonstrates significant efficiency gains, enabling more effective parallelization and resource utilization for large-scale modularized MoE-LLMs.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models organize computation into modules, but their sparse execution creates hardware challenges. Mozart addresses these issues by designing the training algorithm and hardware organization together for 3.5D wafer-scale chiplet architectures.

A fine-grained scheduler streams tokens and experts to improve overlap between communication and computation. On the architecture side, it places different modules together on specialized chiplets using a 2.5D NoP-Tree topology and hierarchical memory structure.

These components coordinate where computation happens, how data moves, and when operations run. The design uses the modular structure of chiplets to support the modular structure of the model. Evaluation across three popular MoE models reports significant efficiency improvements, including more effective parallelization and resource utilization. The findings concern the combined algorithm–hardware framework for the targeted chiplet architecture.
summary.tldr: Mozart jointly designs expert placement, scheduling, and chiplet architecture to improve the efficiency of large-scale MoE training.

title: Mozart: Modularized and Efficient MoE Training on 3.5D Wafer-Scale Chiplet Architectures

abstract: Recent advancements in text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models have enabled high-fidelity and realistic video synthesis. However, current T2V models often struggle to generate physically plausible content due to their limited inherent ability to accurately understand physics. We found that while the representations within T2V models possess some capacity for physics understanding, they lag significantly behind those from recent video self-supervised learning methods. To this end, we propose a novel framework called {VideoREPA}, which distills physics understanding capability from video understanding foundation models into T2V models by aligning token-level relations. This closes the physics understanding gap and enables more physics-plausible generation. Specifically, we introduce the {Token Relation Distillation (TRD) loss}, leveraging spatio-temporal alignment to provide soft guidance suitable for finetuning powerful pre-trained T2V models—a critical departure from prior representation alignment (REPA) methods. To our knowledge, VideoREPA is the first REPA method designed for finetuning T2V models and specifically for injecting physical knowledge. Empirical evaluations show that VideoREPA substantially enhances the physics commonsense of baseline method, CogVideoX, achieving significant improvement on relevant benchmarks and demonstrating a strong capacity for generating videos consistent with intuitive physics. Code and more video results are available at https://videorepa.github.io/.

paragraphs: A generated video can look realistic while depicting motion or interactions that violate intuitive physics. The authors find that text-to-video diffusion models contain some physics-relevant information, but their representations lag behind those of recent self-supervised video-understanding models. VideoREPA aims to transfer that stronger understanding into an already pretrained video generator.

The method aligns relationships between tokens using a Token Relation Distillation loss. Its guidance spans space and time, encouraging the generator to learn relational structure from a video-understanding foundation model. The authors emphasize that this soft guidance is suitable for fine-tuning powerful pretrained text-to-video systems, distinguishing it from earlier representation-alignment approaches.

Experiments using CogVideoX report substantial improvements in physical commonsense and relevant benchmark performance, alongside examples of videos that better follow intuitive physics. The findings support relational alignment as a way to improve physical plausibility through knowledge transfer. The demonstrated benefit concerns the evaluated generator and settings: the contribution is an effective fine-tuning framework for injecting physics-relevant understanding, rather than a guarantee that generated videos always obey physical laws.
summary.tldr: VideoREPA transfers relational knowledge from video-understanding models to improve the physical plausibility of generated videos.

title: VideoREPA: Learning Physics for Video Generation through Relational Alignment with Foundation Models

abstract: The way humans interact with each other, including interpersonal distances, spatial configuration, and motion, varies significantly across different situations. To enable machines to understand such complex, context-dependent behaviors, it is essential to model multiple people in relation to the surrounding scene context. In this paper, we present a novel research problem to model the correlations between two people engaged in a shared interaction involving an object. We refer to this formulation as Human-Human-Object Interactions (HHOIs). To overcome the lack of dedicated datasets for HHOIs, we present a newly captured HHOIs dataset and a method to synthesize HHOI data by leveraging image generative models. As an intermediary, we obtain individual human-object interaction (HOIs) and human-human interaction (HHIs) from the HHOIs, and with these data, we train an text-to-HOI and text-to-HHI model using score-based diffusion model. Finally, we present a unified generative framework that integrates the two individual model, capable of synthesizing complete HHOIs in a single advanced sampling process. Our method extends HHOI generation to multi-human settings, enabling interactions involving more than two individuals. Experimental results show that our method generates realistic HHOIs conditioned on textual descriptions, outperforming previous approaches that focus only on single-human HOIs. Furthermore, we introduce multi-human motion generation involving objects as an application of our framework.

This paper formulates that task as Human-Human-Object Interaction generation and develops a text-conditioned framework that models people in relation to each other and the surrounding object.

To supply training material, the authors introduce a captured dataset and a method for synthesizing additional interaction data using image generative models. They extract human-object and human-human interactions as intermediate representations, then train separate text-conditioned score-based diffusion models for those two kinds of relationships. This decomposition lets each model learn one part of the larger interaction.

A unified sampling process combines the two models to generate complete interactions. The framework also extends to settings with more than two people and supports multi-human motion generation involving objects. Experiments report realistic text-conditioned outputs and improvements over earlier approaches focused on single-person human-object interactions. The findings support combining complementary relationship models to generate richer shared activities.
summary.tldr: The paper combines human-object and human-human diffusion models to generate text-described interactions involving multiple people and objects.

title: Learning to Generate Human-Human-Object Interactions from Textual Descriptions

abstract: Finetuning large language models (LLMs) enables user-specific customization but introduces critical safety risks: even a few harmful examples can compromise safety alignment. A common mitigation strategy is to update the model more strongly on examples deemed safe, while downweighting or excluding those flagged as unsafe. However, because safety context can shift within a single example, updating the model equally on both harmful and harmless parts of a response is suboptimal — an atomic treatment we term static safety shaping. In contrast, we propose dynamic safety shaping (DSS), a dynamic shaping framework that uses fine-grained safety signals to reinforce learning from safe segments of a response while suppressing unsafe content. To enable such fine-grained control during finetuning, we introduce a key insight: guardrail models, traditionally used for filtering, can be repurposed to evaluate partial responses, tracking how safety risk evolves throughout the response, segment by segment. This leads to the Safety Trajectory Assessment of Response (STAR), a token-level signal that enables shaping to operate dynamically over the training sequence. Building on this, we present ★DSS, a DSS method guided by STAR scores that robustly mitigates finetuning risks and delivers substantial safety improvements across diverse threats, datasets, and model families, all without compromising capability on intended tasks. We encourage future safety research to build on dynamic shaping principles for stronger mitigation against evolving finetuning risks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/poloclub/star-dss

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can weaken a language model’s safety alignment even when only a few training examples are harmful. A common defense assigns a safety weight to each complete example. This paper argues that such treatment is too coarse because a response can shift between harmless and harmful content as it unfolds.

Dynamic safety shaping instead adjusts learning within the response. The authors repurpose guardrail models to assess partial responses, tracking changes in risk segment by segment. This produces Safety Trajectory Assessment of Response, or STAR, a token-level signal that can guide how strongly different parts of the training sequence affect the model.

The resulting STAR-guided method reinforces learning from safe segments while suppressing unsafe content. Across the reported threats, datasets, and model families, it substantially improves safety without compromising capability on the intended tasks. The findings support using the evolving safety context of a response during fine-tuning. The central contribution is the finer control made possible by turning guardrail assessments into a signal that changes throughout a training example.
summary.tldr: STAR-guided dynamic safety shaping adjusts learning within responses to improve fine-tuning safety while preserving tested task capabilities.

title: Shape it Up! Restoring LLM Safety during Finetuning

abstract: Synthetic time series generated by diffusion models enable sharing privacy-sensitive datasets, such as patients' functional MRI records. Key criteria for synthetic data include high data utility and traceability to verify the data source. Recent watermarking methods embed in homogeneous latent spaces, but state-of-the-art time series generators operate in data space, making latent-based watermarking incompatible. This creates the challenge of watermarking directly in data space while handling feature heterogeneity and temporal dependencies. We propose TimeWak, the first watermarking algorithm for multivariate time series diffusion models. To handle temporal dependence and spatial heterogeneity, TimeWak embeds a temporal chained-hashing watermark directly within the temporal-feature data space. The other unique feature is the $\epsilon$-exact inversion, which addresses the non-uniform reconstruction error distribution across features from inverting the diffusion process to detect watermarks. We derive the error bound of inverting multivariate time series while preserving robust watermark detectability. We extensively evaluate TimeWak on its impact on synthetic data quality, watermark detectability, and robustness under various post-editing attacks, against five datasets and baselines of different temporal lengths. Our results show that TimeWak achieves improvements of 61.96% in context-FID score, and 8.44% in correlational scores against the strongest state-of-the-art baseline, while remaining consistently detectable.

title: TimeWak: Temporal Chained-Hashing Watermark for Time Series Data

abstract: Diffusion models, such as diffusion policy, have achieved state-of-the-art results in robotic manipulation by imitating expert demonstrations. While diffusion models were originally developed for vision tasks like image and video generation, many of their inference strategies have been directly transferred to control domains without adaptation. In this work, we show that by tailoring the denoising process to the specific characteristics of embodied AI tasks—particularly the structured, low-dimensional nature of action distributions---diffusion policies can operate effectively with as few as 5 neural function evaluations (NFE). Building on this insight, we propose a population-based sampling strategy, genetic denoising, which enhances both performance and stability by selecting denoising trajectories with low out-of-distribution risk. Our method solves challenging tasks with only 2 NFE while improving or matching performance. We evaluate our approach across 14 robotic manipulation tasks from D4RL and Robomimic, spanning multiple action horizons and inference budgets. In over 2 million evaluations, our method consistently outperforms standard diffusion-based policies, achieving up to 20\% performance gains with significantly fewer inference steps.

It selects denoising trajectories with low risk of going outside the learned distribution, aiming to improve both performance and stability. The results support tailoring diffusion sampling to robot-action structure when seeking faster, effective control.
summary.tldr: Genetic denoising selects low-risk action trajectories, enabling two-evaluation diffusion policies with matching or improved manipulation performance.

title: Two-Steps Diffusion Policy for Robotic Manipulation via Genetic Denoising

abstract: We propose an adaptive sampling framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that leverages comprehensive multi-view photometric error signals within a unified Metropolis-Hastings approach. Vanilla 3DGS heavily relies on heuristic-based density-control mechanisms (e.g., cloning, splitting, and pruning), which can lead to redundant computations or premature removal of beneficial Gaussians. Our framework overcomes these limitations by reformulating densification and pruning as a probabilistic sampling process, dynamically inserting and relocating Gaussians based on aggregated multi-view errors and opacity scores. Guided by Bayesian acceptance tests derived from these error-based importance scores, our method substantially reduces reliance on heuristics, offers greater flexibility, and adaptively infers Gaussian distributions without requiring predefined scene complexity. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including Mip-NeRF360, Tanks and Temples and Deep Blending, show that our approach reduces the number of Gaussians needed, achieving faster convergence while matching or modestly surpassing the view-synthesis quality of state-of-the-art models.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs scenes using collections of Gaussians whose number and placement must be adjusted during optimization. Standard density-control procedures use rules for cloning, splitting, and pruning. The paper argues that these heuristics can waste computation or remove Gaussians that would have helped the reconstruction.

The proposed framework treats densification and pruning as probabilistic sampling within a unified Metropolis-Hastings approach. It aggregates photometric errors across multiple views and combines them with opacity scores to guide insertion and relocation. Bayesian acceptance tests derived from these importance scores decide which proposed changes to accept. This allows the representation to adapt without requiring a predefined level of scene complexity.

Experiments on Mip-NeRF360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending show that the method needs fewer Gaussians and converges faster while matching or modestly exceeding leading view-synthesis quality. The result is a more economical scene representation in the reported evaluations. Its main contribution is to make decisions about representation density depend on probabilistic tests informed by multi-view reconstruction errors.
summary.tldr: A Metropolis-Hastings framework adapts Gaussian scene representations using multi-view errors, achieving faster convergence with fewer Gaussians and comparable or modestly better quality.

title: Metropolis-Hastings Sampling for 3D Gaussian Reconstruction

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong generalization across diverse tasks, yet the internal decision-making processes behind their predictions remain opaque. In this work, we study the geometry of hidden representations in LLMs through the lens of intrinsic dimension (ID), focusing specifically on decision-making dynamics in a multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting. We perform a large-scale study, with 28 open-weight transformer models and estimate ID across layers using multiple estimators, while also quantifying per-layer performance on MCQA tasks. Our findings reveal a consistent ID pattern across models: early layers operate on low-dimensional manifolds, middle layers expand this space, and later layers compress it again, converging to decision-relevant representations. Together, these results suggest LLMs implicitly learn to project linguistic inputs onto structured, low-dimensional manifolds aligned with task-specific decisions, providing new geometric insights into how generalization and reasoning emerge in language models.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language models' internal representations change as they work toward a multiple-choice answer. Its main lens is intrinsic dimension: a measure of the effective dimensional structure of those representations. The goal is to connect that geometry with decision-making, giving a more concrete description of otherwise opaque internal processing.

The authors examine 28 open-weight transformer models. They estimate intrinsic dimension at different layers with multiple estimators and also measure multiple-choice performance layer by layer. Combining these measurements lets them study representation geometry alongside the emergence of task-relevant predictions, rather than treating hidden-state structure as an isolated property.

Across the models, the study finds a recurring pattern: early representations have low intrinsic dimension, middle layers expand the space, and later layers compress it toward decision-relevant representations. The authors interpret this as evidence that models implicitly project linguistic inputs onto structured, low-dimensional spaces aligned with particular decisions. This is a suggested explanation grounded in the observed multiple-choice setting, offering a geometric perspective on reasoning and generalization.
summary.tldr: A study of 28 language models finds that representation dimension expands in middle layers and contracts toward decision-relevant structure in later layers.

title: Geometry of Decision Making in Language Models

abstract: We consider the problem of how many samples from a Gaussian multi-index model are required to weakly reconstruct the relevant index subspace. Despite its increasing popularity as a testbed for investigating the computational complexity of neural networks, results beyond the single-index setting remain elusive. In this work, we introduce spectral algorithms based on the linearization of a message passing scheme tailored to this problem. Our main contribution is to show that the proposed methods achieve the optimal reconstruction threshold. Leveraging a high-dimensional characterization of the algorithms, we show that above the critical threshold the leading eigenvector correlates with the relevant index subspace, a phenomenon reminiscent of the Baik–Ben Arous–Peche (BBP) transition in spiked models arising in random matrix theory. Supported by numerical experiments and a rigorous theoretical framework, our work bridges critical gaps in the computational limits of weak learnability in multi-index model.

Our main contribution is to show that the proposed methods achieve the optimal reconstruction threshold. These models provide a setting for studying computational questions about neural networks, but extending results beyond a single index has been difficult.

Their main result shows that the proposed methods attain the optimal reconstruction threshold. A high-dimensional analysis identifies what happens above that threshold: the leading eigenvector becomes correlated with the relevant index subspace.

Rigorous analysis and numerical experiments support the result. The contribution pinpoints a sample threshold for weak learning in the studied Gaussian multi-index setting and provides algorithms that reach it, connecting an abstract learnability boundary to a concrete eigenvector-based procedure.
summary.tldr: Spectral algorithms derived from message passing achieve the optimal weak-reconstruction threshold in the studied Gaussian multi-index setting.

title: Optimal Spectral Transitions in High-Dimensional Multi-Index Models

abstract: Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) is an efficient approximation algorithm for computing sparse representations. However, prior research has shown that the representations computed by OMP may be of inferior quality, as they deliver suboptimal classification accuracy on several im- age datasets. We have found that this problem is caused by OMP’s relatively weak stability under data variations, which leads to unreliability in supervised classifier training. We show that by imposing a simple nonnegativity constraint, this nonnegative variant of OMP (NOMP) can mitigate OMP’s stability issue and is resistant to noise overfitting. In this work, we provide extensive analysis and experimental results to examine and validate the stability advantage of NOMP. In our experiments, we use a multi-layer deep architecture for representation learning, where we use K-means for feature learning and NOMP for representation encoding. The resulting learning framework is not only efficient and scalable to large feature dictionaries, but also is robust against input noise. This framework achieves the state-of-the-art accuracy on the STL-10 dataset.

title: Stable and Efficient Representation Learning with Nonnegativity Constraints

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of online stochastic optimization of a locally smooth function under bandit feedback. We introduce the high-confidence tree (HCT) algorithm, a novel anytime \mathcal X-armed bandit algorithm, and derive regret bounds matching the performance of state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of the dependency on number of steps and the near-optimality dimension. The main advantage of HCT is that it handles the challenging case of correlated bandit feedback (reward), whereas existing methods require rewards to be conditionally independent. HCT also improves on the state-of-the-art in terms of the memory requirement, as well as requiring a weaker smoothness assumption on the mean-reward function in comparison with the existing anytime algorithms. Finally, we discuss how HCT can be applied to the problem of policy search in reinforcement learning and we report preliminary empirical results.

paragraphs: Online stochastic optimization with bandit feedback requires finding good inputs while observing rewards only for the choices made. This paper considers locally smooth objectives in a setting where reward observations can be correlated. Such dependence creates a challenge for existing methods that require rewards to be conditionally independent.

The proposed high-confidence tree algorithm, HCT, is an anytime method, meaning it can operate without a fixed stopping horizon. Its regret bounds match leading algorithms in their dependence on the number of steps and the near-optimality dimension. The contribution preserves those aspects of statistical performance while accommodating correlated feedback.

HCT also reduces memory requirements and uses a weaker smoothness assumption than existing anytime algorithms. These properties address storage and modeling demands alongside dependence between rewards. The authors discuss applying HCT to policy search in reinforcement learning and provide preliminary empirical results. That application illustrates the method’s potential use, while the main stated guarantees concern its regret behavior in the analyzed optimization setting.
summary.tldr: HCT handles correlated bandit rewards with competitive regret bounds, lower memory needs, and weaker smoothness requirements than existing anytime methods.

title: Online Stochastic Optimization under Correlated Bandit Feedback

abstract: We present a new class of density estimation models, Structural Maxent models, with feature functions selected from possibly very complex families. The design of our models is motivated by data-dependent convergence bounds and benefits from new data-dependent learning bounds expressed in terms of the Rademacher complexities of the sub-families composing the family of features considered. We prove a duality theorem, which we use to derive our Structural Maxent algorithm. We give a full description of our algorithm, including the details of its derivation and report the results of several experiments demonstrating that its performance compares favorably to that of existing regularized Maxent. We further similarly define conditional Structural Maxent models for multi-class classification problems. These are conditional probability models making use of possibly complex feature families. We also prove a duality theorem for these models which shows the connection between these models and existing binary and multi-class deep boosting algorithms.

paragraphs: Structural Maxent models estimate probability distributions using features drawn from potentially complex families. The central design question is how to benefit from expressive features while controlling learning behavior. This paper builds the model around data-dependent convergence and learning bounds, so the theoretical treatment reflects properties of the feature families and observed data.

The new bounds use the Rademacher complexities of the subfamilies composing the overall feature collection. These quantities describe aspects of how flexible the candidate features are. The authors prove a duality theorem and use it to derive the Structural Maxent algorithm, connecting the model definition to a concrete training procedure.

Experiments show favorable performance compared with existing regularized Maxent models. The paper also develops conditional Structural Maxent models for multiclass classification, extending the same broad idea to conditional probability estimation. A further duality theorem connects those conditional models to existing binary and multiclass deep boosting algorithms. The contribution combines a new modeling framework, learning guarantees, an algorithm, and a theoretical relationship to boosting.
summary.tldr: Structural Maxent uses data-dependent complexity bounds to organize expressive feature families for density estimation and multiclass classification.

title: Structural Maxent Models

abstract: The Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is an extremely powerful sequence model that is often difficult to train. The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a specific RNN architecture whose design makes it much easier to train. While wildly successful in practice, the LSTM’s architecture appears to be ad-hoc so it is not clear if it is optimal, and the significance of its individual components is unclear. In this work, we aim to determine whether the LSTM architecture is optimal or whether much better architectures exist. We conducted a thorough architecture search where we evaluated over ten thousand different RNN architectures, and identified an architecture that outperforms both the LSTM and the recently-introduced Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) on some but not all tasks. We found that adding a bias of 1 to the LSTM’s forget gate closes the gap between the LSTM and the GRU.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks model sequences, but training them can be difficult. Long short-term memory networks address that difficulty through a particular architectural design. Their practical success leaves a further question: which parts of that design matter, and could a substantially different recurrent architecture work better? This paper investigates those questions through a large empirical search.

The authors evaluate more than ten thousand recurrent network architectures. They identify one that performs better than both LSTM and the gated recurrent unit on some tasks. The qualification matters: the discovered architecture does not win on every task, so the search provides evidence for task-dependent improvements rather than establishing a universally best recurrent design.

The study also finds that setting the LSTM forget-gate bias to 1 closes the observed gap between LSTM and GRU. This result shows that a small architectural setting can materially affect comparisons between network families. Together, the findings connect broad architecture exploration with a simple adjustment to an established model, clarifying why both design and configuration deserve attention.
summary.tldr: A search of over ten thousand recurrent architectures finds task-dependent improvements and a simple LSTM forget-gate adjustment.

title: An Empirical Exploration of Recurrent Network Architectures

abstract: We consider a non-linear generalization of low-rank matrix completion to the case where the data belongs to an algebraic variety, i.e., each data point is a solution to a system of polynomial equations. In this case the original matrix is possibly high-rank, but it becomes low-rank after mapping each column to a higher dimensional space of monomial features. Algebraic varieties capture a range of well-studied linear models, including affine subspaces and their union, but also quadratic and higher degree curves and surfaces. We study the sampling requirements for a general variety model with a focus on the union of affine subspaces. We propose an efficient matrix completion algorithm that minimizes a convex or non-convex surrogate of the rank of the lifted matrix. Our algorithm uses the well-known “kernel trick” to avoid working directly with the high-dimensional lifted data matrix and scales efficiently with data size. We show the proposed algorithm is able to recover synthetically generated data up to the predicted sampling complexity bounds. The algorithm also outperforms standard techniques in experiments with real data.

paragraphs: Matrix completion fills in missing entries by exploiting structure in the data. This paper extends the usual low-rank view to data lying on an algebraic variety: a set described by polynomial equations. Such data can form a high-rank matrix in its original representation while still having exploitable nonlinear structure.

The key step maps each data column into a larger collection of monomial features, where the resulting matrix becomes low-rank. This framework covers affine subspaces and unions of them, as well as higher-degree curves and surfaces. The proposed algorithm minimizes a convex or nonconvex approximation to the lifted matrix's rank. A kernel computation avoids explicitly constructing that potentially large feature representation.

The authors study how many observations recovery requires, with particular attention to unions of affine subspaces. Synthetic experiments recover data up to the predicted sampling bounds, while real-data experiments outperform standard techniques. These results support nonlinear structure as a useful basis for completion even when low rank is absent from the original matrix.
summary.tldr: Polynomial structure enables matrix completion by making potentially high-rank data low-rank in an implicit expanded feature space.

title: Algebraic Variety Models for High-Rank Matrix Completion

abstract: Entropy Search (ES) and Predictive Entropy Search (PES) are popular and empirically successful Bayesian Optimization techniques. Both rely on a compelling information-theoretic motivation, and maximize the information gained about the $\arg\max$ of the unknown function; yet, both are plagued by the expensive computation for estimating entropies. We propose a new criterion, Max-value Entropy Search (MES), that instead uses the information about the maximum function value. We show relations of MES to other Bayesian optimization methods, and establish a regret bound. We observe that MES maintains or improves the good empirical performance of ES/PES, while tremendously lightening the computational burden. In particular, MES is much more robust to the number of samples used for computing the entropy, and hence more efficient for higher dimensional problems.

paragraphs: Information-based Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations according to how much they are expected to reveal about an unknown function's optimum. Entropy Search and Predictive Entropy Search seek information about the input where the maximum occurs. Although empirically successful, their entropy calculations are expensive, making the selection of evaluations computationally burdensome.

Max-value Entropy Search changes the information target to the maximum function value itself. The distinction is between learning where the best point lies and learning how high the function can go. The authors relate this criterion to other Bayesian optimization methods and establish a regret bound, giving the proposal a theoretical connection to optimization performance.

Empirically, the method maintains or improves the performance of the earlier entropy-search methods while greatly reducing computation. It is also less sensitive to the number of samples used to estimate entropy. The reported robustness makes these calculations more efficient in higher-dimensional problems, where the cost of choosing an evaluation is especially consequential.
summary.tldr: Max-value Entropy Search lowers Bayesian optimization overhead by seeking information about the best function value.

title: Max-value Entropy Search for Efficient Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We extend the fair machine learning literature by considering the problem of proportional centroid clustering in a metric context. For clustering n points with k centers, we define fairness as proportionality to mean that any n/k points are entitled to form their own cluster if there is another center that is closer in distance for all n/k points. We seek clustering solutions to which there are no such justified complaints from any subsets of agents, without assuming any a priori notion of protected subsets. We present and analyze algorithms to efficiently compute, optimize, and audit proportional solutions. We conclude with an empirical examination of the tradeoff between proportional solutions and the k-means objective.

For clustering n points with k centers, we define fairness as proportionality to mean that any n/k points are entitled to form their own cluster if there is another center that is closer in distance for all n/k points. We seek clustering solutions to which there are no such justified complaints from any subsets of agents, without assuming any a priori notion of protected subsets. We present and analyze algorithms to efficiently compute, optimize, and audit proportional solutions. We conclude with an empirical examination of the tradeoff between proportional solutions and the k-means objective.

paragraphs: Clustering typically seeks a good overall arrangement of centers, but an aggregate objective can leave groups dissatisfied. This paper defines fairness through proportional representation in a metric space. With n points and k centers, a group of n/k points has a claim to its own cluster if another center would be closer for every member.

A proportional solution admits no such justified complaint from any qualifying subset. The definition does not require protected groups to be specified in advance. Instead, the relevant groups arise from the points' shared preference for a closer center. Fairness is therefore expressed through the relationship between group size, the available number of centers, and distances.

The authors develop and analyze efficient algorithms for computing proportional solutions, optimizing them, and auditing whether they satisfy the criterion. They also empirically examine the tradeoff between proportionality and the k-means objective. This makes the proposed fairness notion operational: it supplies both a standard for evaluating an allocation of centers and procedures for finding or checking solutions against that standard.
summary.tldr: Proportional clustering gives sufficiently large groups a distance-based claim to a center without requiring predefined protected groups.

title: Proportionally Fair Clustering

abstract: Data augmentation (DA) is commonly used during model training, as it significantly improves test error and model robustness. DA artificially expands the training set by applying random noise, rotations, crops, or even adversarial perturbations to the input data. Although DA is widely used, its capacity to provably improve robustness is not fully understood. In this work, we analyze the robustness that DA begets by quantifying the margin that DA enforces on empirical risk minimizers. We first focus on linear separators, and then a class of nonlinear models whose labeling is constant within small convex hulls of data points. We present lower bounds on the number of augmented data points required for non-zero margin, and show that commonly used DA techniques may only introduce significant margin after adding exponentially many points to the data set.

paragraphs: Data augmentation expands a training set through transformations such as noise, rotations, crops, or adversarial perturbations. Although it often improves test performance and robustness, those benefits do not by themselves explain what robustness it can guarantee. This paper investigates the question through classification margin, a measure of separation between data and a classifier's decision boundary.

The analysis asks how much margin augmentation enforces on empirical risk minimizers, the models selected by minimizing training error. It first considers linear separating boundaries. It then extends to a class of nonlinear models whose labels remain constant inside small convex hulls of data points. That structural condition defines the nonlinear setting covered by the analysis.

The authors establish lower bounds on the number of augmented examples needed to enforce a nonzero margin. They show that commonly used augmentation methods may need exponentially many added points before producing a significant margin. This is a qualified theoretical warning about how much augmentation can enforce, rather than a claim that augmentation never helps: observed improvements and provable separation are distinct questions.
summary.tldr: Theoretical analysis shows that common augmentation methods may require exponentially many added examples to enforce a significant classification margin.

title: Does Data Augmentation Lead to Positive Margin?

abstract: Handling previously unseen tasks after given only a few training examples continues to be a tough challenge in machine learning. We propose TapNets, neural networks augmented with task-adaptive projection for improved few-shot learning. Here, employing a meta-learning strategy with episode-based training, a network and a set of per-class reference vectors are learned across widely varying tasks. At the same time, for every episode, features in the embedding space are linearly projected into a new space as a form of quick task-specific conditioning. The training loss is obtained based on a distance metric between the query and the reference vectors in the projection space. Excellent generalization results in this way. When tested on the Omniglot, miniImageNet and tieredImageNet datasets, we obtain state of the art classification accuracies under various few-shot scenarios.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a model to handle previously unseen tasks after seeing only a small number of training examples. TapNet addresses this challenge by combining representations learned across tasks with a projection that adapts to each individual task. The aim is to make shared features useful for the particular classification problem currently being solved.

During episode-based meta-training, the method learns both a neural network and a set of per-class reference vectors across varied tasks. Within each episode, it linearly projects embedded features into a new space for quick task-specific conditioning. The training loss uses distances between query examples and reference vectors in that projected space.

The projection connects shared learning with immediate task adaptation: comparisons are made in a space conditioned on the current episode. Evaluations on Omniglot, miniImageNet, and tieredImageNet achieve state-of-the-art classification accuracy across various few-shot settings. These results support task-adaptive projection as a useful addition to a learned embedding and reference-vector system for generalizing from few examples.
summary.tldr: TapNet adapts few-shot classification to each task by projecting learned features and comparing queries with learned class reference vectors.

title: TapNet: Neural Network Augmented with Task-Adaptive Projection for Few-Shot Learning

abstract: We propose a novel gradient-based tractable approach for the Blahut-Arimoto (BA) algorithm to compute the rate-distortion function where the BA algorithm is fully parameterized. This results in a rich and flexible framework to learn a new class of stochastic encoders, termed PArameterized RAte-DIstortion Stochastic Encoder (PARADISE). The framework can be applied to a wide range of settings from semi-supervised, multi-task to supervised and robust learning. We show that the training objective of PARADISE can be seen as a form of regularization that helps improve generalization. With an emphasis on robust learning we further develop a novel posterior matching objective to encourage smoothness on the loss function and show that PARADISE can significantly improve interpretability as well as robustness to adversarial attacks on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. In particular, on the CIFAR-10 dataset, our model reduces standard and adversarial error rates in comparison to the state-of-the-art by 50% and 41%, respectively without the expensive computational cost of adversarial training.

This produces PARADISE, a framework for learning stochastic encoders. The framework is intended to support several learning settings, including supervised, semi-supervised, multi-task, and robust learning, through a flexible parameterized formulation.

The authors show that the PARADISE training objective can be interpreted as regularization that helps generalization. For robust learning, they introduce an additional posterior-matching objective that encourages smoothness in the loss function. This connects the encoder construction to two practical goals: better behavior on unseen data and greater resistance to adversarial perturbations.

On CIFAR-10, the reported standard and adversarial error rates decrease by 50% and 41%, respectively, relative to the state-of-the-art comparison, without the expensive computational cost of adversarial training. These are experimental results for the evaluated setting, supporting the usefulness of the rate-distortion formulation as a learning objective.
summary.tldr: PARADISE turns rate-distortion optimization into a trainable stochastic encoder framework with reported gains in generalization, interpretability, and adversarial robustness.

title: Parameterized Rate-Distortion Stochastic Encoder

abstract: The output of a neural network depends on its architecture and weights in a highly nonlinear way, and it is often assumed that a network’s parameters cannot be recovered from its output. Here, we prove that, in fact, it is frequently possible to reconstruct the architecture, weights, and biases of a deep ReLU network by observing only its output. We leverage the fact that every ReLU network defines a piecewise linear function, where the boundaries between linear regions correspond to inputs for which some neuron in the network switches between inactive and active ReLU states. By dissecting the set of region boundaries into components associated with particular neurons, we show both theoretically and empirically that it is possible to recover the weights of neurons and their arrangement within the network, up to isomorphism.
originalAbstract: The output of a neural network depends on its architecture and weights in a highly nonlinear way, and it is often assumed that a network’s parameters cannot be recovered from its output. Here, we prove that, in fact, it is frequently possible to reconstruct the architecture, weights, and biases of a deep ReLU network by observing only its output. We leverage the fact that every ReLU network defines a piecewise linear function, where the boundaries between linear regions correspond to inputs for which some neuron in the network switches between inactive and active ReLU states. By dissecting the set of region boundaries into components associated with particular neurons, we show both theoretically and empirically that it is possible to recover the weights of neurons and their arrangement within the network, up to isomorphism.

paragraphs: A neural network’s outputs depend on its architecture and parameters in a complicated nonlinear way. That complexity can suggest that observing outputs is insufficient to reconstruct the network. This paper proves that reconstruction is frequently possible for deep ReLU networks, including their architecture, weights, and biases.

The approach exploits the piecewise linear structure of the function represented by a ReLU network. Different input regions follow different linear rules, and boundaries arise where neurons switch between inactive and active states. The authors dissect these boundaries into components associated with individual neurons. Those components provide information about both neuron weights and the neurons’ arrangement within the network.

The paper supports this reconstruction approach theoretically and empirically. Recovery is up to isomorphism, meaning that equivalent arrangements are not distinguished merely by how their components are labeled. The result does not claim that every network is always recoverable. It shows that, in the cases covered, the geometry visible through outputs contains enough information to reconstruct internal structure that might otherwise appear inaccessible.
summary.tldr: Deep ReLU networks can frequently be reconstructed from outputs by analyzing boundaries between their linear regions, with recovery up to isomorphism.

title: Reverse-engineering deep ReLU networks

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a powerful and efficient framework for direct optimization of ranking metrics. The problem is ill-posed due to the discrete structure of the loss, and to deal with that, we introduce two important techniques: stochastic smoothing and novel gradient estimate based on partial integration. We show that classic smoothing approaches may introduce bias and present a universal solution for a proper debiasing. Importantly, we can guarantee global convergence of our method by adopting a recently proposed Stochastic Gradient Langevin Boosting algorithm. Our algorithm is implemented as a part of the CatBoost gradient boosting library and outperforms the existing approaches on several learning-to-rank datasets. In addition to ranking metrics, our framework applies to any scale-free discrete loss function.

paragraphs: Ranking metrics have a discrete structure that makes them difficult to optimize directly. StochasticRank addresses this problem with a framework aimed at the ranking metric itself. Its main tools are stochastic smoothing and a new gradient estimator derived using partial integration, providing a way to optimize an otherwise problematic loss.

The paper shows that conventional smoothing can introduce bias and develops a general correction for it. This matters because smoothing should make optimization tractable without silently changing the goal in an undesirable way. By adopting Stochastic Gradient Langevin Boosting, the authors also obtain a global convergence guarantee for their method.

The algorithm is implemented in CatBoost and outperforms existing approaches on several learning-to-rank datasets. Its scope extends beyond ranking to any scale-free discrete loss. The contribution therefore combines a treatment of smoothing bias, a gradient-estimation technique, and a convergence result with an implementation and empirical evidence. The global convergence claim is tied to the specified optimization approach used in the framework.
summary.tldr: StochasticRank directly optimizes ranking metrics using corrected stochastic smoothing and gradient estimation, with global convergence through Langevin boosting.

title: StochasticRank: Global Optimization of Scale-Free Discrete Functions

abstract: Feature selection problems have been extensively studied in the setting of linear estimation (e.g. LASSO), but less emphasis has been placed on feature selection for non-linear functions. In this study, we propose a method for feature selection in neural network estimation problems. The new procedure is based on probabilistic relaxation of the $\ell_0$ norm of features, or the count of the number of selected features. Our $\ell_0$-based regularization relies on a continuous relaxation of the Bernoulli distribution; such relaxation allows our model to learn the parameters of the approximate Bernoulli distributions via gradient descent. The proposed framework simultaneously learns either a nonlinear regression or classification function while selecting a small subset of features. We provide an information-theoretic justification for incorporating Bernoulli distribution into feature selection. Furthermore, we evaluate our method using synthetic and real-life data to demonstrate that our approach outperforms other commonly used methods in both predictive performance and feature selection.

paragraphs: Feature selection asks which inputs a predictive model actually needs. Although this problem has been widely studied for linear models, the paper focuses on selecting inputs while learning nonlinear functions with neural networks. Its goal is to train an effective regression or classification model while retaining only a small subset of the available features.

The method penalizes the number of selected features, expressed through the zero norm. Because discrete selection is difficult to optimize directly with gradient descent, the authors use a continuous relaxation of Bernoulli variables. These relaxed stochastic gates allow the selection parameters to be learned alongside the predictive function, bringing the choice of inputs into the same optimization process as prediction.

The paper provides an information-theoretic argument for using Bernoulli distributions in feature selection. Experiments on synthetic and real data report improvements over commonly used methods in both predictive performance and feature selection. These findings support the value of learning sparsity together with nonlinear relationships, rather than judging input usefulness only through a linear estimation setting.
summary.tldr: Stochastic gates make feature-count regularization trainable with gradient descent, jointly selecting inputs and learning nonlinear predictors.

title: Feature Selection using Stochastic Gates

abstract: Learning sensorimotor control policies from high-dimensional images crucially relies on the quality of the underlying visual representations. Prior works show that structured latent space such as visual keypoints often outperforms unstructured representations for robotic control. However, most of these representations, whether structured or unstructured are learned in a 2D space even though the control tasks are usually performed in a 3D environment. In this work, we propose a framework to learn such a 3D geometric structure directly from images in an end-to-end unsupervised manner. The input images are embedded into latent 3D keypoints via a differentiable encoder which is trained to optimize both a multi-view consistency loss and downstream task objective. These discovered 3D keypoints tend to meaningfully capture robot joints as well as object movements in a consistent manner across both time and 3D space. The proposed approach outperforms prior state-of-art methods across a variety of reinforcement learning benchmarks. Code and videos at https://buoyancy99.github.io/unsup-3d-keypoints/.

Structured representations such as keypoints can help, but many existing approaches learn them in two dimensions even when the agent acts in a three-dimensional world. This paper learns a 3D keypoint representation directly from images to better align visual structure with the control setting.

A differentiable encoder maps input images into latent 3D keypoints. Training combines a multi-view consistency loss with the downstream task objective, so the representation is shaped by both geometric agreement and its usefulness for control. The framework learns this structure end to end in an unsupervised manner, without relying on manually specified keypoint identities.

The discovered keypoints tend to track robot joints and object motion consistently across time and 3D space. Across a variety of reinforcement-learning benchmarks, the approach outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using learned spatial structure as part of visual control, while the correspondence to meaningful joints and movements remains an observed tendency.
summary.tldr: Learning consistent 3D keypoints directly from images improves visual control across evaluated reinforcement-learning benchmarks.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Visual 3D Keypoints for Control

abstract: Bandit and reinforcement learning (RL) problems can often be framed as optimization problems where the goal is to maximize average performance while having access only to stochastic estimates of the true gradient. Traditionally, stochastic optimization theory predicts that learning dynamics are governed by the curvature of the loss function and the noise of the gradient estimates. In this paper we demonstrate that the standard view is too limited for bandit and RL problems. To allow our analysis to be interpreted in light of multi-step MDPs, we focus on techniques derived from stochastic optimization principles (e.g., natural policy gradient and EXP3) and we show that some standard assumptions from optimization theory are violated in these problems. We present theoretical results showing that, at least for bandit problems, curvature and noise are not sufficient to explain the learning dynamics and that seemingly innocuous choices like the baseline can determine whether an algorithm converges. These theoretical findings match our empirical evaluation, which we extend to multi-state MDPs.

paragraphs: Policy optimization often improves decisions using noisy estimates of a performance gradient. A conventional explanation of its behavior emphasizes two factors: the curvature of the objective and the noise in those estimates. This paper asks whether that explanation is sufficient for bandit problems and reinforcement learning, where gradient estimates arise from the agent’s decision process.

The authors study methods connected to stochastic optimization, including natural policy gradient and EXP3. They show that some assumptions used in standard optimization theory fail in these settings. Their theoretical results establish that, at least in bandit problems, curvature and gradient noise do not fully explain learning dynamics. A baseline choice can determine whether an algorithm converges.

The empirical results agree with this theoretical picture, and the experiments extend to multi-state Markov decision processes. The practical implication is that baselines deserve attention beyond their familiar role in reducing variance. The theoretical convergence findings are specifically established for bandits, while the broader reinforcement-learning evidence comes from the empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Baselines can affect whether policy optimization converges, beyond their usual role in reducing gradient variance.

title: Beyond Variance Reduction: Understanding the True Impact of Baselines on Policy Optimization

abstract: Recent contrastive representation learning methods rely on estimating mutual information (MI) between multiple views of an underlying context. E.g., we can derive multiple views of a given image by applying data augmentation, or we can split a sequence into views comprising the past and future of some step in the sequence. Contrastive lower bounds on MI are easy to optimize, but have a strong underestimation bias when estimating large amounts of MI. We propose decomposing the full MI estimation problem into a sum of smaller estimation problems by splitting one of the views into progressively more informed subviews and by applying the chain rule on MI between the decomposed views. This expression contains a sum of unconditional and conditional MI terms, each measuring modest chunks of the total MI, which facilitates approximation via contrastive bounds. To maximize the sum, we formulate a contrastive lower bound on the conditional MI which can be approximated efficiently. We refer to our general approach as Decomposed Estimation of Mutual Information (DEMI). We show that DEMI can capture a larger amount of MI than standard non-decomposed contrastive bounds in a synthetic setting, and learns better representations in a vision domain and for dialogue generation.

paragraphs: Contrastive representation learning often tries to capture information shared by different views of the same underlying content. These views might be augmented versions of an image or different portions of a sequence. The paper addresses a weakness of common contrastive objectives: their lower bounds can substantially underestimate mutual information when the views share a large amount.

Decomposed Estimation of Mutual Information, or DEMI, divides this large estimation problem into smaller pieces. One view is split into subviews that progressively reveal more information. Applying the mutual-information chain rule produces unconditional and conditional terms, each responsible for a smaller part of the total. The authors also formulate an efficiently approximated contrastive lower bound for the conditional terms.

In a synthetic setting, DEMI captures more mutual information than standard contrastive bounds without decomposition. Experiments also show better learned representations in a vision domain and for dialogue generation. These findings support estimating shared information in manageable portions: the decomposition preserves the overall information objective while making its individual components more suitable for contrastive approximation.
summary.tldr: DEMI divides mutual-information estimation into smaller contrastive problems to reduce underestimation and improve learned representations.

title: Decomposed Mutual Information Estimation for Contrastive Representation Learning

abstract: Physical modeling is critical for many modern science and engineering applications. From a data science or machine learning perspective, where more domain-agnostic, data-driven models are pervasive, physical knowledge {—} often expressed as differential equations {—} is valuable in that it is complementary to data, and it can potentially help overcome issues such as data sparsity, noise, and inaccuracy. In this work, we propose a simple, yet powerful and general framework {—} AutoIP, for Automatically Incorporating Physics {—} that can integrate all kinds of differential equations into Gaussian Processes (GPs) to enhance prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification. These equations can be linear or nonlinear, spatial, temporal, or spatio-temporal, complete or incomplete with unknown source terms, and so on. Based on kernel differentiation, we construct a GP prior to sample the values of the target function, equation related derivatives, and latent source functions, which are all jointly from a multivariate Gaussian distribution. The sampled values are fed to two likelihoods: one to fit the observations, and the other to conform to the equation. We use the whitening method to evade the strong dependency between the sampled function values and kernel parameters, and we develop a stochastic variational learning algorithm. AutoIP shows improvement upon vanilla GPs in both simulation and several real-world applications, even using rough, incomplete equations.

paragraphs: Physical equations can supply information that observations alone do not provide, particularly when data are sparse or noisy. AutoIP brings this information into Gaussian processes, models that support predictions together with uncertainty estimates. The framework accommodates linear and nonlinear differential equations involving space, time, or both, including incomplete equations with unknown source terms.

Using derivatives of the kernel, AutoIP constructs a joint Gaussian prior over function values, relevant derivatives, and latent source functions. Samples from that prior enter two likelihoods: one measures agreement with observed data, while the other measures agreement with the physical equation. This gives observations and physical relationships explicit roles within the same learning framework.

The authors use whitening to reduce strong dependencies between sampled values and kernel parameters, then develop a stochastic variational learning algorithm. Evaluations in simulations and several real applications show improvements over ordinary Gaussian processes, even when the equations are rough or incomplete. The findings suggest that useful physical guidance need not amount to a complete, exact description of the system.
summary.tldr: AutoIP combines observations and differential equations within Gaussian processes, showing benefits even with rough or incomplete physical knowledge.

title: AutoIP: A United Framework to Integrate Physics into Gaussian Processes

abstract: Even though Shapley value provides an effective explanation for a DNN model prediction, the computation relies on the enumeration of all possible input feature coalitions, which leads to the exponentially growing complexity. To address this problem, we propose a novel method SHEAR to significantly accelerate the Shapley explanation for DNN models, where only a few coalitions of input features are involved in the computation. The selection of the feature coalitions follows our proposed Shapley chain rule to minimize the absolute error from the ground-truth Shapley values, such that the computation can be both efficient and accurate. To demonstrate the effectiveness, we comprehensively evaluate SHEAR across multiple metrics including the absolute error from the ground-truth Shapley value, the faithfulness of the explanations, and running speed. The experimental results indicate SHEAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods across different evaluation metrics, which demonstrates its potentials in real-world applications where the computational resource is limited.

paragraphs: Shapley explanations assign importance to input features by considering how they contribute alongside different combinations of other features. For deep neural networks, calculating these values exactly requires examining all possible feature coalitions. The number of combinations grows exponentially, making this explanation approach expensive as inputs become larger.

The paper introduces SHEAR, which computes explanations using only a small selection of coalitions. Its selection strategy follows a proposed Shapley chain rule and aims to minimize absolute error relative to exact Shapley values. The central idea is to choose informative combinations carefully, so reducing computation also preserves the accuracy of the resulting feature scores.

The evaluation examines three distinct concerns: numerical agreement with exact values, faithfulness of the explanations, and execution speed. SHEAR consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods across the reported metrics. These findings support its potential for explaining neural predictions when computing resources are limited, while grounding that potential in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SHEAR accelerates Shapley explanations by selecting a small set of informative feature coalitions while preserving explanation accuracy.

title: Accelerating Shapley Explanation via Contributive Cooperator Selection

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful framework to learn representations from raw data without supervision. Yet in practice, engineers face issues such as instability in tuning optimizers and collapse of representations during training. Such challenges motivate the need for a theory to shed light on the complex interplay between the choice of data augmentation, network architecture, and training algorithm. % on the resulting performance in downstream tasks. We study such an interplay with a precise analysis of generalization performance on both pretraining and downstream tasks in kernel regimes, and highlight several insights for SSL practitioners that arise from our theory.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning builds representations from raw data without supervision, but its training behavior can be difficult to manage. Optimizer tuning may be unstable, and representations can collapse during training. This paper treats those challenges as motivation for understanding how data augmentation, network architecture, and the training algorithm interact.

The authors study that interaction in kernel regimes, where they carry out a precise analysis of generalization. Their analysis covers both the pretraining task and downstream tasks. Considering both stages matters because learning a representation and using that representation for another task are distinct parts of the self-supervised learning process.

The contribution is a theoretical account connecting these design choices to generalization performance, along with practitioner insights arising from that account. Its stated scope is the kernel setting, which supplies the framework for the analysis. The abstract does not enumerate the individual insights; its central message is that augmentation, architectural bias, and training dynamics should be understood together when analyzing self-supervised representations.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how augmentations, architecture, and training interact to shape self-supervised generalization in kernel regimes.

title: The SSL Interplay: Augmentations, Inductive Bias, and Generalization

abstract: This paper proposes an understandable neural network whose score function is modeled as an additive sum of univariate spline functions. It extends usual understandable models like generative additive models, spline-based models, and neural additive models. It is shown that this neural network can be approximated by a logistic regression whose inputs are obtained with a non-linear preprocessing of input data. This preprocessing depends on the neural network initialization but this paper establishes that it can be replaced by a non random kernel-based preprocessing that no longer depends on the initialization. Hence, the convergence of the training process is guaranteed and the solution is unique for a given training dataset.

This preprocessing depends on the neural network initialization but this paper establishes that it can be replaced by a non random kernel-based preprocessing that no longer depends on the initialization. paragraphs: This paper develops an understandable neural network whose prediction score is a sum of separate spline functions, each acting on one input variable. The additive structure makes the contribution associated with each variable explicit. The proposed network extends existing approaches built around additive models, splines, and neural additive models.

The authors show that this network can be approximated by logistic regression applied to nonlinearly transformed inputs. Initially, the transformation depends on the neural network’s random initialization. They then establish that a deterministic kernel-based transformation can replace it, removing that dependence on the initial random network.

This replacement leads to guaranteed convergence of training and a unique solution for a given training dataset in the resulting formulation. The contribution connects an interpretable nonlinear score with a training problem whose outcome is mathematically well determined. The approximation statement is central: the paper links the proposed network to kernel logistic regression, rather than claiming that every ReLU network admits the same interpretable structure or training guarantee.
summary.tldr: An additive spline neural network admits a kernel logistic regression approximation with deterministic preprocessing and guaranteed training convergence.

title: Kernel Logistic Regression Approximation of an Understandable ReLU Neural Network

abstract: There is an emerging interest in generating robust counterfactual explanations that would remain valid if the model is updated or changed even slightly. Towards finding robust counterfactuals, existing literature often assumes that the original model $m$ and the new model $M$ are bounded in the parameter space, i.e., $\|\text{Params}(M){-}\text{Params}(m)\|{<}\Delta$. However, models can often change significantly in the parameter space with little to no change in their predictions or accuracy on the given dataset. In this work, we introduce a mathematical abstraction termed naturally-occurring model change, which allows for arbitrary changes in the parameter space such that the change in predictions on points that lie on the data manifold is limited. Next, we propose a measure – that we call Stability – to quantify the robustness of counterfactuals to potential model changes for differentiable models, e.g., neural networks. Our main contribution is to show that counterfactuals with sufficiently high value of Stability as defined by our measure will remain valid after potential “naturally-occurring” model changes with high probability (leveraging concentration bounds for Lipschitz function of independent Gaussians). Since our quantification depends on the local Lipschitz constant around a data point which is not always available, we also examine practical relaxations of our proposed measure and demonstrate experimentally how they can be incorporated to find robust counterfactuals for neural networks that are close, realistic, and remain valid after potential model changes.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe changes to an input that would produce a different prediction. Their usefulness can depend on whether they remain valid after the model changes. This paper questions measuring such changes only through parameter distance, since parameters can shift substantially while predictions on the data remain almost unchanged.

The authors define naturally-occurring model change by limiting prediction changes on the data manifold while allowing arbitrary parameter changes. They introduce a Stability measure for counterfactuals in differentiable models. Using concentration bounds for Lipschitz functions of independent Gaussian variables, they show that sufficiently high Stability gives a high-probability guarantee of validity after changes covered by their framework.

The measure depends on a local Lipschitz constant, which may not be available in practice. The authors therefore examine practical relaxations and experimentally incorporate them into counterfactual search. The resulting explanations are reported to be close, realistic, and resilient to potential model changes. The theoretical guarantee remains tied to sufficiently high Stability and the specified model-change framework.
summary.tldr: A Stability measure gives probabilistic robustness guarantees for counterfactual explanations under a prediction-based model of model change.

title: Robust Counterfactual Explanations for Neural Networks With Probabilistic Guarantees

abstract: We consider stochastic unconstrained bilevel optimization problems when only the first-order gradient oracles are available. While numerous optimization methods have been proposed for tackling bilevel problems, existing methods either tend to require possibly expensive calculations regarding Hessians of lower-level objectives, or lack rigorous finite-time performance guarantees. In this work, we propose a Fully First-order Stochastic Approximation (F2SA) method, and study its non-asymptotic convergence properties. Specifically, we show that F2SA converges to an $\epsilon$-stationary solution of the bilevel problem after $\epsilon^{-7/2}, \epsilon^{-5/2}$, and $\epsilon^{-3/2}$ iterations (each iteration using $O(1)$ samples) when stochastic noises are in both level objectives, only in the upper-level objective, and not present (deterministic settings), respectively. We further show that if we employ momentum-assisted gradient estimators, the iteration complexities can be improved to $\epsilon^{-5/2}, \epsilon^{-4/2}$, and $\epsilon^{-3/2}$, respectively. We demonstrate even superior practical performance of the proposed method over existing second-order based approaches on MNIST data-hypercleaning experiments.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves two linked optimization problems: the upper problem depends on the outcome of the lower one. This paper studies stochastic, unconstrained problems where the available tools provide only gradients. That setting matters because methods requiring second derivatives of the lower objective can involve expensive calculations.

The authors introduce Fully First-order Stochastic Approximation, or F2SA, and establish finite-time convergence guarantees. Reaching an epsilon-stationary solution takes epsilon to the powers of −7/2, −5/2, and −3/2 iterations when noise affects both objectives, only the upper objective, or neither objective, respectively. Each iteration uses a constant number of samples. Stationarity is the target of these guarantees; it does not assert a globally optimal solution.

Adding momentum-assisted gradient estimates improves the first two iteration bounds to epsilon to the powers of −5/2 and −2, while leaving the deterministic bound unchanged. The paper also reports better practical performance than existing second-order approaches in MNIST data-hypercleaning experiments. Together, these results give a gradient-only method both theoretical support and an application-level demonstration.
summary.tldr: F2SA solves stochastic bilevel problems using only gradients, with finite-time stationarity guarantees and improved bounds from momentum.

title: A Fully First-Order Method for Stochastic Bilevel Optimization

abstract: To deal with the challenge of high cost of annotating all relevant labels for each example in multi-label learning, single-positive multi-label learning (SPMLL) has been studied in recent years, where each example is annotated with only one positive label. By adopting pseudo-label generation, i.e., assigning pseudo-label to each example by various strategies, existing methods have empirically validated that SPMLL would significantly reduce the amount of supervision with a tolerable damage in classification performance. However, there is no existing method that can provide a theoretical guarantee for learning from pseudo-label on SPMLL. In this paper, the conditions of the effectiveness of learning from pseudo-label for SPMLL are shown and the learnability of pseudo-label-based methods is proven. Furthermore, based on the theoretical guarantee of pseudo-label for SPMLL, we propose a novel SPMLL method named MIME, i.e., Mutual label enhancement for sIngle-positive Multi-label lEarning and prove that the generated pseudo-label by MIME approximately converges to the fully-supervised case. Experiments on four image datasets and five MLL datasets show the effectiveness of our methods over several existing SPMLL approaches.
