paragraphs: An example in multi-label learning can have several relevant labels, making complete annotation expensive. Single-positive multi-label learning reduces that burden by providing only one positive label per example. Existing methods use generated pseudo-labels to fill in supervision, but their empirical success had not been accompanied by theoretical guarantees for learning in this setting.

The paper establishes conditions under which learning from these pseudo-labels is effective and proves learnability for pseudo-label-based methods. Building on that analysis, the authors introduce MIME, a method for mutual label enhancement. They also prove that the pseudo-labels generated by MIME approximately converge toward the fully supervised case.

The approximate nature of that result matters: it supports recovering useful supervision without claiming that every missing label is always reconstructed exactly. Experiments on four image datasets and five multi-label learning datasets show effectiveness relative to several existing approaches. The contribution combines a theoretical account of when pseudo-labeling can work with a method designed around that account.
summary.tldr: MIME builds on conditions for learning from pseudo-labels to improve multi-label classification when each example has only one annotated positive label.

title: Revisiting Pseudo-Label for Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning

abstract: Indiscriminate data poisoning attacks aim to decrease a model’s test accuracy by injecting a small amount of corrupted training data. Despite significant interest, existing attacks remain relatively ineffective against modern machine learning (ML) architectures. In this work, we introduce the notion of model poisoning reachability as a technical tool to explore the intrinsic limits of data poisoning attacks towards target parameters (i.e., model-targeted attacks). We derive an easily computable threshold to establish and quantify a surprising phase transition phenomenon among popular ML models: data poisoning attacks can achieve certain target parameters only when the poisoning ratio exceeds our threshold. Building on existing parameter corruption attacks and refining the Gradient Canceling attack, we perform extensive experiments to confirm our theoretical findings, test the predictability of our transition threshold, and significantly improve existing indiscriminate data poisoning baselines over a range of datasets and models. Our work highlights the critical role played by the poisoning ratio, and sheds new insights on existing empirical results, attacks and mitigation strategies in data poisoning.

This paper investigates the intrinsic limits of attacks that try to steer training toward particular model parameters. Its central question is whether an attacker can reach a chosen parameter target with a given amount of poisoned data.

The authors introduce model poisoning reachability and derive an easily computed threshold for popular machine learning models. The experiments confirm the theoretical findings, examine how well the threshold predicts the transition, and substantially improve existing poisoning baselines across datasets and models. The threshold describes reachability of specified targets; exceeding it should not be read as a claim that every attack necessarily succeeds. The analysis also helps interpret existing attack results and mitigation strategies.
summary.tldr: A computable poisoning-ratio threshold reveals when certain target model parameters become reachable through corrupted training data.

title: Exploring the Limits of Model-Targeted Indiscriminate Data Poisoning Attacks

abstract: We introduce a new class of spatially stochastic physics and data informed deep latent models for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) which operate through scalable variational neural processes. We achieve this by assigning probability measures to the spatial domain, which allows us to treat collocation grids probabilistically as random variables to be marginalised out. Adapting this spatial statistics view, we solve forward and inverse problems for parametric PDEs in a way that leads to the construction of Gaussian process models of solution fields. The implementation of these random grids poses a unique set of challenges for inverse physics informed deep learning frameworks and we propose a new architecture called Grid Invariant Convolutional Networks (GICNets) to overcome these challenges. We further show how to incorporate noisy data in a principled manner into our physics informed model to improve predictions for problems where data may be available but whose measurement location does not coincide with any fixed mesh or grid. The proposed method is tested on a nonlinear Poisson problem, Burgers equation, and Navier-Stokes equations, and we provide extensive numerical comparisons. We demonstrate significant computational advantages over current physics informed neural learning methods for parametric PDEs while improving the predictive capabilities and flexibility of these models.

The approach uses scalable variational neural processes for both forward and inverse problems, leading to Gaussian-process models of solution fields. The central benefit is that the spatial sampling structure becomes part of the probabilistic model, allowing physics constraints and irregularly located measurements to be handled within the same approach.
summary.tldr: Random-grid neural processes treat spatial grids probabilistically to solve parametric PDEs efficiently while incorporating noisy measurements at arbitrary locations.

title: Random Grid Neural Processes for Parametric Partial Differential Equations

abstract: In model-free reinforcement learning, recent methods based on a phasic policy gradient (PPG) framework have shown impressive improvements in sample efficiency and zero-shot generalization on the challenging Procgen benchmark. In PPG, two design choices are believed to be the key contributing factors to its superior performance over PPO: the high level of value sample reuse and the low frequency of feature distillation. However, through an extensive empirical study, we unveil that policy regularization and data diversity are what actually matters. In particular, we can achieve the same level of performance with low value sample reuse and frequent feature distillation, as long as the policy regularization strength and data diversity are preserved. In addition, we can maintain the high performance of PPG while reducing the computational cost to a similar level as PPO. Our comprehensive study covers all 16 Procgen games in both sample efficiency and generalization setups. We hope it can advance the understanding of PPG and provide insights for future works.

paragraphs: Phasic Policy Gradient has shown strong sample efficiency and zero-shot generalization on Procgen. Its advantages over PPO were commonly attributed to extensive reuse of value-learning samples and infrequent feature distillation. This paper tests that explanation through an empirical study of which design choices actually sustain the observed performance.

The experiments identify policy regularization and data diversity as the crucial factors in the studied settings. The authors obtain comparable performance with less value-sample reuse and more frequent feature distillation when regularization strength and data diversity are preserved. This separates the effects of the training schedule from other properties that change alongside it.

The study covers all 16 Procgen games in both sample-efficiency and generalization setups. It also shows that PPG’s high performance can be maintained while reducing computation to a level similar to PPO. The findings provide an empirical basis for simplifying PPG and suggest that future designs should pay close attention to regularization and the diversity of training data.
summary.tldr: A Procgen study finds that policy regularization and data diversity sustain PPG’s performance, allowing computational cost to fall to a level similar to PPO.

title: PPG Reloaded: An Empirical Study on What Matters in Phasic Policy Gradient

abstract: Learning with expert advice and multi-armed bandit are two classic online decision problems which differ on how the information is observed in each round of the game. We study a family of problems interpolating the two. For a vector $\mathbf{m}=(m_1,…,m_K)\in \mathbb N^K$, an instance of $\mathbf m$-MAB indicates that the arms are partitioned into $K$ groups and the $i$-th group contains $m_i$ arms. Once an arm is pulled, the losses of all arms in the same group are observed. We prove tight minimax regret bounds for $\mathbf m$-MAB and design an optimal PAC algorithm for its pure exploration version, $\mathbf m$-BAI, where the goal is to identify the arm with minimum loss with as few rounds as possible. We show that the minimax regret of $\mathbf m$-MAB is $\Theta\left(\sqrt{T\sum_{k=1}^K\log (m_k+1)}\right)$ and the minimum number of pulls for an $(\varepsilon,0.05)$-PAC algorithm of $\mathbf m$-BAI is $\Theta\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\cdot \sum_{k=1}^K\log (m_k+1)\right)$. Both our upper bounds and lower bounds for $\mathbf m$-MAB can be extended to a more general setting, namely the bandit with graph feedback, in terms of the clique cover and related graph parameters. As consequences, we obtained tight minimax regret bounds for several families of feedback graphs.

paragraphs: Online decision problems differ in how much feedback a choice reveals. This paper studies a setting between expert advice and multi-armed bandits: options are divided into groups, and choosing one option reveals the losses of every option in its group. The group sizes determine how informative each observation can be.

For T rounds and group sizes m₁ through mK, the authors prove that minimax regret scales as the square root of T times the sum of log(mk + 1). Matching upper and lower bounds establish the optimal order of this dependence. The result captures how both the number of groups and their sizes affect achievable decision performance.

The paper also gives an optimal pure-exploration algorithm for identifying an approximately best option. At the stated confidence level, its sample requirement scales with that same logarithmic sum divided by the squared accuracy tolerance. Extensions to graph feedback use clique covers and related graph parameters, yielding tight regret bounds for several graph families and connecting grouped observations to more general feedback structures.
summary.tldr: The paper derives optimal regret and exploration bounds when choosing an option reveals feedback for an entire group of options.

title: On Interpolating Experts and Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: We present Neural Quantile Estimation (NQE), a novel Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) method based on conditional quantile regression. NQE autoregressively learns individual one dimensional quantiles for each posterior dimension, conditioned on the data and previous posterior dimensions. Posterior samples are obtained by interpolating the predicted quantiles using monotonic cubic Hermite spline, with specific treatment for the tail behavior and multi-modal distributions. We introduce an alternative definition for the Bayesian credible region using the local Cumulative Density Function (CDF), offering substantially faster evaluation than the traditional Highest Posterior Density Region (HPDR). In case of limited simulation budget and/or known model misspecification, a post-processing calibration step can be integrated into NQE to ensure the unbiasedness of the posterior estimation with negligible additional computational cost. We demonstrate that NQE achieves state-of-the-art performance on a variety of benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Neural Quantile Estimation, or NQE, performs simulation-based inference by learning conditional quantiles of a posterior distribution. It models one posterior dimension at a time, conditioning each on the observed data and the preceding dimensions. This autoregressive organization builds a multidimensional posterior from a sequence of one-dimensional quantile predictions.

To generate posterior samples, NQE interpolates its predicted quantiles with monotonic cubic Hermite splines. The procedure includes special handling of distribution tails and multiple modes. The paper also proposes a Bayesian credible-region definition based on the local cumulative distribution function, reporting substantially faster evaluation than the traditional highest-posterior-density-region approach.

For limited simulation budgets or known model misspecification, the authors introduce an optional post-processing calibration step intended to ensure unbiased posterior estimation with negligible additional computational expense. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across several benchmark problems. The overall contribution combines a quantile-based posterior representation, a sampling procedure, and a faster credible-region construction, with calibration available for the stated situations where simulation resources or model accuracy are constrained.
summary.tldr: NQE builds simulation-based posteriors through conditional quantile regression, with spline sampling, faster credible-region evaluation, and optional calibration.

title: Simulation-Based Inference with Quantile Regression

abstract: Current theoretical and empirical research in neural networks suggests that complex datasets require large network architectures for thorough classification, yet the precise nature of this relationship remains unclear. This paper tackles this issue by defining upper and lower bounds for neural network widths, which are informed by the polytope structure of the dataset in question. We also delve into the application of these principles to simplicial complexes and specific manifold shapes, explaining how the requirement for network width varies in accordance with the geometric complexity of the dataset. Moreover, we develop an algorithm to investigate a converse situation where the polytope structure of a dataset can be inferred from its corresponding trained neural networks. Through our algorithm, it is established that popular datasets such as MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR10 can be efficiently encapsulated using no more than two polytopes with a small number of faces.

paragraphs: The idea that more complex datasets need larger neural networks leaves an important question unanswered: which aspects of complexity determine the required architecture? This paper studies that relationship through the geometric structure of datasets. It uses their polytope structure to derive upper and lower bounds on network width for classification.

These bounds connect architectural size to a specific geometric description instead of treating dataset complexity as an informal property. The authors extend the analysis to simplicial complexes and particular manifold shapes, examining how different forms of geometric complexity affect width requirements. This provides a way to reason about the relationship between the shape of the data and network capacity.

The paper also investigates the reverse direction, developing an algorithm that infers a dataset's polytope structure from trained networks. Through this algorithm, the authors establish that MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR10 can be efficiently described using at most two polytopes with relatively few faces. The result concerns the inferred geometric description of these datasets and complements the theoretical bounds on architecture.
summary.tldr: The paper connects neural network width bounds to dataset geometry and infers compact polytope descriptions from trained networks.

title: Defining Neural Network Architecture through Polytope Structures of Datasets

abstract: Reasoning is a fundamental ability towards artificial general intelligence (AGI). Fueled by the success of deep learning, the neural logic machines models (NLMs) have introduced novel neural-symbolic structures and demonstrate great performance and generalization on reasoning and decision-making tasks. However, the original training approaches of the NLMs are still far from perfect, the models would repeat similar mistakes during the training process which leads to sub-optimal performance. To mitigate this issue, we present a novel framework named Failure Reflection Guided Regularizer (FRGR). FRGR first dynamically identifies and summarizes the root cause if the model repeats similar mistakes during training. Then it penalizes the model if it makes similar mistakes in future training iterations. In this way, the model is expected to avoid repeating errors of similar root causes and converge faster to a better-performed optimum. Experimental results on multiple relational reasoning and decision-making tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of FRGR in improving performance, generalization, training efficiency, and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Neural logic machines combine neural and symbolic structures for reasoning and decision-making. Although they can generalize well, their original training procedures can repeatedly produce similar mistakes, leading to suboptimal performance. This paper focuses on using those recurring failures as information that can guide subsequent training.

The proposed Failure Reflection Guided Regularizer first detects repeated mistakes and dynamically summarizes their root causes. It then penalizes the model when similar mistakes occur in later training iterations. This creates a feedback mechanism in which the model's history of failure shapes the regularization applied as learning continues.

The intended effect is to reduce repeated errors with similar causes and help training reach a better-performing solution more quickly. Experiments on multiple relational reasoning and decision-making tasks show improvements in performance, generalization, training efficiency, and data efficiency. These results support making recurring failure patterns an explicit part of the training objective, with benefits demonstrated across several aspects of learning in the evaluated neural logic machines.
summary.tldr: A regularizer that identifies and penalizes recurring error causes improves neural logic machines' reasoning performance and learning efficiency in experiments.

title: Improving Neural Logic Machines via Failure Reflection

abstract: We study interactive imitation learning, where a learner interactively queries a demonstrating expert for action annotations, aiming to learn a policy that has performance competitive with the expert, using as few annotations as possible. We focus on the general agnostic setting where the expert demonstration policy may not be contained in the policy class used by the learner. We propose a new oracle-efficient algorithm MFTPL-P (abbreviation for Mixed Follow the Perturbed Leader with Poisson perturbations) with provable finite-sample guarantees, under the assumption that the learner is given access to samples from some “explorative” distribution over states. Our guarantees hold for any policy class, which is considerably broader than prior state of the art. We further propose Bootstrap-DAgger, a more practical variant that does not require additional sample access.

paragraphs: Interactive imitation learning lets a learner ask an expert which action to take in particular states. The aim is to become competitive with that expert while requesting few annotations. This paper studies the agnostic setting: the learner’s available policy class may be unable to represent the expert’s policy exactly, making perfect imitation an unsuitable starting assumption.

The authors introduce MFTPL-P, short for Mixed Follow the Perturbed Leader with Poisson perturbations. It is an oracle-efficient algorithm with finite-sample guarantees that apply to any policy class. Those guarantees depend on access to samples from an additional explorative distribution over states. The broader coverage of policy classes is a central theoretical advance over the previous state of the art described in the abstract.

The paper also proposes Bootstrap-DAgger as a more practical variant that removes the need for this additional sample access. Together, the contributions address both formal learning guarantees under an explicit sampling assumption and an algorithm intended for a less demanding data-access setting.
summary.tldr: The paper develops broadly applicable guarantees for interactive imitation learning and a practical variant that avoids extra exploratory samples.

title: Agnostic Interactive Imitation Learning: New Theory and Practical Algorithms

abstract: Continual learning (CL) is a fundamental topic in machine learning, where the goal is to train a model with continuously incoming data and tasks. Due to the memory limit, we cannot store all the historical data, and therefore confront the “catastrophic forgetting” problem, i.e., the performance on the previous tasks can substantially decrease because of the missing information in the latter period. Though a number of elegant methods have been proposed, the catastrophic forgetting phenomenon still cannot be well avoided in practice. In this paper, we study the problem from the gradient perspective, where our aim is to develop an effective algorithm to calibrate the gradient in each updating step of the model; namely, our goal is to guide the model to be updated in the right direction under the situation that a large amount of historical data are unavailable. Our idea is partly inspired by the seminal stochastic variance reduction methods (e.g., SVRG and SAGA) for reducing the variance of gradient estimation in stochastic gradient descent algorithms. Another benefit is that our approach can be used as a general tool, which is able to be incorporated with several existing popular CL methods to achieve better performance. We also conduct a set of experiments on several benchmark datasets to evaluate the performance in practice.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model as new data and tasks arrive, without assuming that all earlier examples remain available. Memory constraints make this difficult: updates based on recent information can substantially damage performance on previous tasks. This paper addresses that forgetting problem by examining the gradients that determine each model update.

The proposed approach calibrates the gradient at every updating step. Its aim is to guide learning in a useful direction even when much of the historical data is missing. The idea draws partly on stochastic variance reduction methods, including SVRG and SAGA, which improve gradient estimation. Here, that inspiration is applied to the problem of learning across a changing sequence of tasks.

The method is also presented as a general tool that can be incorporated into several existing continual learning approaches to improve performance. The authors evaluate it on multiple benchmark datasets. The contribution is an update-level intervention that can complement existing methods, rather than requiring access to a complete archive of previous training data.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes calibrating each gradient update to reduce forgetting when continual learning cannot retain all historical data.

title: An Effective Dynamic Gradient Calibration Method for Continual Learning

abstract: No-reference image- and video-quality metrics are widely used in video processing benchmarks. The robustness of learning-based metrics under video attacks has not been widely studied. In addition to having success, attacks on metrics that can be employed in video processing benchmarks must be fast and imperceptible. This paper introduces an Invisible One-Iteration (IOI) adversarial attack on no-reference image and video quality metrics. The proposed method uses two modules to ensure high visual quality and temporal stability of adversarial videos and runs for one iteration, which makes it fast. We compared our method alongside eight prior approaches using image and video datasets via objective and subjective tests. Our method exhibited superior visual quality across various attacked metric architectures while maintaining comparable attack success and speed. We made the code available on GitHub: https://github.com/katiashh/ioi-attack.

paragraphs: No-reference quality metrics assess images or videos without comparing them with a reference version. These metrics are widely used in video-processing benchmarks, making their robustness relevant to how processing systems are evaluated. This paper investigates attacks that alter metric behavior while keeping the resulting media visually convincing.

The proposed Invisible One-Iteration attack, or IOI, runs for a single iteration to keep computation fast. It includes two modules aimed at preserving visual quality and temporal stability. The temporal requirement matters for videos because preserving individual frames alone does not address whether the sequence remains visually stable over time.

The authors compare IOI with eight previous approaches on image and video datasets, using both objective measurements and subjective tests. They report superior visual quality across different attacked metric architectures, with attack success and speed comparable to the alternatives. The finding is a favorable tradeoff among these requirements, particularly visual quality. It shows that effective attacks on the tested metrics can coexist with high-quality-looking media and fast execution.
summary.tldr: IOI attacks image and video quality metrics in one iteration, achieving better reported visual quality with comparable attack success and speed.

title: IOI: Invisible One-Iteration Adversarial Attack on No-Reference Image- and Video-Quality Metrics

abstract: We present a new algorithm for imitation learning in infinite horizon linear MDPs dubbed ILARL which greatly improves the bound on the number of trajectories that the learner needs to sample from the environment. In particular, we remove exploration assumptions required in previous works and we improve the dependence on the desired accuracy $\epsilon$ from $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-5})$ to $\mathcal{O} (\epsilon^{-4})$. Our result relies on a connection between imitation learning and online learning in MDPs with adversarial losses. For the latter setting, we present the first result for infinite horizon linear MDP which may be of independent interest. Moreover, we are able to provide a strengthen result for the finite horizon case where we achieve $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$. Numerical experiments with linear function approximation shows that ILARL outperforms other commonly used algorithms.

paragraphs: Imitation learning aims to learn behavior from demonstrations, but the learner may still need to collect trajectories from its environment. This paper introduces ILARL for infinite-horizon linear Markov decision processes and improves the theoretical bound on how many such trajectories are needed to reach a desired accuracy.

The result removes exploration assumptions used in earlier work. It also improves the accuracy dependence from an inverse fifth power to an inverse fourth power: as the required error tolerance becomes smaller, the bound grows less steeply. These are guarantees within the stated linear decision-process setting, where the structure of the problem supports the analysis.

The proof connects imitation learning to online learning in decision processes with adversarial losses. The authors develop an infinite-horizon result for that setting and obtain a stronger inverse-square accuracy dependence in the finite-horizon case. Experiments using linear function approximation also show ILARL outperforming commonly used alternatives. Together, the contributions combine improved sampling guarantees with empirical evidence in the evaluated approximation setting.
summary.tldr: ILARL improves imitation-learning trajectory bounds in linear decision processes while removing exploration assumptions required by prior work.

title: Imitation Learning in Discounted Linear MDPs without exploration assumptions

abstract: Causal representation learning aims at identifying high-level causal variables from perceptual data. Most methods assume that all latent causal variables are captured in the high-dimensional observations. We instead consider a partially observed setting, in which each measurement only provides information about a subset of the underlying causal state. Prior work has studied this setting with multiple domains or views, each depending on a fixed subset of latents. Here, we focus on learning from unpaired observations from a dataset with an instance-dependent partial observability pattern. Our main contribution is to establish two identifiability results for this setting: one for linear mixing functions without parametric assumptions on the underlying causal model, and one for piecewise linear mixing functions with Gaussian latent causal variables. Based on these insights, we propose two methods for estimating the underlying causal variables by enforcing sparsity in the inferred representation. Experiments on different simulated datasets and established benchmarks highlight the effectiveness of our approach in recovering the ground-truth latents.

This paper considers measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state, with the visible subset changing from one example to another. The observations are also unpaired, so the learner cannot rely on matched views of the same state to connect the missing pieces.

title: A Sparsity Principle for Partially Observable Causal Representation Learning

abstract: Agents built with large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential across a wide range of domains. However, in complex decision-making tasks, pure LLM-based agents tend to exhibit intrinsic bias in their choice of actions, which is inherited from the model’s training data and results in suboptimal performance. To develop strategic language agents, i.e., agents that generate flexible language actions and possess strong decision-making abilities, we propose a novel framework that powers LLM-based agents with reinforcement learning (RL). We consider Werewolf, a popular social deduction game, as a challenging testbed that emphasizes versatile communication and strategic gameplay. To mitigate the intrinsic bias in language actions, our agents use an LLM to perform deductive reasoning and generate a diverse set of action candidates. Then an RL policy trained to optimize the decision-making ability chooses an action from the candidates to play in the game. Extensive experiments show that our agents overcome the intrinsic bias and outperform existing LLM-based agents in the Werewolf game. We also conduct human-agent experiments and find that our agents achieve human-level performance and demonstrate strong strategic play.

paragraphs: Language models can produce flexible dialogue, but their preferred actions may reflect biases inherited from training data rather than sound strategy. This paper studies that problem in Werewolf, a social deduction game requiring both communication and decision-making. The aim is to combine language generation with action selection trained for strategic play.

The framework assigns different responsibilities to the language model and the reinforcement learning policy. The language model performs deductive reasoning and generates a diverse set of possible actions. The trained policy then chooses which candidate to use in the game. This gives the decision-making component alternatives beyond the language model’s own preferred response.

Experiments show that the resulting agents overcome the identified action bias and outperform existing language-model agents in Werewolf. In human-agent experiments, they also achieve human-level performance and exhibit strong strategic play. These findings support separating candidate generation from learned strategic selection in this testbed. The human-level result refers to the evaluated game setting, rather than unrestricted human-level reasoning.
summary.tldr: An LLM generates candidate actions while a reinforcement learning policy selects strategically effective moves in Werewolf.

title: Language Agents with Reinforcement Learning for Strategic Play in the Werewolf Game

abstract: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) methods have obtained promising results with moderate model complexity. These approaches primarily focus on a lightweight architecture design, but neglect to further reduce network redundancy. While some model compression techniques try to achieve more lightweight SR models with neural architecture search, knowledge distillation, or channel pruning, they typically require considerable extra computational resources or neglect to prune weights. To address these issues, we propose a flexible meta pruning (FMP) for lightweight image SR, where the network channels and weights are pruned simultaneously. Specifically, we control the network sparsity via channel vectors and weight indicators. We feed them into a hypernetwork, whose parameters act as meta-data for the parameters of the SR backbone. Consequently, for each network layer, we conduct structured pruning with channel vectors, which control the output and input channels. Besides, we conduct unstructured pruning with weight indicators to influence the sparsity of kernel weights, resulting in flexible pruning. During pruning, the sparsity of both channel vectors and weight indicators are regularized. We optimize the channel vectors and weight indicators with proximal gradient and SGD. We conduct extensive experiments to investigate critical factors in the flexible channel and weight pruning for image SR, demonstrating the superiority of our FMP when applied to baseline image SR architectures.

paragraphs: Lightweight image super-resolution models aim to improve image resolution with moderate computational complexity. Designing a small architecture can still leave redundant channels and weights inside it. Flexible Meta Pruning, or FMP, addresses both forms of redundancy together, extending compression beyond removing only whole channels.

FMP represents the pruning decisions with channel vectors and weight indicators. Channel vectors control the input and output channels of each layer, providing structured pruning. Weight indicators control the sparsity of individual kernel weights, providing unstructured pruning. Both are supplied to a hypernetwork whose parameters serve as metadata for the super-resolution backbone’s parameters, linking the pruning controls with the model being compressed.

During pruning, the method regularizes the sparsity of both kinds of controls and optimizes them using proximal gradient and stochastic gradient descent. Experiments examine factors affecting joint channel and weight pruning and report superior results when FMP is applied to baseline super-resolution architectures. The contribution is a flexible mechanism for combining two levels of compression within the same model, supported by the reported experimental comparisons.
summary.tldr: Flexible Meta Pruning compresses image super-resolution networks by jointly pruning whole channels and individual weights through hypernetwork-based controls.

title: Lightweight Image Super-Resolution via Flexible Meta Pruning

abstract: As a data-driven paradigm, offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been formulated as sequence modeling that conditions on the hindsight information including returns, goal or future trajectory. Although promising, this supervised paradigm overlooks the core objective of RL that maximizes the return. This overlook directly leads to the lack of trajectory stitching capability that affects the sequence model learning from sub-optimal data. In this work, we introduce the concept of max-return sequence modeling which integrates the goal of maximizing returns into existing sequence models. We propose Reinforced Transformer (Reinformer), indicating the sequence model is reinforced by the RL objective. Reinformer additionally incorporates the objective of maximizing returns in the training phase, aiming to predict the maximum future return within the distribution. During inference, this in-distribution maximum return will guide the selection of optimal actions. Empirically, Reinformer is competitive with classical RL methods on the D4RL benchmark and outperforms state-of-the-art sequence model particularly in trajectory stitching ability. Code is public at https://github.com/Dragon-Zhuang/Reinformer.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can be treated as sequence prediction using recorded experience and information such as eventual rewards or goals. The paper argues that this supervised formulation can neglect the central reinforcement learning objective of maximizing return. That omission limits trajectory stitching: the ability to combine useful portions of recorded trajectories when the available behavior is suboptimal.

Reinformer adds return maximization directly to sequence-model training. It aims to predict the highest future return within the data distribution, then uses that predicted return to guide action selection at inference time. The distinction is consequential: the model is trained to identify a high-return target supported by its distribution, as well as to model sequences conditioned on outcomes.

On the D4RL benchmark, Reinformer is competitive with classical reinforcement learning methods and outperforms the state-of-the-art sequence model considered, particularly in trajectory stitching. These results support integrating the optimization objective into sequence learning when recorded trajectories are imperfect. The predicted maximum remains explicitly tied to the distribution, which defines the kind of return the method aims to pursue.
summary.tldr: Reinformer trains sequence models to maximize in-distribution future returns, improving their ability to stitch together useful recorded behavior.

title: Reinformer: Max-Return Sequence Modeling for Offline RL

abstract: A key component of transformers is the attention mechanism orchestrating how each token influences the propagation of every other token along the layers of a transformer. In this paper we provide a rigorous, mathematical analysis of the asymptotic properties of attention in transformers. Although we present several results based on different assumptions, all of them point to the same conclusion, all tokens asymptotically converge to each other, a phenomenon that has been empirically reported in the literature. Our findings are carefully compared with existing theoretical results and illustrated by simulations and experimental studies using the GPT-2 model.

In this paper we provide a rigorous, mathematical analysis of the asymptotic properties of attention in transformers. paragraphs: Attention determines how tokens influence one another as their representations pass through transformer layers. This paper asks what happens to those representations asymptotically: what behavior emerges as the propagation process continues toward its limiting regime? The focus is a mathematical account of attention's long-term behavior, connecting the mechanism's interactions to the eventual relationship among tokens.

The authors establish several results under different assumptions. Across those results, token representations converge toward one another, producing a form of consensus. This gives theoretical support to a phenomenon previously observed empirically. The assumptions remain part of each result: the shared conclusion describes the analyzed settings rather than establishing that every finite transformer computation must make all tokens identical.

The paper compares its findings with earlier theoretical work and illustrates them through simulations and experiments involving GPT-2. Together, these elements connect limiting mathematical behavior with observations in a language model. The significance is a clearer account of how attention can progressively reduce differences among token representations, and a framework for interpreting the convergence observed in the studied systems.
summary.tldr: Under several analyzed sets of assumptions, attention makes token representations converge toward one another asymptotically.

title: Consensus Is All You Get: The Role of Attention in Transformers

abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) provide more nuanced supervision compared to outcome reward models (ORMs) for optimizing policy models, positioning them as a promising approach to enhancing the capabilities of LLMs in complex reasoning tasks. Recent efforts have advanced PRMs from step-level to token-level granularity by integrating reward modeling into the training of generative models, with reward scores derived from token generation probabilities. However, the conflict between generative language modeling and reward modeling may introduce instability and lead to inaccurate credit assignments. To address this challenge, we revisit token-level reward assignment by decoupling reward modeling from language generation and derive a token-level reward model through the optimization of a discriminative policy, termed the Q-function Reward Model (Q-RM). We theoretically demonstrate that Q-RM explicitly learns token-level Q-functions from preference data without relying on fine-grained annotations. In our experiments, Q-RM consistently outperforms all baseline methods across various benchmarks. For example, when integrated into PPO/REINFORCE algorithms, Q-RM enhances the average Pass@1 score by 5.85/4.70 points on mathematical reasoning tasks compared to the ORM baseline, and by 4.56/5.73 points compared to the token-level PRM counterpart. Moreover, reinforcement learning with Q-RM significantly enhances training efficiency, achieving convergence 12$\times$ faster than ORM on GSM8K and 11$\times$ faster than step-level PRM on MATH. Code and data are available at https://github.com/homzer/Q-RM.

paragraphs: Reward models can judge an entire answer or provide finer feedback during its construction. Token-level feedback offers detailed credit assignment, but deriving rewards from generation probabilities mixes language generation with reward modeling. The authors argue that these objectives can conflict, causing unstable training and inaccurate judgments about individual tokens.

Their Q-function Reward Model separates reward modeling from generation by optimizing a discriminative policy. These results link improved reward assignment with both stronger answers and faster training in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Q-RM learns token-level rewards from preferences independently of language generation, improving reasoning performance and training speed in reported evaluations.

title: Discriminative Policy Optimization for Token-Level Reward Models

abstract: Inductive knowledge graph completion aims to predict missing triplets in an incomplete knowledge graph that differs from the one observed during training. While subgraph reasoning models have demonstrated empirical success in this task, their theoretical properties, such as stability and generalization capability, remain unexplored. In this work, we present the first theoretical analysis of the relationship between the stability and the generalization capability for subgraph reasoning models. Specifically, we define stability as the degree of consistency in a subgraph reasoning model’s outputs in response to differences in input subgraphs and introduce the Relational Tree Mover’s Distance as a metric to quantify the differences between the subgraphs. We then show that the generalization capability of subgraph reasoning models, defined as the discrepancy between the performance on training data and test data, is proportional to their stability. Furthermore, we empirically analyze the impact of stability on generalization capability using real-world datasets, validating our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Inductive knowledge graph completion predicts missing relationships in a graph different from the one used for training. Subgraph reasoning models have performed well empirically on this task, but their ability to transfer raises a theoretical question: how does sensitivity to changes in local graph structure relate to the gap between training and test performance?

The paper defines stability through the consistency of a model’s outputs when its input subgraphs differ. To measure those input differences, the authors introduce Relational Tree Mover’s Distance. This supplies a way to relate changes in relational graph structure to changes in the predictions produced by a subgraph reasoning model.

The analysis establishes a proportional relationship between the stability quantity and generalization, expressed as the discrepancy between training and test performance. Experiments on real-world datasets examine the effect of stability and validate the theoretical findings. The contribution gives a formal account of an observed modeling concern: understanding transfer to a new knowledge graph requires examining how predictions respond to differences in the subgraphs used for reasoning.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis connects subgraph reasoning models’ sensitivity to structural changes with their training-to-test generalization gap.

title: Stability and Generalization Capability of Subgraph Reasoning Models for Inductive Knowledge Graph Completion

abstract: To defend against privacy leakage of user data, differential privacy is widely used in federated learning, but it is not free. The addition of noise randomly disrupts the semantic integrity of the model and this disturbance accumulates with increased communication rounds. In this paper, we introduce a novel federated learning framework with rigorous privacy guarantees, named FedCEO, designed to strike a trade-off between model utility and user privacy by letting clients "C*ollaborate with Each Other". Specifically, we perform efficient tensor low-rank proximal optimization on stacked local model parameters at the server, demonstrating its capability to flexibly truncate high-frequency components in spectral space. This capability implies that our FedCEO can effectively recover the disrupted semantic information by smoothing the global semantic space for different privacy settings and continuous training processes. Moreover, we improve the SOTA utility-privacy trade-off bound by order of $\sqrt{d}$, where $d$ is the input dimension. We illustrate our theoretical results with experiments on representative datasets and observe significant performance improvements and strict privacy guarantees under different privacy settings. The *code is available at https://github.com/6lyc/FedCEO_Collaborate-with-Each-Other.

FedCEO addresses the resulting tension between privacy protection and model usefulness by processing clients’ models together at the server.

Together, the results support coordinated server-side processing as a way to improve useful learning while retaining the framework’s stated privacy guarantees.
summary.tldr: FedCEO jointly smooths client model parameters to improve the utility-privacy trade-off in federated learning with rigorous privacy guarantees.

title: Clients Collaborate: Flexible Differentially Private Federated Learning with Guaranteed Improvement of Utility-Privacy Trade-off

abstract: Constrained optimization problems arise in various engineering systems such as inventory management and power grids. Standard deep neural network (DNN) based machine learning proxies are ineffective in practical settings where labeled data is scarce and training times are limited. We propose a semi-supervised Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) based optimization proxy for this complex regime, wherein training commences in a sandwiched fashion, alternating between a supervised learning step for minimizing cost, and an unsupervised learning step for enforcing constraint feasibility. We show that the proposed semi-supervised BNN outperforms DNN architectures on important non-convex constrained optimization problems from energy network operations, achieving up to a tenfold reduction in expected maximum equality gap and halving the inequality gaps. Further, the BNN’s ability to provide posterior samples is leveraged to construct practically meaningful probabilistic confidence bounds on performance using a limited validation data, unlike prior methods.

paragraphs: Engineering optimization often requires reducing a cost while satisfying strict constraints. Learned proxies aim to approximate these decisions, but the authors identify limited labeled data and short training budgets as difficult conditions for standard deep neural networks. They propose a semi-supervised Bayesian neural network designed for this constrained setting.

Training alternates between two complementary steps. A supervised step learns to minimize cost, and an unsupervised step works on constraint feasibility. This alternating arrangement gives both the objective and the constraints an explicit role in training. The Bayesian model also provides posterior samples, which the authors use to construct probabilistic confidence bounds on performance from limited validation data.

On important non-convex problems in energy network operations, the proposed model outperforms the evaluated deep neural network architectures. Reported gains include up to a tenfold reduction in the expected maximum equality gap and a halving of inequality gaps. These findings concern how closely proposed solutions satisfy constraints, while the confidence bounds provide an additional way to assess expected performance under scarce validation data.
summary.tldr: A semi-supervised Bayesian optimization proxy improves constraint satisfaction under limited data and training time while providing probabilistic performance bounds.

title: Optimization Proxies using Limited Labeled Data and Training Time – A Semi-Supervised Bayesian Neural Network Approach

abstract: Minority samples are underrepresented instances located in low-density regions of a data manifold, and are valuable in many generative AI applications, such as data augmentation, creative content generation, etc. Unfortunately, existing diffusion-based minority generators often rely on computationally expensive guidance dedicated for minority generation. To address this, here we present a simple yet powerful guidance-free approach called Boost-and-Skip for generating minority samples using diffusion models. The key advantage of our framework requires only two minimal changes to standard generative processes: (i) variance-boosted initialization and (ii) timestep skipping. We highlight that these seemingly-trivial modifications are supported by solid theoretical and empirical evidence, thereby effectively promoting emergence of underrepresented minority features. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that Boost-and-Skip greatly enhances the capability of generating minority samples, even rivaling guidance-based state-of-the-art approaches while requiring significantly fewer computations. Code is available at https://github.com/soobin-um/BnS.

paragraphs: This paper aims to generate examples from parts of a data distribution that are poorly represented. Here, minority samples mean instances in low-density regions of the data manifold. Producing such examples can be useful for applications including data augmentation and creative generation, but existing diffusion approaches often use costly guidance specifically designed for that purpose.

Boost-and-Skip changes two parts of the diffusion generation process: it increases the variance of the initialization and skips timesteps. It requires no dedicated minority-generation guidance. The authors support these changes with theoretical analysis and empirical evidence showing that they encourage underrepresented features to appear in generated samples.

The reported experiments show a substantial improvement in minority generation, with results that rival leading guidance-based approaches while using significantly less computation. The significance lies in achieving that behavior through small changes to the generation procedure. The findings support this simpler route to exploring underrepresented regions without asserting that it outperforms guided generation in every setting.
summary.tldr: Boost-and-Skip promotes underrepresented diffusion samples through higher-variance initialization and timestep skipping, rivaling guided approaches with less computation in the reported experiments.

title: Boost-and-Skip: A Simple Guidance-Free Diffusion for Minority Generation

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown great potential in general robotic decision-making tasks via imitation learning. However, the variable quality of training data often constrains the performance of these models. On the other hand, offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) excels at learning robust policy models from mixed-quality data. In this paper, we introduce Reinforced robot GPT (ReinboT), a novel end-to-end VLA model that integrates the RL principle of maximizing cumulative reward. ReinboT achieves a deeper understanding of the data quality distribution by predicting dense returns that capture the nuances of manipulation tasks. The dense return prediction capability enables the robot to generate more robust decision-making actions, oriented towards maximizing future benefits. Extensive experiments show that ReinboT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN mixed-quality dataset and exhibits superior few-shot learning and out-of-distribution generalization capabilities in real-world tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models connect visual observations and language to robot decisions, often learning by imitating recorded behavior. Their performance can be constrained when demonstrations vary in quality. ReinboT introduces an end-to-end model that incorporates the reinforcement learning objective of maximizing cumulative reward to make better use of mixed-quality training data.

The model predicts dense returns that capture differences in manipulation behavior and its expected future benefits. These predictions provide a way to represent the quality distribution within the data and guide action generation toward more rewarding outcomes. This connects the model’s understanding of observations and instructions with an explicit assessment of the consequences of its decisions.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN mixed-quality dataset, along with superior few-shot learning and out-of-distribution generalization in real-world tasks. The results support incorporating reward-oriented learning into vision-language-action modeling. In particular, they show the value of distinguishing behavior by its anticipated return when the available examples contain a mixture of stronger and weaker robot performance.
summary.tldr: ReinboT uses dense return prediction to bring reward-maximizing learning into a vision-language-action model, improving robot performance with mixed-quality data.

title: ReinboT: Amplifying Robot Visual-Language Manipulation with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this work, we address the test-time adaptation challenge in graph neural networks (GNNs), focusing on overcoming the limitations in flexibility and generalization inherent in existing data-centric approaches. To this end, we propose a novel research problem, test-time graph neural dataset search, which seeks to learn a parameterized test-time graph distribution to enhance the inference performance of unseen test graphs on well-trained GNNs. Specifically, we propose a generative Projection based test-time Graph Neural Dataset Search method, named PGNDS, which maps the unseen test graph distribution back to the known training distribution through a generation process guided by well-trained GNNs. The proposed PGNDS framework consists of three key modules: (1) dual conditional diffusion for GNN-guided generative projection through test-back-to-training distribution mapping; (2) dynamic search from the generative sampling space to select the most expressive test graphs; (3) ensemble inference to aggregate information from original and adapted test graphs. Extensive experiments on real-world graphs demonstrate the superior ability of our proposed PGNDS for improved test-time GNN inference.

summary.tldr: PGNDS generates and searches adapted test graphs, then combines them with original graphs to improve GNN inference.

title: Test-Time Graph Neural Dataset Search With Generative Projection

abstract: Recently, long-context large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in information retrieval and long-document QA. However, to tackle the most challenging intellectual problems, LLMs must reason effectively in long and complex contexts (e.g., frontier mathematical research). Studying how LLMs handle increasing reasoning complexity and context length is essential, yet existing benchmarks lack a solid basis for quantitative evaluation. Inspired by the abstraction of GSM-8K problems as computational graphs—and the ability to introduce noise by adding unnecessary nodes and edges—we develop a grade-school math problem generator capable of producing arithmetic problems with infinite difficulty and context length under fine-grained control. Using our newly synthesized GSM-$\infty$ benchmark, we comprehensively evaluate existing LLMs. We find a consistent sigmoid decline in reasoning performance as complexity increases, along with a systematic inference scaling trend: exponentially increasing inference computation yields only linear performance gains. These findings underscore the fundamental limitations of current long-context LLMs and the key challenges in scaling reasoning capabilities. Our GSM-$\infty$ benchmark provides a scalable and controllable testbed for systematically studying and advancing LLM reasoning in long and complex contexts.

paragraphs: Success at retrieving information from long documents leaves open how well language models reason when both context and problem complexity grow. GSM-∞ provides a controlled way to study this question using generated arithmetic problems. Its generator can increase difficulty and context length without a fixed ceiling, making the benchmark extensible as model capabilities change.

The approach represents grade-school math problems as computational graphs. Necessary calculations define the reasoning structure, while unnecessary nodes and edges introduce distracting information. This construction provides fine-grained control over problem complexity and context length, allowing the authors to examine how performance changes as the generated tasks become more demanding.

The evaluated models show a consistent sigmoid-shaped decline in reasoning performance as complexity increases. The benchmark's main value is its controllable generation process, which supports systematic investigation of those patterns.
summary.tldr: GSM-∞ generates controllably harder and longer math problems, revealing declining reasoning performance and limited gains from increased inference computation.

title: GSM-$∞$: How Do your LLMs Behave over Infinitely Increasing Reasoning Complexity and Context Length?

abstract: When developing new large language models (LLMs), a key step is evaluating their final performance, often by computing the win-rate against a reference model based on external feedback. Human feedback is the gold standard, particularly for capturing nuanced qualities like coherence, readability, and alignment with human expectations. However, human evaluations are costly—even for large tech companies—and when conducted with active users, they may negatively impact user experience. A promising alternative is synthetic feedback, where evaluations are conducted by other large language models, including reward models. While this eliminates the need for costly human annotations, it introduces biases that may distort the evaluation process. In this work, we propose a statistically principled framework that integrates human and synthetic feedback to reduce reliance on human annotations while maintaining unbiased win-rate calculations. Our experiments demonstrate a reduction in human annotations by up to 12.2% with an off-the-shelf synthetic evaluator and up to 24.8% with a finetuned variant. Apart from being generalizable, scalable, and free of hyper-parameter tuning, our method offers predictable annotation savings, which can be estimated based on data-dependent characteristics.

paragraphs: Evaluating a language model often means estimating how frequently people prefer its answers to those of a reference model. Human judgments capture qualities such as readability and coherence, but collecting them is expensive and can disrupt active users. Synthetic evaluators offer a cheaper source of feedback, although their preferences can introduce bias into the estimated win rate.

This paper develops a statistical framework that combines human judgments with synthetic feedback while preserving unbiased win-rate calculations. The purpose is to reduce the amount of human annotation needed without allowing the synthetic evaluator's biases to distort the final estimate. Human feedback remains part of the evaluation process, while synthetic judgments help make that process more economical.

Experiments report annotation reductions of up to 12.2% using an off-the-shelf synthetic evaluator and up to 24.8% with a fine-tuned evaluator. The method requires no hyperparameter tuning, and its anticipated savings can be estimated from characteristics of the data. These findings make the contribution both an evaluation procedure and a way to anticipate its annotation benefits.
summary.tldr: Combining human and synthetic feedback preserves unbiased win-rate estimates while reducing human annotation needs by up to 24.8% in the reported experiments.

title: Accelerating Unbiased LLM Evaluation via Synthetic Feedback

abstract: Foundation models compress a large amount of information in a single, large neural network, which can then be queried for individual tasks. There are strong parallels between this widespread framework and offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning algorithms: a universal value function is trained on a large number of goals, and the policy is evaluated on a single goal in each test episode. Extensive research in foundation models has shown that performance can be substantially improved through test-time training, specializing the model to the current goal. We find similarly that test-time offline reinforcement learning on experience related to the test goal can lead to substantially better policies at modest compute costs. We propose a novel self-supervised data selection criterion, which selects transitions from an offline dataset according to their relevance to the current state and quality with respect to the evaluation goal. We demonstrate across a wide range of high-dimensional loco-navigation and manipulation tasks that fine-tuning a policy on the selected data for a few gradient steps leads to significant performance gains over standard offline pre-training. Our goal-conditioned test-time training (GC-TTT) algorithm applies this routine in a receding-horizon fashion during evaluation, adapting the policy to the current trajectory as it is being rolled out. Finally, we study compute allocation at inference, demonstrating that, at comparable costs, GC-TTT induces performance gains that are not achievable by scaling model size.

paragraphs: A policy trained for many goals is evaluated on a particular goal during each episode. It finds that a small amount of offline reinforcement learning on goal-related experience can produce better policies at modest computational cost.

summary.tldr: GC-TTT improves goal-conditioned policies during evaluation through brief updates on relevant offline experience.

title: Test-time Offline Reinforcement Learning on Goal-related Experience

abstract: Normalizing Flows (NFs) are a classical family of likelihood based methods that have received revived attention. Recent efforts such as TARFlow have shown that NFs are capable to achieving promising performance on image modeling tasks, making them promising alternatives to other methods such as diffusion models. In this work, we further advance the state of Normalizing Flow generative models by introducing iterative TARFlow (iTARFlow). Unlike diffusion models, iTARFlow maintains a fully end-to-end, likelihood-based objective during training. During sampling, it performs autoregressive generation followed by an iterative denoising procedure inspired by diffusion-style methods. Through extensive experiments, We show that iTARFlow achieves competitive performance across ImageNet resolutions of 64, 128, and 256 pixels, demonstrating its potential as a strong generative model and advances the frontier of Normalizing Flows. In addition, we analyze the characteristic artifacts produced by iTARFlow, offering insights that may shed the light for future improvements.

paragraphs: This paper develops normalizing flows as an approach to image generation by extending TARFlow into iterative TARFlow, or iTARFlow. The motivation is that recent flow models already show promising image-modeling performance, creating an opportunity to improve their generation process while retaining their likelihood-based training formulation.

iTARFlow keeps a fully end-to-end likelihood objective during training. At sampling time, it first generates autoregressively and then applies iterative denoising inspired by diffusion methods. The distinction between these stages matters: the model borrows a refinement procedure associated with diffusion while preserving the training objective characteristic of the flow approach.

The authors also examine characteristic artifacts in the generated images, using them to identify directions that may inform future improvements. summary.tldr: iTARFlow adds iterative denoising during image sampling while retaining end-to-end likelihood-based normalizing-flow training.

title: Normalizing Flows with Iterative Denoising

abstract: Mixed-integer optimization solvers often find optimal solutions early in the search, yet spend the majority of computation time proving optimality. We exploit this by learning when to terminate solvers early on distributions of similar problem instances. Our method trains a neural network to estimate the true optimality gap from the solver state, then uses conformal prediction to calibrate a stopping threshold with rigorous probabilistic guarantees on solution quality. On six problem families from the Distributional MIPLIB library, our method reduces solve time by over 60% while guaranteeing 0.1%-optimal solutions with 95% probability for new instances drawn from the same distribution.

paragraphs: Mixed-integer optimization solvers can find an optimal solution well before they finish proving that no better solution exists. That gap between finding and certifying a solution creates an opportunity to save computation. This paper learns when to stop a solver on recurring problems drawn from a distribution of similar instances.

A neural network examines the solver’s state and estimates the true optimality gap: how far the current solution is from the best possible one. Conformal prediction then calibrates the stopping threshold. This calibration turns a learned estimate into a stopping rule with a probabilistic guarantee on solution quality, allowing termination before a full optimality proof.

Across six problem families from Distributional MIPLIB, the method reduces solve time by more than 60%. Its stated guarantee is a 0.1%-optimal solution with 95% probability for new instances from the same distribution. That distributional condition matters: the result supports faster solving with calibrated quality assurance when future instances follow the problem distribution used by the method.
summary.tldr: A conformally calibrated stopping rule cuts reported solve time by over 60% while guaranteeing 0.1%-optimal solutions with 95% probability on same-distribution instances.

title: Conformal Prediction for Early Stopping in Mixed Integer Optimization

abstract: The advancements of Large Language Models (LLMs) are primarily attributed to massive pretraining data, which also introduces risks like privacy leakage and data contamination. Therefore, it is crucial to determine whether an LLM has been trained on a given target text. Existing detection methods primarily rely on local statistics of isolated tokens (e.g., those with the lowest probabilities), neglecting the probability dynamics during the token generation process. In this paper, we shift the detection paradigm from a local token to a global sequence perspective, grounded in the core intuition that memorized sequences exhibit volatility patterns distinct from those generated via inference. We propose Adaptive Entropic Convolutional Analysis (AECA), a framework that conceptualizes the probability sequence as a dynamic signal, integrating calibration with convolutional filtering to effectively capture memorization signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AECA surpasses previous methods by up to 1.5% in average AUC on the WikiMIA benchmark, with its advantage being particularly pronounced in long-text scenarios.

paragraphs: Determining whether a text appeared in an LLM’s pretraining data matters for investigating privacy leakage and data contamination. Existing detection methods often summarize isolated token probabilities, such as focusing on particularly unlikely tokens. This paper instead examines how probabilities change across a sequence, treating their evolution as potentially informative evidence about memorization.

Adaptive Entropic Convolutional Analysis, or AECA, represents the sequence of token probabilities as a dynamic signal. It combines calibration with convolutional filtering to capture patterns in that signal. The motivating intuition is that memorized sequences have different volatility patterns from sequences handled through inference, making relationships across tokens useful for detection.

On the WikiMIA benchmark, the authors report improvements of up to 1.5% in average AUC over previous methods. The advantage is especially pronounced for longer texts. These findings support considering sequence-wide probability dynamics alongside the local statistics that have dominated earlier detection approaches. The reported result concerns improved discrimination on the benchmark, with the strongest gains appearing in its long-text scenarios.
summary.tldr: AECA detects possible pretraining membership from sequence-wide probability dynamics, improving WikiMIA results especially for long texts.

title: Rethinking Pretraining Data Detection for LLMs: From Local to Global

abstract: To distinguish Markov equivalent graphs in causal discovery, it is necessary to restrict the structural causal model. A flexible class of models that is general and identifiable in most cases are location-scale noise models (LSNMs), in which the effect $Y$ is modeled based on its causes $\boldsymbol{X}$ as $Y = f(\boldsymbol{X}) + g(\boldsymbol{X})N$. To facilitate the estimation of these models, a prominent assumption is that the noise variable $N$ follows a symmetric distribution. We show that when $N$ is a skewed random variable, which is likely in real-world domains, such approaches drop in performance. To address this limitation, we propose SkewD, a likelihood-based method for causal discovery under LSNMs with skewed noise, employing a combination of heuristic search and expectation conditional maximization for parameter estimation. SkewD extends the usual normal distribution framework to the skew-normal setting, enabling reliable inference under symmetric and skewed noise. While our main focus is on bivariate cause-effect inference, we further showcase how SkewD can be extended to the multivariate setting.

paragraphs: Different causal graphs can imply the same observational relationships, so distinguishing them requires restrictions on the causal model. This paper studies location-scale noise models, where causes determine both the central response and the scale of random variation. These models are flexible and identifiable in most cases, but prominent estimation approaches assume symmetric noise.

The authors show that those approaches lose performance when the noise is skewed. Their proposed method, SkewD, extends the usual normal-noise formulation to a skew-normal setting. It uses likelihood-based inference, combining heuristic search with expectation conditional maximization to estimate model parameters.

Allowing skewness enables the method to handle both symmetric and asymmetric noise within the proposed framework. This matters because imposing symmetry can distort the comparison between competing causal explanations when the data's variation is uneven. The paper concentrates on deciding causal direction between two variables and also demonstrates how SkewD can be extended to multivariate problems, giving a path beyond its main bivariate setting.
summary.tldr: SkewD extends location-scale causal discovery to skew-normal noise, addressing performance losses caused by assuming symmetric variation.

title: Skewness-Robust Causal Discovery in Location-Scale Noise Models

abstract: Riemannian diffusion models generalize score-based generative modeling to manifold-supported data via stochastic diffusion equations on the manifold. However, training requires sampling from and differentiating the manifold heat kernel, which is rarely available in closed form beyond a few highly symmetric manifolds. We propose a general approach that approximates the heat kernel by directly solving the manifold heat equation with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). Given an explicit manifold specification, we choose a coordinate system, derive the corresponding heat (Fokker–Planck) equation and a short-time asymptotic approximation, and then train a PINN to learn the log heat kernel. The resulting surrogate enables both forward noising (heat-kernel sampling) and conditional-score evaluation for denoising score matching. We demonstrate the method on diverse manifolds including $S^2$, $SO(3)$, $\mathrm{SPD}(n)$, and permutation-quotiented point clouds.

paragraphs: Diffusion models for manifold-supported data must add and remove noise in ways that respect the underlying geometry. Their training relies on the manifold heat kernel, which describes the diffusion process. Sampling from it and computing its derivatives are difficult because closed-form expressions are available for only a limited set of highly symmetric manifolds.

This paper approximates the heat kernel by solving the manifold heat equation with a physics-informed neural network. Starting from an explicit manifold specification, the authors choose coordinates, derive the associated heat equation and a short-time asymptotic approximation, and train a network to represent the log heat kernel.

The learned surrogate supports both forward noising through heat-kernel sampling and conditional-score evaluation for denoising score matching. The approach is demonstrated on the sphere S², the rotation group SO(3), positive-definite matrix manifolds, and permutation-quotiented point clouds. Its contribution is a general construction for obtaining the diffusion quantities needed for training when an explicit manifold description is available.
summary.tldr: A physics-informed neural network approximates manifold heat kernels, enabling the noising and score calculations needed to train Riemannian diffusion models.

title: Riemannian Diffusion Models on General Manifolds via Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities and generalization in embodied manipulation. However, their decision-making relies on a fast, instinctive process that lacks deliberation. This strategy often leads to suboptimal or catastrophic actions when facing complex or ambiguous scenarios that require greater consideration. In this paper, we introduce VLA-ATTC, a framework that endows VLA models with adaptive test-time compute (TTC). VLA-ATTC employs an uncertainty-based “cognitive clutch” to dynamically transition from reflexive execution to a TTC deliberation phase when necessary. During TTC phase, a novel Relative Action Critic (RAC) model identifies the optimal action from generated candidates via pairwise comparisons. This relative mechanism replaces unstable absolute value estimation, significantly simplifying the learning objective. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient sampling strategy to amortize computational costs and an automated data pipeline that curates preference pairs without manual annotation. On the LIBERO-LONG benchmark, VLA-ATTC reduces the failure rate of the SOTA model PI0.5 by over 50%.
