paragraphs: Vision-language-action models often choose robot actions through a fast response process. In complex or ambiguous situations, that speed can come with poor or catastrophic decisions. VLA-ATTC adds a mechanism for spending extra computation selectively, using uncertainty to determine when the model should move from immediate execution into a deliberation phase.

During deliberation, the framework generates candidate actions and uses a Relative Action Critic to compare them in pairs. This replaces unstable absolute value estimation with a relative learning problem for selecting an action. An efficient sampling strategy spreads computational costs, while an automated data pipeline creates preference pairs without manual annotation.

On LIBERO-LONG, VLA-ATTC reduces PI0.5’s failure rate by more than 50%. This is a reduction in failures on the stated benchmark, rather than an equivalent increase in overall success percentage. The result supports the framework’s core idea: combine uncertainty-triggered extra computation with comparative action evaluation, so deliberation is available when fast action selection needs more consideration.
summary.tldr: VLA-ATTC selectively adds deliberation and pairwise action comparison, reducing PI0.5’s failure rate by over 50% on LIBERO-LONG.

title: VLA-ATTC: Adaptive Test-Time Compute for VLA Models with Relative Action Critic Model

abstract: The de novo generation of high-affinity epitopes tailored to specific major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins is a pivotal challenge in computational immunotherapy. However, current methods struggle to effectively integrate the MHC context into the generation process, and often fail to guarantee high binding affinity due to the neglect of discriminative signals from non-binders. To bridge these gaps, we present EpiCoCo, a probabilistic framework for Epitope generation via MHC-context Co-modeling and Contrastive affinity learning. EpiCoCo treats the pMHC complex as a dynamic, co-adaptive system by operating on the joint E(3) graph. In addition, we introduce Contrastive Affinity Guidance (CAG), an inference mechanism that leverages the gradient difference between learned high- and low-affinity distributions. CAG actively drives the generation trajectory towards high-affinity manifolds while utilizing repulsive signals to filter out candidates with poor binding potential. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that EpiCoCo achieves a mean binding free energy of -45.20 REU, a 23% improvement over the state-of-the-art, while maintaining high structural plausibility. The results validate that context co-modeling and negative-informed guidance are essential for generating valid, high-potency immunotherapeutics.

paragraphs: EpiCoCo addresses the generation of new epitopes tailored to bind particular MHC proteins. The paper identifies two shortcomings in existing approaches: insufficient integration of the MHC context and inadequate use of examples with poor binding. Both matter because generation needs to account for the target protein while distinguishing promising candidates from weak ones.

It also introduces Contrastive Affinity Guidance during generation. This mechanism compares gradients from learned high-affinity and low-affinity distributions, steering candidates toward favorable regions while pushing them away from patterns associated with poor binding.

Evaluations report a mean binding free energy of −45.20 REU, described as a 23% improvement over the state of the art, while maintaining high structural plausibility. The authors interpret the results as validating the importance of joint context modeling and guidance informed by negative examples. The stated evidence concerns generated candidates’ binding-energy and structural evaluations, which are the concrete outcomes reported for the framework.
summary.tldr: EpiCoCo jointly models epitopes and MHC context, using both favorable and unfavorable affinity signals to improve generated candidates.

title: EpiCoCo: De Novo Epitope Generation via MHC-Context Co-Modeling and Contrastive Affinity Guidance

abstract: This paper studies preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL), where agents learn from comparative, trajectory-level feedback rather than numeric rewards. While PbRL has seen rapid empirical and theoretical progress, existing analyses are largely confined to restricted settings and fail to jointly capture the outcome-based and comparison-based nature of preference feedback. We prove that under a broad general function approximation framework, PbRL admits a $\sqrt{T}$ regret guarantee. In particular, we introduce a simple and provably efficient algorithm, Recursive Trajectory-based Preference Q-Learning (RTPQ), and establish its regret bound while explicitly accounting for the trajectory-level and comparative structure of preferences. Our analysis is characterized by a new complexity measure, the Dual Episodic Eluder Dimension (DEED), which quantifies the intrinsic difficulty of PbRL. We show that for linear MDPs, the DEED scales as $\mathcal{O}(dH)$, yielding a regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(dH\sqrt{T}\max(H^{3/2},\,1/\kappa))$, where $\kappa$ is a problem-dependent constant. This bound is near-optimal up to horizon- and problem-dependent factors when compared to standard reward-based linear MDPs. In addition, our framework recovers the best-known regret bounds in the special cases of dueling bandits and standard outcome-based reinforcement learning. Overall, our results provide a general regret guarantee for PbRL with outcome-based preference feedback and broad function approximation.

Regret measures accumulated performance shortfall, so this growth rate implies a declining average shortfall as interactions increase within the analyzed framework. For linear Markov decision processes, the complexity measure scales with representation dimension and episode horizon. The resulting regret bound is near-optimal relative to standard reward-based linear settings up to horizon-dependent and problem-dependent factors. The framework also recovers the best-known bounds for dueling bandits and standard outcome-based reinforcement learning, connecting these special cases to a broader account of preference learning.

title: Rethinking the Hardness of PbRL: A Provable General Regret Bound

abstract: Dirac-Frenkel instantaneous residual minimization evolves nonlinear parametrizations of PDE solutions in time, but ill-conditioning can render the parameter dynamics non-unique. We interpret this non-uniqueness as a gauge freedom: nullspace directions that leave the time derivative unchanged can be used to select better-conditioned parameter velocities. Building on Onsager’s minimum-dissipation principle, we introduce a history variable—interpretable as momentum—and inject it only along the nullspace directions. The resulting Dirac-Frenkel-Onsager dynamics preserve instantaneous residual minimization, in contrast to standard regularization that can introduce bias, while promoting temporally smooth parameter evolution. Examples demonstrate that the approach leads to increased robustness in singular and near-singular regimes.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to evolve a parametrized approximation to a partial differential equation over time. Dirac–Frenkel residual minimization chooses parameter changes that best match the equation at each instant. However, poorly conditioned parametrizations can admit several parameter velocities that produce the same time derivative of the represented solution, leaving the parameter evolution ambiguous.

The authors treat this ambiguity as useful freedom. Certain directions in parameter space do not change the solution’s instantaneous derivative; these are nullspace directions. Drawing on Onsager’s minimum-dissipation principle, they introduce a history variable resembling momentum and apply it only in those directions. This lets past motion influence which equivalent parameter velocity is selected without changing the residual-minimizing solution derivative.

The resulting dynamics retain instantaneous residual minimization while encouraging smoother parameter trajectories. That distinction matters because ordinary regularization can alter the optimization problem and introduce bias. Examples show greater robustness in singular and nearly singular settings, supporting the idea that redundant parameter freedom can help stabilize evolution rather than merely obstruct it.
summary.tldr: Momentum restricted to redundant parameter directions stabilizes PDE solution dynamics while preserving instantaneous residual minimization.

title: A Dirac-Frenkel-Onsager Principle: Instantaneous Residual Minimization with Gauge Momentum for Nonlinear Parametrizations of PDE Solutions

abstract: Self-supervised learning for time-series representation aims to reduce reliance on labeled data while maintaining strong downstream performance, yet many existing approaches incur high computational costs or rely on assumptions that do not hold across diverse temporal dynamics. In this work, we introduce Divide and Contrast (Di-COT), an unsupervised framework that avoids data augmentation and multiple encoder passes by contrasting informative substructures within a window rather than individual timesteps. Di-COT stochastically partitions each window into a small number of overlapping sub-blocks per iteration, enabling efficient and meaningful contrast while mitigating false positives during temporal transitions. To further improve scalability, we adopt a contrastive objective whose computation depends on the batch size and the number of sub-blocks, making loss computation independent of sequence length. Extensive experiments on six large-scale real-world datasets, as well as the UCR and UEA benchmarks, demonstrate that Di-COT learns transferable representations while achieving state-of-the-art performance with substantially reduced training time.

paragraphs: Learning useful time-series features without labels can make those features reusable across downstream tasks. However, existing approaches can require expensive computation or assumptions that fit some temporal patterns poorly. Divide and Contrast, or Di-COT, learns by comparing informative structures inside a time window without creating augmented versions of the data.

At each iteration, the method randomly partitions a window into a few overlapping sub-blocks. These blocks become the units of comparison, replacing comparisons centered on individual timesteps. This design avoids multiple encoder passes and helps reduce false positive pairings around temporal transitions, where nearby observations may represent changing behavior.

Di-COT also uses an objective whose computation depends on batch size and the number of sub-blocks, rather than sequence length. That independence applies specifically to loss computation. Experiments on six large real-world datasets and the UCR and UEA benchmarks report transferable representations, state-of-the-art performance, and substantially shorter training time. The results support substructure-level comparison as an efficient way to learn temporal features.
summary.tldr: Di-COT learns transferable time-series features by contrasting overlapping sub-blocks, reducing training cost without data augmentation.

title: Divide and Contrast: Learning Robust Temporal Features without Augmentation

abstract: Multi-modal neuroimaging-based psychiatric diagnosis must integrate cross-modal agreement with modality-specific complementarity, yet in real multi-site cohorts these signals are frequently entangled with site- and cohort-dependent correlations, yielding shortcut-driven predictions and limited interpretability. We propose Structured Multi-modal Graph Disentanglement (SMGD), which explicitly factorizes multi-modal graph representations into four components with distinct roles: shared diagnostic evidence, complementary diagnostic evidence, incidental cross-modal agreement, and modality-specific non-robust correlations, with the former two forming the diagnostic core and the latter two suppressed as shortcuts. SMGD is realized as geometry-driven structure learning: under a mild distributional assumption, we develop mini-batch estimable surrogate regularizers that shape subspace organization and cross-modal relations, enforcing semantic consistency through relational geometry rather than centroid coincidence while suppressing confounded dependencies. Experiments on large multi-site datasets show improved in-domain diagnosis and more reliable cross-dataset generalization in the presence of a Modality Gap, without relying on expert-crafted diagnostic biomarkers.

paragraphs: SMGD addresses a difficulty in combining neuroimaging modalities for psychiatric diagnosis: agreement between modalities is not always useful diagnostic evidence. In data collected across sites and cohorts, shared patterns can reflect incidental correlations, and modality-specific features can also provide unreliable shortcuts. The method explicitly separates these possibilities within its learned graph representations.

It divides the representation into four components: shared diagnostic evidence, complementary diagnostic evidence, incidental agreement, and modality-specific non-robust correlations. The first two form the diagnostic core, while training suppresses the latter two. Under a mild distributional assumption, the authors derive regularizers estimable from mini-batches that organize subspaces and cross-modal relationships using geometry.

This geometric approach enforces semantic consistency through relationships among representations instead of requiring their centers to coincide. Experiments on large multi-site datasets show improved in-domain diagnosis and more reliable transfer across datasets in the presence of a Modality Gap. The method achieves these results without expert-crafted diagnostic biomarkers, supporting explicit separation of useful agreement, complementary information, and confounded correlations.
summary.tldr: SMGD separates useful diagnostic information from incidental and non-robust correlations to improve multimodal neuroimaging predictions and cross-dataset generalization.

title: Structured Multi-modal Graph Disentanglement for Psychiatric Diagnosis

abstract: We study the problem of computing a U-statistic with a kernel function $f$ of degree $k \geq 2$, i.e., the average of some function $f$ over all $k$-tuples of instances, in a federated learning setting. U-statistics of degree $2$ include several useful statistics such as Kendall’s $\tau$ coefficient, the Area under the Receiver-Operator Curve and the Gini mean difference. Existing methods provide solutions only under the lower-utility local differential privacy model and/or scale poorly in the size of the domain discretization. In this work, we propose a protocol that securely computes U-statistics of degree $k \geq 2$ under central differential privacy by leveraging Multi Party Computation (MPC). Our method substantially improves accuracy when compared to prior solutions. We provide a detailed theoretical analysis of its accuracy, communication and computational properties. We evaluate its performance empirically, obtaining favorable results, e.g., for Kendall’s $\tau$ coefficient, our approach reduces the Mean Squared Error by up to four orders of magnitude over existing baselines.

paragraphs: Many useful statistics depend on relationships among observations rather than on individual observations alone. A U-statistic averages a function over groups of a fixed size, called its degree. Degree-two examples include Kendall’s correlation coefficient, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and the Gini mean difference. This paper studies their computation when data are distributed in a federated setting.

The proposed protocol supports degree two and higher by combining multiparty computation with central differential privacy. Multiparty computation supplies the secure computation component, while differential privacy supplies the privacy guarantee for the statistical result. This addresses shortcomings of earlier approaches that either use the lower-utility local privacy model or scale poorly with domain discretization.

The authors analyze accuracy, communication requirements, and computational cost, then evaluate the protocol empirically. They report substantially improved accuracy, including reductions in mean squared error of up to four orders of magnitude for Kendall’s coefficient compared with existing baselines. That example demonstrates the potential accuracy benefit of the combined protocol without implying an identical improvement for every statistic.
summary.tldr: A secure federated protocol computes higher-degree U-statistics with central differential privacy and substantially better reported accuracy.

title: Accurate, Private, Secure, Federated U-statistics with Higher Degree

abstract: Discovering governing differential equations from observational data is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning. Existing symbolic regression approaches rely primarily on quantitative metrics; however, real-world differential equation modeling also requires incorporating domain knowledge to ensure physical plausibility. To address this gap, we propose DoLQ, a method for discovering ordinary differential equations with LLM-based qualitative and quantitative evaluation. DoLQ employs a multi-agent architecture: a Sampler Agent proposes dynamic system candidates, a Parameter Optimizer refines equations for accuracy, and a Scientist Agent leverages an LLM to conduct both qualitative and quantitative evaluations and synthesize their results to iteratively guide the search. Experiments on multi-dimensional ordinary differential equation benchmarks demonstrate that DoLQ achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, not only attaining higher success rates but also more accurately recovering the correct symbolic terms of ground truth equations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Bon99yun/DoLQ.

paragraphs: DoLQ searches for ordinary differential equations that explain observed changes in a system. A candidate equation can match measurements numerically while still being questionable in light of domain knowledge. The paper addresses this gap by combining quantitative assessment with qualitative judgments about whether a proposed model makes physical sense.

Its architecture divides the search among three roles. A Sampler Agent proposes candidate dynamical systems, and a Parameter Optimizer adjusts their numerical parameters to improve accuracy. A Scientist Agent uses a language model to perform qualitative and quantitative evaluations, combine their conclusions, and guide subsequent proposals. Evaluation therefore feeds back into the search rather than serving only as a final filter.

On benchmarks involving multidimensional ordinary differential equations, DoLQ achieves higher success rates than existing methods and more accurately identifies the symbolic terms in the true equations. Recovering those terms matters because the task is to uncover governing structure, not merely reproduce observed values. The results support incorporating domain-informed evaluation into the equation-discovery loop.
summary.tldr: DoLQ combines equation proposals, parameter fitting, and language-model evaluation to improve recovery of governing differential equations.

title: Discovering Ordinary Differential Equations with LLM-Based Qualitative and Quantitative Evaluation

abstract: Antibody expression ranking is a critical task in antibody design, yet its modelling is severely hindered by the scarcity of labeled experimental data. To address this, we propose a unified preference-based learning framework that integrates scarce quantitative expression data with large-scale weak positive supervision from immunization data. We adapt Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to protein language models by introducing a union-masked log-likelihood approximation and IMGT-based alignment, enabling efficient training on variable-length sequences. Evaluating on a diverse internal dataset of 1254 labeled sequences and 4 million unlabeled camelid-derived antibodies, we show that our method consistently outperforms baselines on most metrics. Our results demonstrate that preference learning can effectively learn from weak supervision, providing a scalable solution for antibody expressibility optimization in data-constrained settings. Project page: https://kisoji-biotechnology-inc.github.io/Preference-Expression-Ranking/.

paragraphs: Ranking antibodies by expression is important for antibody design, but measured expression labels are scarce. This paper develops a preference-learning framework that combines limited quantitative measurements with much larger amounts of weak positive supervision from immunization data. The aim is to make the abundant, less direct evidence useful for learning expression rankings.

The method adapts Direct Preference Optimization to protein language models. It introduces a union-masked approximation to sequence log-likelihood and uses IMGT-based alignment, enabling efficient training with antibody sequences of different lengths. These changes connect the preference-learning objective to the variable-length sequence setting while integrating the two kinds of supervision.

The evaluation uses an internal dataset containing 1,254 labeled sequences and four million unlabeled camelid-derived antibodies. The method consistently outperforms baselines on most reported metrics. This supports preference learning as a way to exploit weak supervision when direct experimental labels are limited. The reported outcome concerns expression ranking and expressibility optimization, with gains demonstrated on the dataset described.
summary.tldr: A protein preference-learning framework combines scarce expression measurements with large-scale weak supervision to improve antibody expression ranking.

title: Preference-based Antibody Expression Ranking: Scaling with Large-scale Weak Supervision

abstract: Sequential learning is order-dependent: from Pile-style next-token domain adaptation to instruction-SFT and DPO, $N$ candidate sources induce $N!$ possible curricula. We show that the local order effect is governed by a computable geometric quantity, the Lie-bracket commutator of gradient update fields, yielding a pairwise score for whether $A \to B$ or $B \to A$ is better for a target domain. The pairwise bracket primitive also defines a Lie-Bracket Tournament: with a shared $\theta_0$ target-gradient reference, Hessian symmetry gives Borda/row-sum scores from one Hessian-vector product per source, $O(N)$ dot products, and an $O(N\log N)$ sort, without materializing the $O(N^2)$ edge matrix. Empirically, the planner reaches 98.1%/98.9% pairwise accuracy at $k=1$ for instruction-SFT/DPO, remains at 73.1%/72.2% at $k=20$, and preserves the original pretraining-domain evidence with 82.4–92.0% accuracy across four LLMs and 91.1% on diffusion. At curriculum scale, it recovers the best of all $3!$ schedules in 87.5% of trials, ranks 85 Stack programming-language source domains for a Python target in the 99th sampled percentile, and reaches the 99.0–99.6th sampled percentile on 56 MMLU subjects, sharply above the reported descending gradient-norm baseline. These results reframe sequential learning as a geometric tournament problem: commutators provide both local pairwise order information and a scalable primitive for many-domain schedules.

paragraphs: Training on the same sources in different orders can produce different outcomes, and the number of possible curricula grows factorially. This paper characterizes the local effect of swapping two sources through the Lie bracket of their gradient-update fields. That quantity yields a score predicting which order is better for a target domain.

The pairwise score also supports a tournament over many sources. With a shared initial target-gradient reference, Hessian symmetry allows row-sum rankings using one Hessian-vector product per source, a linear number of dot products, and a sort. At curriculum scale, the method finds the best of six schedules in 87.5% of trials and achieves high sampled-percentile rankings on larger domain collections. These results support local update geometry as a useful scheduling signal, while the declining accuracy shows that predictive strength varies across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Lie brackets predict local training-order effects and enable scalable curriculum rankings without evaluating every source pair.

title: The Geometry of Sequential Learning: Lie-Bracket Prediction of Transfer Order

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are pretrained on massive amounts of data, their knowledge coverage remains incomplete in specialized, data-scarce domains, motivating extensive efforts to study synthetic data generation for knowledge injection. We propose $\textbf{SPA}$ ($\textbf{S}$caling $\textbf{P}$rompt-engineered $\textbf{A}$ugmentation), a simple but tough-to-beat baseline that uses a small set of carefully designed prompts to generate large-scale synthetic data for knowledge injection. Through systematic comparisons, we find that $\textbf{SPA}$ outperforms several strong baselines. Furthermore, we identify two key limitations of prior approaches: (1) while RL-based methods may improve the token efficiency of LLM-based data augmentation at small scale, they suffer from diversity collapse as data scales, leading to diminishing returns; and (2) while multi-stage prompting may outperform simple augmentation methods, their advantages can disappear after careful prompt tuning. Our results suggest that, for knowledge injection, careful prompt design combined with straightforward large-scale augmentation can be surprisingly effective, and we hope SPA can serve as a strong baseline for future studies in this area. Our code is available at https://github.com/Tangkexian/SPA.

paragraphs: Language models can lack knowledge in specialized domains where training data is scarce. SPA studies whether generating large amounts of synthetic data with a small collection of carefully designed prompts can provide an effective knowledge-injection baseline. The approach focuses on prompt quality and augmentation scale.

Systematic comparisons find that SPA outperforms several strong baselines. The analysis identifies two reasons more elaborate approaches can lose their advantage. Reinforcement-learning-based augmentation may use tokens more efficiently at small scale, but suffers from diversity collapse as generation scales, producing diminishing returns. Multi-stage prompting can outperform simpler augmentation, yet that advantage can disappear when the simpler method’s prompts are carefully tuned.

The findings suggest that complexity alone is an unreliable guide to knowledge-injection effectiveness. Prompt design and the diversity of generated material matter when assessing a method at scale. SPA offers a straightforward reference point for future comparisons, showing that carefully engineered prompts combined with large-scale generation can be competitive without a more involved augmentation procedure.
summary.tldr: SPA shows that carefully tuned prompts and large-scale synthetic augmentation can outperform more elaborate knowledge-injection methods.

title: SPA: A Simple but Tough-to-Beat Baseline for Knowledge Injection

abstract: Recent advances in image and video generation raise hopes that these models possess world modeling capabilities—the ability to generate realistic, physically plausible videos. This could revolutionize applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and scientific simulation. However, before treating these models as world models, we must ask: Do they adhere to physical laws? Current evaluation methods rely on subjective judgments or trajectory matching, limiting their usage for physical reasoning estimation, where many generations could be physically plausible. Thus, we introduce Morpheus, one of the first physics-informed evaluation frameworks for measuring the ability of video generation models to comprehend Newtonian dynamics. Morpheus features 130 real-world videos capturing physical phenomena, guided by conservation laws. Using those as conditioning for video generation, we assess physical plausibility leveraging interpretable metrics evaluated with respect to infallible conservation laws known per physical setting, leveraging advances in physics-informed neural networks and vision-language foundation models. Importantly, Morpheus targets controlled Newtonian rigid-body settings to enable quantitative checks. Our findings reveal that even with advanced prompting and video conditioning, contemporary models struggle to encode physical principles despite generating aesthetically pleasing videos. Code and data available here.

paragraphs: A convincing-looking generated video may still violate physics. Evaluating this through visual judgments is subjective, while requiring a generated trajectory to match one reference can reject other physically plausible outcomes. Morpheus instead assesses video generation through conservation laws that apply to the particular physical setting.

The framework includes 130 real-world videos depicting physical phenomena and uses them to condition generation. It combines advances in physics-informed neural networks and vision-language foundation models to evaluate interpretable measures of physical plausibility. Its scope is deliberately controlled Newtonian rigid-body settings, where the relevant laws support quantitative checks rather than judgments based mainly on appearance.

The findings show that contemporary generators struggle to encode physical principles even with advanced prompting and video conditioning, despite producing aesthetically pleasing results. This separates visual realism from the specific physical consistency needed for world modeling. Morpheus therefore contributes an evaluation approach that asks whether generated motion respects known constraints in the tested settings, allowing multiple possible trajectories without treating one observed sequence as the sole valid answer.
summary.tldr: Morpheus evaluates generated videos against conservation laws and finds persistent physical inconsistencies in controlled Newtonian settings.

title: Evaluating Newtonian Mechanics in Video Generative Models with Real Physical Systems

abstract: Despite the success of knowledge distillation (KD) in Large Language Models (LLMs), the underlying mechanism behind its efficacy remains unclear. In this paper, we propose a unified approach to explore the common mechanism of various KD methods using interactions. Specifically, we decompose the output score of the LLM into the sum of numerous interactions. Each interaction represents a nonlinear relationship involving a set of input variables (e.g., words). Based on the decomposed interactions, we discover that the common mechanism underlying various KD methods is the sparsification of interactions, i.e., student models retain fewer interactions for inference while suppressing other interactions to zero effects. Furthermore, we discover that the performance variance across different KD methods arises from their capabilities in handling complex interactions. A KD method typically yields better performance if it enables the student model to achieve higher sparsity of complex interactions. Motivated by these insights, we propose a plug-and-play loss function called Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) to explicitly enforce the sparsity of complex interactions during the distillation process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating CIP consistently improves the performance of diverse KD methods on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks.

abstract: High-quality data is a cornerstone of large language model (LLM) pretraining, yet its growth has not kept pace with the needs of frontier models. In this paper, we introduce RePro, a novel web recycling method that trains a relatively small LM with reinforcement learning to generate effective and faithful rephrasings of pretraining data. Specifically, we design one quality reward and three faithfulness rewards, optimizing the LM rephraser to convert organic data into high-quality rephrasings while maintaining its core semantics and structure. In our experiment, we train a rephraser as small as 1B parameters to recycle 72B tokens sampled from DCLM-RefinedWeb. Pretraining results on 400M, 1.4B, and 2.8B models demonstrate that RePro delivers 3.7%-14.5% relative accuracy gains over organic-only baseline on 22 downstream tasks, doubling the performance gains achieved by the state-of-the-art web recycling method that prompts a 70B rephraser. Experiments with different amounts of recycled data highlight that RePro improves organic data efficiency by 2-3$\times$. Individual and distributional analyses validate that RePro preserves more critical information and faithfully reflects the characteristics of organic data compared to prompting-based methods. Together, these results show that RePro provides an efficient and controllable path to effectively recycle organic data for pretraining. Our code is available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/RePro.

RePro trains a relatively small language model specifically for this task. title: RePro: Training Language Models to Faithfully Recycle the Web for Pretraining

abstract: Advanced agents are increasingly demonstrating the potential to operate as autonomous engineers, creating a growing demand for evaluation benchmarks that capture the complexity of real-world development. Such environments typically involve both complex code and large-scale data (i.e., file system). However, existing benchmarks usually evaluate code-centric or data-centric capabilities in isolation, leaving a clear gap with real development scenarios. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing CoDA-Bench, the first benchmark to jointly evaluate code and data intelligence in a data-intensive environment. We construct a data-intensive Linux sandbox based on the Kaggle ecosystem (containing hundreds of datasets), where agents must actively explore complex file hierarchies to identify relevant resources and generate code for data-driven analytical tasks. CoDA-Bench comprises 1,009 tasks spanning 31 communities, with each task environment containing an average of 980 files, simulating realistic data scale and noise. Evaluations of advanced agents reveal that even top-performing systems struggle to effectively integrate data discovery with code execution, achieving a success rate of only 61.1%. These results highlight a substantial gap in current agentic capabilities for data-intensive tasks and point to promising directions for future research.

summary.tldr: CoDA-Bench tests coding agents on joint data discovery and programming tasks, where evaluated top systems reach only 61.1% success.

title: CoDA-Bench: Can Code Agents Handle Data-Intensive Tasks?

abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in general video understanding, their capacity to interpret involuntary, and spatio-temporally evolving pathologic motor behaviors such as seizure semiology remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce Seizure-Semiology-Suite (S$^3$), a clinically grounded dataset and benchmark for fine-grained, structured seizure semiology understanding. The dataset includes 438 seizure videos annotated with over 35,000 dense labels covering 20 ILAE-defined semiological features. Building on this dataset, we propose a seven-task hierarchical benchmark that systematically evaluates MLLMs from low-level visual perception to temporal sequencing, narrative report generation, and seizure diagnosis. To enable clinically meaningful evaluation of generated reports, we further introduce the Report Quality Index for Seizure Semiology (Seizure-RQI). Extensive baselines across 11 open-weight MLLMs reveal systematic weaknesses in laterality reasoning, temporal localization, symptom sequencing, and clinically faithful reporting. We show that seizure-specific fine-tuning substantially improves performance across tasks, and that a two-stage neuro-symbolic framework achieves an F1 score of 0.96 on epileptic versus non-epileptic seizure classification. Seizure-Semiology-Suite establishes a rigorous benchmark for evaluating multimodal models in safety-critical medical video understanding and guides the development of clinically reliable, domain-adaptive multimodal intelligence. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LinaZhangUCLA/SeizureSemiologySuite.

Seizure-Semiology-Suite examines these abilities in multimodal language models through a clinically grounded dataset. It contains 438 seizure videos with more than 35,000 dense labels covering 20 semiological features defined by the ILAE.

A seven-task hierarchy evaluates abilities from basic visual perception to symptom ordering, report writing, and seizure diagnosis. The authors also introduce Seizure-RQI to assess the clinical quality of generated reports. This structure makes it possible to examine distinct components of seizure understanding rather than reducing the evaluation to a single classification result.

Seizure-specific fine-tuning substantially improves performance across tasks. A two-stage neuro-symbolic framework achieves an F1 score of 0.96 for distinguishing epileptic from non-epileptic seizures. Together, the dataset, evaluation measures, and model results establish a detailed basis for studying domain-specific medical video understanding.
summary.tldr: Seizure-Semiology-Suite benchmarks detailed seizure-video understanding, exposes recurring model weaknesses, and demonstrates improvements from domain-specific training.

title: Seizure-Semiology-Suite($S^3$): A Clinically Multimodal Dataset, Benchmark, and Models for Seizure Semiology Understanding

abstract: Model merging (MM) has gained significant attention as a cost-effective approach to integrate multiple task-specific models into a unified model. However, recent work reveals that MM is highly susceptible to backdoor attacks. Existing defenses based on task arithmetic often fail to eliminate backdoors without substantially degrading clean-task performance, owing to their reliance on direct parameter-space editing. To address this gap, we propose Linear Feature Path Minimization (LFPM), a backdoor mitigation framework for model merging, which introduces an anti-backdoor task vector into the backdoored merged model. Unlike prior approaches, LFPM formulates the backdoor robustness of the merged model from a unified feature-space perspective under the Cross-Task Linearity (CTL) framework, which leverages the approximate linearity of features across tasks. This perspective guides the optimization of the anti-backdoor task to suppress backdoors while preserving clean-task performance. Furthermore, we introduce an effective optimization mechanism based on gradient accumulation and loss path-integral, ensuring robust backdoor suppression along the interpolation path. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFPM consistently exhibits strong robustness against backdoor attacks in both full fine-tuning and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) settings.

paragraphs: Model merging combines task-specific models into one model at relatively low cost, but it can also carry backdoor behavior into the combined system. Existing defenses that directly edit parameters can suppress unwanted behavior at the expense of ordinary task performance. This paper proposes Linear Feature Path Minimization, or LFPM, to address that tradeoff.

LFPM introduces an anti-backdoor task vector and guides its optimization through the merged model's feature behavior. Its Cross-Task Linearity perspective uses the approximate linearity of features across tasks. This provides a way to target backdoor suppression while seeking to preserve the representations needed for clean tasks, rather than relying only on direct parameter-space changes.

The optimization mechanism combines gradient accumulation with a loss path-integral to suppress backdoors along the interpolation path. Experiments report consistently strong robustness in both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings. The findings support examining how task combinations affect internal features when designing defenses, with protection along the combination path forming an explicit part of the method.
summary.tldr: LFPM uses feature-space guidance to optimize an anti-backdoor task vector for merged models while seeking to preserve clean-task performance.

abstract: We consider reinforcement learning in systems with unknown dynamics. Algorithms such as E 3 (Kearns and Singh, 2002) learn near-optimal policies by using “exploration policies” to drive the system towards poorly modeled states, so as to encourage exploration. But this makes these algorithms impractical for many systems; for example, on an autonomous helicopter, overly aggressive exploration may well result in a crash. In this paper, we consider the apprenticeship learning setting in which a teacher demonstration of the task is available. We show that, given the initial demonstration, no explicit exploration is necessary, and we can attain near-optimal performance (compared to the teacher) simply by repeatedly executing “exploitation policies” that try to maximize rewards. In finite-state MDPs, our algorithm scales polynomially in the number of states; in continuous-state linear dynamical systems, it scales polynomially in the dimension of the state. These results are proved using a martingale construction over relative losses.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with unknown dynamics often uses explicit exploration to visit poorly understood states. The paper notes that this can be impractical in physical systems, where aggressive exploration may cause failure. It instead studies apprenticeship learning, assuming an initial teacher demonstration of the task is available.

Given that demonstration, the authors show that repeatedly executing exploitation policies can attain near-optimal performance compared with the teacher, without explicit exploration. These policies try to maximize rewards while the system's dynamics are initially unknown. The teacher-relative qualification matters: the stated benchmark is the demonstrated performance, rather than an unrestricted claim of global optimality.

The algorithm scales polynomially with the number of states for finite-state Markov decision processes. For continuous-state linear dynamical systems, it scales polynomially with state dimension. The proofs use a martingale construction over relative losses. These results establish a conditional route to effective learning from demonstration, showing that explicit exploration is unnecessary in the analyzed apprenticeship setting without claiming that all subsequent actions are risk-free.
summary.tldr: Given a teacher demonstration, exploitation-only learning achieves near-optimal teacher-relative performance with polynomial scaling in the analyzed settings.

title: Exploration and apprenticeship learning in reinforcement learning

abstract: We introduce flexible algorithms that can automatically learn mappings from images to actions by interacting with their environment. They work by introducing an image classifier in front of a Reinforcement Learning algorithm. The classifier partitions the visual space according to the presence or absence of highly informative local descriptors. The image classifier is incrementally refined by selecting new local descriptors when perceptual aliasing is detected. Thus, we reduce the visual input domain down to a size manageable by Reinforcement Learning, permitting us to learn direct percept-to-action mappings. Experimental results on a continuous visual navigation task illustrate the applicability of the framework.

paragraphs: Learning actions directly from images requires handling a large and varied visual input space. This paper introduces algorithms that learn image-to-action mappings through interaction with an environment. They place an image classifier before a reinforcement learning algorithm, using visual classification to create an input representation the learner can manage.

The classifier divides visual inputs according to whether informative local descriptors are present. Its representation is refined incrementally when perceptual aliasing is detected: situations that need to be distinguished are being treated as visually equivalent. Selecting additional local descriptors allows the classifier to make finer distinctions as learning proceeds.

This connects the development of the visual representation to the needs of learning actions. The system reduces the visual domain while retaining a mechanism for refining distinctions that prove inadequate. Experiments on a continuous visual navigation task illustrate the framework's applicability. The reported finding supports the use of an adaptive visual classifier as an interface between images and reinforcement learning in that task.
summary.tldr: An incrementally refined image classifier makes visual inputs manageable for reinforcement learning of image-to-action mappings.

title: Interactive learning of mappings from visual percepts to actions

abstract: We analyze skewing, an approach that has been empirically observed to enable greedy decision tree learners to learn “difficult” Boolean functions, such as parity, in the presence of irrelevant variables. We prove that, in an idealized setting, for any function and choice of skew parameters, skewing finds relevant variables with probability 1. We present experiments exploring how different parameter choices affect the success of skewing in empirical settings. Finally, we analyze a variant of skewing called Sequential Skewing.

paragraphs: Greedy decision tree learners can struggle with Boolean functions such as parity, particularly when the inputs include irrelevant variables. Earlier empirical work found that skewing could help these learners succeed. This paper investigates why that happens, focusing on whether skewing can identify the variables that actually matter to the target function.

The main theoretical result states that, in an idealized setting, skewing finds relevant variables with probability one for any function and choice of skew parameters. The idealized setting is essential to the scope of that guarantee. The result supplies a theoretical explanation for relevant-variable discovery without asserting identical behavior in every practical learning situation.

The authors also run experiments examining how parameter choices affect empirical success and analyze a variant called Sequential Skewing. These parts connect the theoretical result to questions about how the method behaves when used in practice. The contribution combines an explanation of skewing's ability to expose relevant inputs with an empirical investigation of choices that influence its effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Skewing is proved to find relevant Boolean variables with probability one in an idealized setting, alongside empirical analysis of parameter choices.

title: Why skewing works: learning difficult Boolean functions with greedy tree learners

abstract: An efficient and general multiple kernel learning (MKL) algorithm has been recently proposed by Sonnenburg et al. (2006). This approach has opened new perspectives since it makes the MKL approach tractable for largescale problems, by iteratively using existing support vector machine code. However, it turns out that this iterative algorithm needs several iterations before converging towards a reasonable solution. In this paper, we address the MKL problem through an adaptive 2-norm regularization formulation. Weights on each kernel matrix are included in the standard SVM empirical risk minimization problem with a `1 constraint to encourage sparsity. We propose an algorithm for solving this problem and provide an new insight on MKL algorithms based on block 1-norm regularization by showing that the two approaches are equivalent. Experimental results show that the resulting algorithm converges rapidly and its efficiency compares favorably to other MKL algorithms.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines several kernel matrices within a learning problem. The paper begins with an existing iterative approach that made large-scale multiple kernel learning practical by reusing support vector machine software. Its remaining drawback is that reaching a reasonable solution can require several iterations, motivating a more efficient formulation and solver.

The authors formulate the problem through adaptive 2-norm regularization. They include weights for the kernel matrices directly in the standard SVM empirical-risk objective and impose an ℓ₁ constraint to encourage sparsity. This makes the relative contributions of the kernels part of the optimization while favoring a solution that uses fewer of them.

The paper proposes an algorithm for this formulation and shows that it is equivalent to approaches based on block 1-norm regularization. That equivalence connects two ways of understanding multiple kernel learning, alongside the practical algorithmic contribution. Experiments report rapid convergence and efficiency that compares favorably with other multiple kernel learning algorithms. These results support the proposed solver as a practical improvement in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: An adaptive regularization formulation yields an efficient multiple-kernel solver and connects it to block 1-norm regularization.

title: More efficiency in multiple kernel learning

abstract: In this paper we propose a discriminant learning framework for problems in which data consist of linear subspaces instead of vectors. By treating subspaces as basic elements, we can make learning algorithms adapt naturally to the problems with linear invariant structures. We propose a unifying view on the subspace-based learning method by formulating the problems on the Grassmann manifold, which is the set of fixed-dimensional subspaces of a Euclidean space. Previous methods on the problem typically adopt an inconsistent strategy: feature extraction is performed in the Euclidean space while non-Euclidean dissimilarity measures are used. In our approach, we treat each subspace as a point in the Grassmann space, and perform feature extraction and classification in the same space. We show feasibility of the approach by using the Grassmann kernel functions such as the Projection kernel and the Binet-Cauchy kernel. Experiments with real image databases show that the proposed method performs well compared with state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Some learning problems represent each example as a linear subspace rather than a single vector. This paper develops discriminant learning around that representation. Treating the subspace itself as the basic data object lets the learning framework accommodate problems with linear invariant structure, instead of forcing every example into an ordinary vector-based treatment.

The framework uses the Grassmann manifold, the collection of fixed-dimensional subspaces of a Euclidean space. Each example becomes a point in that space, and both feature extraction and classification are performed there. This addresses an inconsistency identified in earlier methods, which extracted features using Euclidean geometry but assessed dissimilarity using non-Euclidean measures.

The authors demonstrate feasibility with Grassmann kernel functions, including the Projection and Binet-Cauchy kernels. Experiments on real image databases show good performance relative to state-of-the-art algorithms. The main contribution is a coherent geometric framework for subspace-based learning, with the experiments supporting its practical usefulness rather than establishing that it always dominates other image classification approaches.
summary.tldr: Grassmann discriminant analysis places subspace examples, feature extraction, and classification in a shared geometric framework.

title: Grassmann discriminant analysis: a unifying view on subspace-based learning

abstract: The GroupLASSO method for finding important explanatory factors suffers from the potential non-uniqueness of solutions and also from high computational costs. We formulate conditions for the uniqueness of GroupLASSO solutions which lead to an easily implementable test procedure. In addition to merely detecting ambiguities in solutions, this testing procedure identifies all potentially active groups. These results are used to derive an efficient algorithm that can deal with input dimensions in the millions and can approximate the solution path efficiently. The derived methods are applied to large-scale learning problems where they exhibit excellent performance. We show that the proposed testing procedure helps to avoid misinterpretations of GroupLASSO solutions.

These results are used to derive an efficient algorithm that can deal with input dimensions in the millions and can approximate the solution path efficiently. paragraphs: GroupLASSO identifies important explanatory factors organized into groups, but its solutions can be ambiguous and expensive to compute. Ambiguity matters when interpreting which groups are selected: a reported solution may not be unique. This paper addresses both the mathematical uniqueness question and the computational burden of large problems.

The authors formulate conditions for uniqueness that yield an easily implemented testing procedure. The test also identifies all groups that could potentially be active. This gives information beyond a single fitted solution, helping expose ambiguity in which explanatory groups the method may select.

These results support an efficient algorithm capable of handling input dimensions in the millions and efficiently approximating the solution path. Applications to large-scale learning problems exhibit excellent reported performance. The authors also show that the test helps prevent misinterpretations of GroupLASSO results. The contribution connects reliable interpretation with scalable computation by using information about possible solutions to guide both.
summary.tldr: A GroupLASSO uniqueness test identifies potentially active groups and supports efficient optimization with millions of input dimensions.

title: The Group-Lasso for generalized linear models: uniqueness of solutions and efficient algorithms

abstract: Many different topic models have been used successfully for a variety of applications. However, even state-of-the-art topic models suffer from the important flaw that they do not capture the tendency of words to appear in bursts; it is a fundamental property of language that if a word is used once in a document, it is more likely to be used again. We introduce a topic model that uses Dirichlet compound multinomial (DCM) distributions to model this burstiness phenomenon. On both text and non-text datasets, the new model achieves better held-out likelihood than standard latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA). It is straightforward to incorporate the DCM extension into topic models that are more complex than LDA
originalAbstract: Many different topic models have been used successfully for a variety of applications. However, even state-of-the-art topic models suffer from the important flaw that they do not capture the tendency of words to appear in bursts; it is a fundamental property of language that if a word is used once in a document, it is more likely to be used again. We introduce a topic model that uses Dirichlet compound multinomial (DCM) distributions to model this burstiness phenomenon. On both text and non-text datasets, the new model achieves better held-out likelihood than standard latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA). It is straightforward to incorporate the DCM extension into topic models that are more complex than LDA

paragraphs: Words tend to recur within a document: after a word appears once, another occurrence becomes more likely. This burstiness is a property of language that the paper argues existing topic models fail to capture adequately. The issue concerns how repeated observations are modeled, even when a topic model otherwise works well for its applications.

The authors introduce a topic model using Dirichlet compound multinomial distributions to represent this behavior. These distributions provide a way to account for concentrated repetition within a document. The approach makes burstiness part of the probabilistic model, so the model can reflect the tendency for occurrences to arrive in groups.

On both text and non-text datasets, the proposed model obtains better held-out likelihood than standard latent Dirichlet allocation. This indicates a better probabilistic fit to unseen data in those evaluations; it is not a claim about every possible downstream task. The authors also state that the extension can be incorporated straightforwardly into topic models more complex than LDA, giving the modeling idea a broader potential role.
summary.tldr: Modeling repeated occurrences with Dirichlet compound multinomial distributions improves held-out likelihood over standard LDA on the evaluated datasets.

title: Accounting for burstiness in topic models

abstract: Many temporal processes can be naturally modeled as a stochastic system that evolves continuously over time. The representation language of continuous-time Bayesian networks allows to succinctly describe multi-component continuous-time stochastic processes. A crucial element in applications of such models is inference. Here we introduce a variational approximation scheme, which is a natural extension of Belief Propagation for continuous- time processes. In this scheme, we view messages as inhomogeneous Markov processes over individual components. This leads to a relatively simple procedure that allows to easily incorporate adaptive ordinary differential equation (ODE) solvers to perform individual steps. We provide the theoretical foundations for the approximation, and show how it performs on a range of networks. Our results demonstrate that our method is quite accurate on singly connected networks, and provides close approximations in more complex ones.

paragraphs: Some temporal systems evolve continuously rather than only at fixed observation steps. Continuous-time Bayesian networks provide a compact representation for such systems when they contain multiple components. This paper addresses inference in those models by introducing a variational approximation that extends belief propagation to processes evolving in continuous time.

The key modeling choice is to represent messages as inhomogeneous Markov processes over individual components. In other words, the information exchanged during inference is itself expressed as a process whose behavior can vary with time. This leads to a relatively simple procedure in which individual computational steps can use adaptive ordinary differential equation solvers.

The authors provide theoretical foundations for the approximation and evaluate its behavior across a range of networks. They report quite accurate results on singly connected networks and close approximations on more complicated ones. These findings support the method as an approximate inference procedure across the tested structures. Its practical appeal comes from connecting continuous-time message passing to established adaptive numerical solvers.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time extension of belief propagation represents messages as Markov processes and yields accurate approximate inference on evaluated networks.

title: Continuous-Time Belief Propagation

abstract: Functional neuroimaging can measure the brain’s response to an external stimulus. It is used to perform brain mapping: identifying from these observations the brain regions involved. This problem can be cast into a linear supervised learning task where the neuroimaging data are used as predictors for the stimulus. Brain mapping is then seen as a support recovery problem. On functional MRI (fMRI) data, this problem is particularly challenging as i) the number of samples is small due to limited acquisition time and ii) the variables are strongly correlated. We propose to overcome these difficulties using sparse regression models over new variables obtained by clustering of the original variables. The use of randomization techniques, e.g. bootstrap samples, and hierarchical clustering of the variables improves the recovery properties of sparse methods. We demonstrate the benefit of our approach on an extensive simulation study as well as two publicly available fMRI datasets.

paragraphs: Brain mapping seeks to identify regions involved in responses to an external stimulus. The paper frames this as supervised learning: brain measurements predict the stimulus, and recovering the relevant predictors identifies the associated regions. In fMRI, this is difficult because acquisition time limits sample counts and the measured variables are strongly correlated.

The proposed approach clusters the original variables to construct new predictors, then fits sparse regression models using them. It combines hierarchical clustering with randomization techniques such as bootstrap sampling. These operations change the variables presented to the sparse method and improve its ability to recover the relevant support.

An extensive simulation study and experiments on two public fMRI datasets demonstrate benefits from the approach. The findings concern identifying relevant variables under small-sample, strongly correlated conditions. The contribution is therefore a way to improve sparse recovery by changing the representation through clustering and incorporating randomization, with brain mapping providing both the motivation and the application.
summary.tldr: Randomization and hierarchical clustering improve sparse recovery for brain mapping with limited samples and strongly correlated fMRI measurements.

title: Small-sample brain mapping: sparse recovery on spatially correlated designs with randomization and clustering
